units.tr: Preface to Petrus Bertius, professor at Leiden.

units.la: {H}Yperaspistes tuus, clarissime Berti, heretica Borboritarum deliramenta, blasphemos Manichæorum furores, asperiores Stoicorū sententias, horrenda crypticæ theologiæ dogmata & à Christi schola ad porticum Zenonis defectionem innocentiæ meæ, quin imò summis nostræ tempestatis theologis pronuper non sine insigni injuria, sine omni pudore & verecundia publicè, suspiciosè, accusatoriè & acerbè imputavit. Etenim, Confer nunc, ait, cum iis (nempe Borboritarum, Manichæorum & Stoicorū erroribus) ea quæ ipse docès. Agnoscis enim hæc tua. Nihil potest dici verius, quàm, Cre-
units.tr: Your Hyperaspistes, most distinguished Bertius, has publicly, suspiciously, accusingly and bitterly charged my innocence with the heretical ravings of the Borborites, the blasphemous fury of the Manichaeans, the harsher opinions of the Stoics, and the horrid dogmas of the mystical theology, with a defection from Christ's school to the Porch of Zeno. He has done this, without shame or restraint, against the most eminent theologians of our age, and not without notable injury to them. "Confer now," he says, "with those (namely, the errors of the Borborites, Manichaeans and Stoics) the things you yourself teach. For you acknowledge these as your own." Nothing can be said more truthfully than this: [the following].

units.la: den» detes ne peccatis quidem suis pos- » se separari à dilectione Dei: Pecca- » ta ipsis proficere ad salutem: Cre- » dentes, etsi peccent contra con- » scientiam, tamen obsignatos esse » in diem redemtionis: Oves Christi » non posse degenerare: Credentes » nunquam desinere credere, itaque » semper manere in Christo, ac perse- » verare usque ad finem, nec penitus » posse deficere. Alia Borboritarum & » Manichaeorum dogmata imputare tibi » adhuc non possum, tum ob concisam scripti » tui brevitatem, tum quia argumentum » tractans de perseverantia & apostasia san- » ctorum, non nisi obiter principia ista, et ut » canis è Nilo solet, degustasti, occultatis iis, » quae de reprobatione ad crypticam theolo- » giam à VESTRIS referuntur. Hoc tan- » tum suggeram, si illis assentiris, qui docet, » adulteria et homicidia esse opus Dei mo- » toris, auctoris, impulsoris; Deum eos impel- » lere ad peccandum; Necessaria esse Deo » hominum peccata; Deum peccatoribus opus » habere; Deum absolute decrevisse, ut pec- » catant; Deum facere, ut homines pec- » cent, ient; atque alia ipsius farina (neque vero potes ignorare à quibus ista dicantur, defendantur divulgentur) jam Te no Mani chaorum vesaniam æquare, sed etiam multis-partibus superare. Hem accusatione capitalem! Egone vero à te, Berti, quē christianum, quem amicum, quem fratrem æstimabam, tantorum facinorum ac tam atrocium crimina susciperem? Sane quidem non tam à gravi & moderato theologo hæc tam falsæ, tamque iniquæ ac virulentæ criminationes oblatæ videntur, quàm ab Hercule quodam furente, aut à Furiis ipsis, & Eumenidum aliqua aut furibunda Didone, quæ Savit inops animi, totamque infensa per urbem Bacchatur, qualis commotis excita sacris Thyas, ubi audito stimulant trieterica Baccho Orgia, nocturnusque vocat clamore Cithaeron.
units.tr: "Believers cannot be separated even by their sins from the love of God. Sins actually advance them to salvation. Believers, even if they sin against conscience, are nevertheless sealed for the day of redemption. The sheep of Christ cannot degenerate. Believers never cease to believe, and so always remain in Christ and persevere to the end, and cannot fail utterly." I cannot yet impute to you the other dogmas of the Borborites and Manichaeans, both because your writing is brief and because, in treating the argument concerning the perseverance and apostasy of the saints, you have only touched on these principles in passing, as a dog drinks from the Nile, and you have kept hidden what is referred to our people concerning reprobation in the mystical theology. I will only suggest this: if you agree with those who teach that adulteries and murders are the work of God as mover, author and impeller; that God impels men to sin; that men's sins are necessary to God; that God has need of sinners; that God absolutely decreed that they should sin; that God makes men sin, and other things of the same kind (and you cannot be ignorant by whom these things are said, defended and published), then you not only equal the madness of the Manichaeans but surpass it in many respects. Oh, what a capital accusation! Should I, Bertius, whom I esteemed as a Christian, a friend and a brother, accept from you charges of such great and atrocious crimes? Indeed, these false, unjust and virulent accusations seem to have been brought not so much by a grave and moderate theologian as by some raging Hercules, or by the Furies themselves, or by one of the Eumenides, or by a frenzied Dido, who "raged, lacking in mind, and through the whole city ran wild in anger, like a Thyas roused by sacred rites, when the triennial rites of Bacchus stir her, and Cithaeron calls her with nocturnal clamour."

units.la: Itaque tibi, obsecro te, quid est, mi Berti? Quis tibi morbus est in pectore, qui nec adhuc omnes Expulit astus: sed ut ingenti Vexata Noto servat longos Unda tumultus, & jam vento Cessante tumet?
units.tr: So then, I beg you, what is wrong with you, my dear Bertius? What sickness is in your breast, one that has not yet been driven out by all its fits? It is like a sea that, though the wind has dropped, still swells, keeping up the long turmoil it caught from the violent South Wind.

units.la: Cogitanti sane mihi quomodo has
units.tr: Indeed, as I considered how I might repel these accusations brought against me,

units.la: ate àte oblatas criminationes depelle-rem, varia in mentem veniunt. Mi-ror Bertium, qui me judicat ORNA-TISSIMUM, qui SUUM, qui ERA-TREM appellat, simul tamen Bor-boritam, Manichæum, Stoicum, a-postatam, Zenonis discipulum non tam barbara voce, quàm mente ciiminari & toto orbe differre po-tuisse, nedum voluisse. Contemplor mores seculi, Paulinum de eo vati-cinium recordor: Illud autem scito, fo-reut extremis diebus instent tempora mo-lesta. Erunt enim homines sui amantes, avari, gloriosi, superbi, maledici, parentibus immorigeri, ingrati, profani, charitatis expertes, nescii sederis, calumniatores, in-temperantes, immites, minime amantes bonorum, proditores, praecipites, inflati, vo-luptatum amantes potius quàm Dei: Ha-bentes formam pietatis, sed qui vim ejus abnegarint. Dubito an tu quoque, Berti, seculo conformatus in horum censum imprudens veneris. Illata à te crimina id suadent, praeter amo-ris mei, quo te olim complexus sum, fincesinceritatem & constantiam, quod dissuadeat, nihil video. Occurrit illud Ciceronis de amicitia. Ne criminibus inferendis deleCtetur amicus, aut credat oblatis. Occurrit, truces animos à misericordi natura debilitari: occurrit tandem crescere licentia spiritus. Quid facerem? Tam inconsulta, tamque iniqua de me & aliis veri patronis judicia non quidem vetare, attamen leni aliquo & moderato scripto declinare, dissuadere, iram animi tui misericordia frangere, & denique fraterna te monitione ad meliorem mentem revocare, id vero æquum & amicum duxi. Vetare nolo, quoniam hæc magnifica nimis & superba vox est imperatoris aut prætoris, quin & tibi intolerabilis. Occinis enim mihi ex Ctorū rubricis illud: Prætori extra territorium suum jus dicenti impune non paretur. Esto. Itaque nō ut prætor extra territorium meum tibi quicquam mando, sed tanquam amicus, cujus hæc jurisdictio sine territorio, vel potius in omni territorio, torio, opinor, est, ut candidè monea-at, ferio suadeat, & hortetur ad o-ptima eligenda atque capescenda, Tibi ℘ Christiana amicitia nostra aurem vellico, tequead æquanimi-tatem, ad judicii moderationem & prudetiam spiritualem humaniter invito, fraternéq; hortor, ut omnia tua studia in istud unum mecū con-feras, ne ultra quàm par est sapien-tes veritatis & charitatis divortium unquam moliamur aut meditemur.
units.tr: various thoughts came to mind. I am amazed that Bertius, who calls me "most distinguished," "his own," and "brother," could accuse me, in no barbarous word but in his mind, of being a Borborite, a Manichaean, a Stoic, an apostate, a disciple of Zeno, and could differ from the whole world, let alone want to. I look at the morals of the age and recall Paul's prophecy about it: But know this, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good, traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God; having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof. I wonder, Bertius, whether you too, conformed to this age, have unwittingly come into the number of these. The charges you have brought suggest it, and apart from the affection with which I once embraced you, and the sincerity and constancy of my friendship, I see nothing to dissuade me from thinking so. The saying of Cicero on friendship comes to mind: A friend should not delight in bringing accusations, nor believe those brought. Also comes to mind: fierce minds are weakened by a merciful nature; and finally: licence of spirit grows. What was I to do? I did not wish to forbid such rash and unjust judgments of me and of others who are true defenders of the truth, but I thought it right and friendly to turn them aside with some gentle and moderate writing, to dissuade you, to break the anger of your mind with mercy, and at last, by a brotherly admonition, to call you back to a better mind. I do not wish to forbid, since this is too grand and proud a word for an emperor or a praetor, and it would be intolerable to you too. For you chant to me from the rubrics of the Code: No one obeys with impunity a praetor who gives judgment outside his own territory. Very well. So I do not command you anything as a praetor outside my territory, but as a friend, whose jurisdiction is without territory, or rather is in every territory, I think, so that I may frankly advise you, gently persuade you, and urge you to choose and embrace what is best. For the sake of our Christian friendship I touch your ear, I kindly invite you to equanimity, to moderation of judgment and to spiritual prudence, and I earnestly urge you to devote all your zeal to this one thing with me, that we never attempt or plan a rift between truth and charity beyond what wise people allow.

units.la: Nam ut pro me, quę tu criminaris, primò & privatim tibi respondeam, quid, amabo te, est quod me pesti-lentissimum hæreticum esse voci-fereris? quòd me omnibus sacri Ro-mani imperii sub quo vivo privile-giis excidisse clamites? quòd impe-ratorum denique in Borboritas & Manichęos edicta in me cites? Hæc-cine ego tanta crimina & pœnas nulla re alia, quàm à te allegatis de perseverantia sanctorum effatis meis commeruì? Ita sane est. Nec tu qui-dem causam nunc dicis aut profers aliam. Ex hac igitur una æquus iudex me aut damnet aut absolvat. Et vero tui ipse Berti, quo es acumine, huius sive causæ sive culpæ levitate, aut, ut plenius licet minus latine cū I C. dicam, nullitatem, vel si Græce mavis ἀδίκεια facillime deprehendisses, si ea quæ tractatibus quatuor de perseverantia sanctorum disserui paulo diligentius ruminasses, non autem, ut hic proverbium a te contra me siniistre usurpatum in te aliquanto dexterius mihi retorquere liceat, obiter & ut canis e Nilo solet, degustasses. Verum enim quia arx controversiæ effatis istis cōtinetur, hic ea velle operose tueri, nimis lōgum foret. Itaque horum declarationem & firmamen libro quinto nostro de sanctorum perseverantia, quo Hyperaspistæ tui omne robur enervatur, perspicue videre poteris. Istactenus ergo accusationes tuas non horreo: sed interim ad suspiciones tuas istis nihilo meliores accedo, quibus dum aliorum me errores
units.tr: For, to answer what you charge against me, first and privately, tell me, I pray, why do you cry out that I am a most pestilent heretic? Why do you claim that I have fallen from all the privileges of the holy Roman empire under which I live? Why, finally, do you cite against me the imperial edicts against the Borborites and Manichaeans? Did I earn these great charges and penalties by nothing else than my statements on the perseverance of the saints that you have cited? That is indeed so. Nor do you now plead or bring forward any other cause. Let a fair judge therefore either condemn or acquit me on this single ground. And indeed, Bertius, with your keen wit you could very easily have detected the flimsiness, or as I may more fully but less Latinely put it with the jurists, the nullity of this cause or fault (or, if you prefer Greek, adikeia [ἀδίκεια]), if you had chewed over a little more carefully what I discussed in my four treatises on the perseverance of the saints, instead of, to turn back somewhat more adroitly upon you the proverb you have misused against me, having merely tasted it in passing, as a dog does the Nile. But since the citadel of the controversy is contained in those statements, to defend them at length here would be far too long. So you can clearly see their explanation and confirmation in our fifth book on the perseverance of the saints, by which the whole strength of your Hyperaspistes is weakened. So far, then, I am not alarmed by your accusations. But in the meantime I come to your suspicions, which are no better than those charges, by which, while you do not dare to charge me with the errors of others...

units.la: [The last line is partly illegible, ~4 letters aster "errores" at the page foot.] rum reum agere non audes, alios tamen & quidé præcipuos seculi nostri theologos nimis temere accusas. Nunquam enim, Seneca auctore, subsistit lassa crudelitas, immanium ferarum modo: qua plus quam exigit fames, mordent. Ego quidem neque huic fusspicioni crimen, nec invidiæ isti materiam dedi. Quid verò sit, quòd impia illa & nefaria enunciata theologis nostris exprobrares, diu miratus sum: attamen in disputationem tuam de revelata & occulta theologia, quam per auditorem quendam nostrum mihi huc misisti, incidens demum vidi notare te Lutherum, Zwinglium, Calvinum, Bezam, Ursinum, Zanchiū, Perkinsum, Bucanum, Piscatorem, D. Sibrandū & alios de ecclesia Dei optimè meritos viros, idque agere ut difficiliora illorum dicta etiam contra publicas abillis editas confessiones, cōtestationes, & protestationes finistre accipias, & interpretationis malignitate exasperes. Hoccine, Berti, est humahumanū factum autinceptum, ne-dum Christianum! Id mihi admo-dum improbari, dissimulare non possum. Etsi enim ex primis illis veritatis post reformationem à pa-patu factam doctoribus mihi deos non faciam, nec arbitrer, quod illi ignoraverint, scire posse neminem: aut ei, qui vel tantillū de spatio cir-culóque per eos trito deflexerit, ad-eo non præbeam aures, ut etiam ve-hementer fuccenseam: tamē ii quo-que mihi videntur admonendi, qui-bus post primos Deus aliquid patefecerit, ut ad ea in medium afferen-da magna utantur dexteritate, ne insolenter alios impetant, quasi cri-mini dantes, quod non omnia vide-rint, aut non satis cōmodē eloquuti sint, nequid maligne voluisse vel te-gere vel depravare privatis ullis ad-ductos rationibus interpretentur. Non enim decet Christianum ho-minem fusspiciosus animus, neque vero in eos ingratus, per quos Deus ecclesiæ suæ magnum aliquod con-tulit lit beneficium. Jam vero quæso te Berti, cogita quàm probe tu hæc observaveris, quando viros de universa Dei ecclesia meritissimos manichæorum vesaniam non æquare, sed multis partibus superare publicè scribere non dubitasti. Qua insuper etiam mente aut prudentia præfatos Dei servos magis nostros, quàm vestros scribas, ignorare malo, quàm suspicari. Non desunt tamen, qui id summam interpretentur imprudétiam, quę illorum doctrinam tuo calculo nō probari arguat, quæ Bellarmini, Becani, Graweri, Menzeri & aliorum hoc sæculo ecclesiæ alastorum scomata confirmet, sarcasmos exasperet, cōvicia exacuat, quæ mediocria & simpliciora ingenia perturbet, quæ denique in religiosa veritate ex ædificet neminem. Sed ego ista jam nolo, quod alioqui mihi licere poterat, tägere pressius. Interea redi, mi Berti, ad meliorem mentem: irarum enim satis est.
units.tr: ...you nonetheless rashly accuse other theologians of our age, and especially the most eminent ones. For, as Seneca says, cruelty never stops when it is weary, but like savage beasts it bites beyond what hunger demands. I, for my part, have given neither cause for this suspicion nor material for this hatred. I have long wondered why you reproach our theologians with those impious and nefarious statements. Yet when I came at last, in your disputation on revealed and hidden theology, which a certain hearer of ours sent to me here, I saw that you note Luther, Zwingli, Calvin, Beza, Ursinus, Zanchius, Perkins, Bucanus, Piscator, Sibrandus, and other men who deserved very well of the Church of God, and that you act so that you take their harder sayings in a sinister sense, even against the public confessions, testimonies and protestations published by them, and exasperate them with malignant interpretation. Bertius, is this a humane deed, or even a Christian one? I cannot dissemble that I utterly disapprove of it. For although I do not make gods of those first teachers of the truth after the reformation from the papacy, nor think that no one can know what they did not know, nor do I so refuse to listen to anyone who has strayed even slightly from the path trodden by them, that I do not even grow vehemently angry, yet it seems to me that those too must be admonished to whom God has revealed something after the first teachers, that they may use great skill in bringing such things forward, lest they assail others insolently, as if blaming them that they did not see everything or did not express themselves with sufficient clarity, and lest they interpret as malicious any silence or distortion, led by private reasons. For a suspicious mind does not befit a Christian man, nor does ingratitude toward those through whom God has bestowed some great benefit on his Church. Now, I beg you, Bertius, consider how well you have observed these things, when you did not hesitate to write publicly that men most deserving of the whole Church of God do not equal the madness of the Manichaeans but surpass it in many respects. Moreover, I would rather not know, than suspect, whether with what mind or prudence you have written about these servants of God as scribes more of ours than of yours. Yet there are some who will interpret this as the highest imprudence, which argues that their doctrine is not approved by your calculus, and which confirms the slanders of Bellarmine, Becanus, Grawer, Menzer and others of this age against the Church, sharpens sneers, sharpens insults, disturbs the mediocre and simpler minds, and in short builds up no one in religious truth. But I do not now wish to touch on these matters more closely, though I might otherwise be permitted to do so. Meanwhile, return, my dear Bertius, to a better mind, for there has been enough of anger.

units.la: pelle infamos
units.tr: Drive away the infamous ones.

units.la: Fluctus animi, redeat pietas / Virtusque viro.
units.tr: Let the tumult of your mind subside, and let piety and manly virtue return to you.

units.la: Nam ab accusatione tua, quæ virorum certe innocentium famam bacchatim discerpit, quæ Christianæ reipublicæ quietem labefactat, quæ animi incōpositi æstus est, quæ nec accusatore nec reis digna est, quæ deniq; prudentiorum judicio tanti est, quanti est fungus putidus, illa abiisse longissimè & exsulare videtur. Da igitur hoc ecclesiæ, da patriæ, da piorum votis, da tantorum virorum meritis ac sudoribus, ne Chami de more partes illorum tegendas universo orbi denudes, auctoritatem minuas, veritatis defensionem eis detrahas: sed modestè, sed piè, sed verè judices eos ex publicis ecclesiarum confessionibus, quarum illi plerunq; scriptores fuerunt. Cogita hic tutò ambulare, qui simpliciter ambulat: & crede jurātibus, quibus etiam injuratis credere oportebat. Nemo illorum Borborita est, nemo Manichæus, Stoicus. eus nemo. Neverò tu idem contra conscientiam tuam de iis sentire te debere quiriteris, age copendiario disputationis tuæ examine per Dei gratiam sum effecturus, ut nec præfatos theologos nec me ppositum habere aliud, quàm veritati in NA-TURA & SCRIPTURA divinitus revelatæ patrocinari, clarissime intelligas. Pone itaque præjudicium, pone affectus, pone animo præceptas opiniones, quæ nocent judicio, & ex re judica. Faxit Deus ter Opt. Max., ut sincero ac constanti veritatis, pietatis & mutuæ charitatis studio ardeamus omnes, & tandem in Christo Jesu salutem consequamur, Amen.
units.tr: For your accusation, which tears the reputation of innocent men to pieces in a frenzy, which shakes the peace of the Christian commonwealth, which is the agitation of an unsettled mind, which is worthy neither of an accuser nor of the accused, and which, in the judgment of wiser people, is worth no more than a rotten mushroom, seems to have gone far away and to be in exile. Grant therefore this to the Church, grant it to the fatherland, grant it to the prayers of the godly, grant it to the merits and labours of such great men: do not, like Ham, expose to the whole world the parts that ought to be covered, diminish their authority, and take away from them the defence of the truth. Rather, judge them moderately, piously, and truthfully, from the public confessions of the churches, of which they were for the most part the writers. Consider that he walks safely who walks simply, and believe those who swear oaths, whom one ought to have believed even when they were not sworn. None of them is a Borborite, none a Manichaean, none a Stoic. Yet you complain that you ought not to think of them in this way against your own conscience. Go on, and by God's grace I shall bring it about, by a brief examination of your disputation, that you clearly understand that neither the aforementioned theologians nor I have any purpose other than to defend the truth divinely revealed in NATURE and in SCRIPTURE. Put aside, therefore, prejudgment, put aside emotions, put aside opinions prescribed to the mind, which harm judgment, and judge from the matter itself. May God, the best and greatest, grant that we all burn with a sincere and steadfast zeal for truth, piety, and mutual love, and at last obtain salvation in Christ Jesus. Amen.

units.la: INDEX CAPITUM.
units.tr: INDEX OF CHAPTERS.

units.la: I. Num aliunde potius regula humanarum actionum petenda sit, quam ex lege & euangelio?
units.tr: I. Whether the rule of human actions is to be sought from anywhere else rather than from the law and the gospel?

units.la: II. An in Deo sint dua & quidem contraria voluntates?
units.tr: II. Whether there are in God two wills, and indeed contrary ones?

units.la: III. An dua ista voluntates conciliari possint?
units.tr: III. Whether these two wills can be reconciled?

units.la: IV. An Deus velit peccata & ipsa per se decreverit?
units.tr: IV. Whether God wills sins and has decreed them in themselves?

units.la: V. An Deus efficaciter ordinarit, decreverit & voluerit, ut Adam laberetur?
units.tr: V. Whether God efficaciously ordained, decreed and willed that Adam should fall?

units.la: VI. An omnia absoluta necessitate germantur?
units.tr: VI. Whether all things come about by absolute necessity?

units.la: VII. Quodnam sit primum Dei decretum?
units.tr: VII. What is the first decree of God?

units.la: VIII. Quaenam sit forma decretorum Dei?
units.tr: VIII. What is the form of the decrees of God?

units.la: IX. An credentes postquam semel verae fide donati sunt, possint peccatis suis gratia Dei & sua salute excidere?
units.tr: IX. Whether believers, once they have been endowed with true faith, can fall away from the grace of God and their salvation through their sins?

units.la: X. Annon Bertius quemadmodum theologi, quorum sententiam arrodit, duplicem Dei voluntatem asserat?
units.tr: X. Does not Bertius, like the theologians whose opinion he undermines, assert a twofold will of God?

units.la: CAP. I. Num aliunde potius regula humanarum actionum petenda sit quàm ex lege & euangelio?
units.tr: CHAPTER I. Should the rule of human actions be sought from anywhere other than the law and the gospel?

units.la: Rimariam actionum humanarum regulam esse legem & euangelium sine mora intelligit, qui viam salutis ex sacris divini verbi monumentis religiosè inquirere instituit: imò, sidè religiosis & salutaribus sermo sit, solam. Ita testatur divinus apostolus: Tota scriptura diuinitus est inspirata & utilis ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem quae est in iustitia: ut perfectus sit homo Dei ad omne opus bonum perfectè instructus. Ita & Salvator noster: Habent Mosen & prophetas: audiant eos. Et post pauxillum: Si Mosen & prophetas non audiunt, neque si quidem quispiam ex mortuis excitetur, assentientur. Ad solam scripturam ille discipulos suos amandavit:
units.tr: Whoever sets out to seek the way of salvation religiously from the sacred records of God's Word understands at once that the law and the gospel are the sole rule for searching out human actions. Indeed, if the word is to be religious and salutary for the faithful, it is the only one. The divine apostle bears witness to this: All Scripture is inspired by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly equipped for every good work. Our Saviour likewise says: They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them. And a little later: If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded though one rise from the dead. It was to Scripture alone that he sent his disciples:

units.la: Hi sunt sermones quos locutus sum vobis, quū adhuc essem vobiscum, oportere impleri omnia, quae scripta sunt in lege Mosis & prophetis & psalmis de me. Tunc aperuit eorum mentem, ut intelligerent scripturas. Rursus suo id exemplo docet Paulus; In nobis discatis, supra id quod scriptum est non sapere. Et ab aliis doctrinis avocat Colosienses: Videte ne quis vos depraedetur per philosophiam & inanem deceptionem, secundum traditionem hominum. Nihil scripturis addi aut detrahi vult Salomon: Ne addas verbis ejus, ne te redarguat, & mendax convincaris. Sermo Dei est ignitus, est clypeus sperantibus in se. Idem orthodoxi patres senserunt. Basilius in regulis brevioribus, regula 95. Quae ad usum pertinentia sunt, ea ut unusquisque ex divinis literis edificat & rectum & necessarium est, tum ad majorem expletionem animi in pietate, tum etiam ut ne humanis constitutionibus assuefiat. Ambrosius lib. 1. de poenit. cap. 4. Deus non alienis assertionibus sed suis aestimandus est vocibus. Tertullianus adversus Hermogenem, Non recipio quod extra scripturas de tuo infers. Epiphanius in haeresi 55. Divina scriptura omnia cum bono ordine muniens, veritatem per omnia firmavit. Et in Panario: Ex non scriptis legentes, ex arena funiculos nectunt. Quid opus est pluribus in tanta luce veritatis? An adhuc existimare potes, quotquot viam salutis ex sacris divini verbi monumentis religiose inquirere instituunt, quomodo scripsisti perplexari?
units.tr: These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you, that all things must be fulfilled which are written in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms concerning me. Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures. Paul likewise teaches this by his own example: In us you may learn not to think beyond what is written. And he calls the Colossians away from other teachings: See that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men. Solomon wills that nothing be added to or taken away from Scripture: Do not add to his words, lest he reprove you and you be found a liar. The word of God is refined, a shield to those who trust in him. The orthodox Fathers held the same view. Basil, in the Shorter Rules, rule 95: What is useful for life, each person should build from the divine letters; this is both right and necessary, both for the fuller perfecting of the soul in godliness and so that we may not become accustomed to human constitutions. Ambrose, On Repentance, book 1, chapter 4: God is to be valued not by foreign assertions but by his own voice. Tertullian, against Hermogenes: I do not accept what you bring in from your own mind beyond the Scriptures. Epiphanius, in heresy 55: Divine Scripture, fortifying all things in good order, has confirmed the truth in every respect. And in the Panarion: Those who read what is not written weave ropes out of sand. What need is there of more in such a light of truth? Or can you still think that all who undertake to seek the way of salvation religiously from the sacred records of God's Word are perplexed in the way you have written?

units.la: Quaenā, te obsecro, esse potest illis religio, qui in scripturis religiosè versantes, aliunde potiùs quàm ex illis actionum suarum regulam expetunt? Irreligiosa quidem ingenia fanaticorum, enthusiastarum, ponti-ficiorum, non religiosa christianorum pe-ctora id moliuntur. Et quorsum illud tuum Potius? Religiosis verbo Dei nihil est potius, nihil prius, nihil antiquius, necesse debet. Cur etiam indefinitè scribis, humanarum actionum regulam? Humanae enim dicuntur actiones non modo quae religiosae, sed & omnes quae liberae, & in potestate ejus sunt, qui vult agere. Illarum sola scriptura est norma, fideliis loquaris, quibus eam legere aut audire contingit, alioquin secus se res habet, si ad totum genus humanum indefinita oratione id referas. Harum etiam aliae sunt regulae. Cur etiam de lege dicis, quae varias admittit significationes? An solam scriptam legem intelligis? Si hanc solam, utique lex naturae, quae non scripta est, sed innata, non etit ex regulis actionum humanarum exterminanda. Ita Paulus: Nam quum gentes, quae legem non habent, naturaliter quae legis sunt, faciunt, ipsi legem non habentes, sibi ipsis sunt lex: ut qui ostendant opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis, una testimonium reddente ipsorum conscientia, & cogitationibus sese mutuo accusantibus.
units.tr: Tell me, I beg you, what religion can those have who, while occupied religiously with the Scriptures, seek the rule of their actions from anywhere rather than from them? It is the irreligious minds of fanatics, enthusiasts and Papists that attempt this, not the religious hearts of Christians. And what is the meaning of your word "rather"? For the religious, nothing is preferable to the Word of God, nothing comes before it, nothing is older. Why also do you write indefinitely the rule of human actions? For actions are called human not only when they are religious but also when they are free and within the power of the one who wishes to act. Scripture alone is the norm of these, you would speak faithfully, to those who have the opportunity to read or hear it; otherwise the matter stands differently if you refer this to the whole human race in indefinite terms. Some other rules also apply to these. Why also do you speak of the law, a word that admits of various meanings? Do you mean only the written law? If you mean only that, then surely the law of nature, which is not written but innate, will not be cast out of the rules of human actions. So Paul: For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves; they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness with them, and their thoughts accusing or else excusing one another.

units.la: Rom. 2. v. 14. 15. accusantibus & excusantibus. Duo autem sunt gravissimi lapsus tui in hoc argumento, de quibus es monendus. Prior est, quòd illiberali plane artificio ethnicos, Plautinum Lyconidem, Euripideam Dianam, Homericum Agamemnonem, Libertinorum pessimum Quintinum cum non paucis eruditionis & pietatis fama claris viris in errore conferruminas. Quàm enim alieni sint ab illis clarissimi viri ac inter eos nominatim Calvinus theologorum gravissimus tum cætera illius monumenta, tum instructio adversus Libertinos luculenter declarant. Quis verò orthodoxorum dicere sustinet? Ita & se & actiones suas actionumque omnium principia, causas, ac ἀρχάς arcana illa ac potenti voluntate Dei regi, ut quacunque dicunt, faciunt, cogitant, etiam MALA ex illo fonte fluant: atque in hac voluntate ipsi contra omnem rationem, & contra manifestum Dei verbum acquiescant: imò vero hac ipsa doctrina perstringant oculos imperitiorum, inq; dubiis, & explicatu difficilibus quæstionibus, ad hanc unam recurrant.&c. Tuam fidem, mi Berti. Quibus in locis & à quibus ista scribuntur? Ab ethnicis, fateor, & Libertinis, à nostris theologis nusquam. Absterge igitur quam illis ignominiam aspersisti: non enim sic veritas manifestatur, non Deo justitiæ & misericordiæ laus asse-ritur. eritur. Posterior est, quòd tu ipse aliunde potius quàm ex lege & euangelio actionum humanarum regulam petis. Quid enim? Fidem procul dubio in humanis actionibus numeras. Ejus vero triplicem enumeras regulam, dum ita scribis: Et sunt qui contra rationem & naturam Dei ipsamque apertam scripturam folicitentur credere. Ecce hic duas alias regulas quàm legem & euangelium, nempe rationem & naturam Dei. Hoc ex Castellionis haustum' lacunis patet puteque. Clarius admonitio tua ad Christianum lectorem, quàm apologetico tuo praestruxisti, eundem errorem errat, quando de judicio humano disserit, Judicium humanum haud dubiè est actio humana. Ejus vero canone & regulam statuis aliam quàm legem & euangelium. Verba tua agnoscis: Eam (canonem) fere post rationem naturalem, & veritatem divinitus tibi insculpitam, logicam apodixin, quàm si ad ea quae in scripturis legis, quae in creaturis conspicis, quae in temetipsa sentis, plaeide & cum religione adhibeas, fieri non potest ut à vero aberres. Ita plures actionum humanarum regulas, quàm legem & euangelium, architectaris ipse. Mèlius Calvinus contra Libertinos c.15. Quod attinet ad opera quae nos facimus, consideranda à nobis vo-luntatem Dei, qualiter eam ipse declaret, ut, exempli emplì gratia, quum iubetissimum cuique seruari: ne cui damnum aut iniuria inferatur: ibi vo-luntas ejus perspicua est. Quid igitur rei placeat amplius disquirinon oportet. Scimus enim nos, si id facimus, ejus voluntati obsequuturos: sin minus et minime gratos fore. Ecce tibi hic regulam actionum humanarum Dei verbum nobis revelatum. In hoc sine tergiuersatione & calumnia acquiescamus.
units.tr: Rom. 2:14, 15. Now there are two very serious slips in your treatment of this subject, and you must be warned about them. The first is that, by a quite ungenerous trick, you join the pagans, the Plautine Lyconides, the Euripidean Diana, the Homeric Agamemnon, and Quintin, the worst of the Libertines, in error with not a few men famous for learning and piety. For how remote from these views are those most distinguished men, and among them Calvin, the most weighty of theologians, as his other writings and especially his instruction against the Libertines clearly show! And who of the orthodox would dare to say such things? Thus both themselves and their actions, and the principles [ἀρχάς], causes and secret origins of all their actions, are governed by the hidden and powerful will of God, so that whatever they say, do or think, even evil things, flow from that source; and in this will they acquiesce against all reason and against the plain word of God; indeed, by this very doctrine they dazzle the eyes of the unskilled, and in doubtful and difficult questions they have recourse to this one thing alone, etc. Your good faith, my dear Bertius! In what places, and by whom, are these things written? By pagans, I grant, and Libertines, but nowhere by our theologians. Wipe away, then, the disgrace you have cast upon them; for the truth is not thus made manifest, nor is praise of God's justice and mercy thereby asserted. The second slip is that you yourself seek the rule of human actions from somewhere other than the law and the gospel. For what do you do? Without doubt you count faith among human actions. Yet you list for it a threefold rule, when you write: And there are those who, against reason and the nature of God and the plain Scripture itself, are inclined to believe. Here you name two rules other than the law and the gospel, namely reason and the nature of God. This is plainly drawn from the pools and wells of Castellio. Your admonition to the Christian reader, which you set out in your apologetic, is more clearly in error on the same point, when it treats of human judgment: human judgment is undoubtedly a human action, and yet you lay down for its canon a rule other than the law and the gospel. Acknowledge your own words: This canon is, after natural reason and the truth divinely engraved in you, a logical demonstration, which, if you apply calmly and religiously to what you see in the Scriptures of the law, in creatures, and in yourself, it cannot happen that you go astray from the truth. Thus you yourself construct more rules of human actions than the law and the gospel. Calvin, against the Libertines, chapter 15, does better: As regards the works which we perform, we must consider the will of God, as he himself declares it; for example, when he commands that each one be kept safe, that no one be harmed or wronged; there his will is plain. Therefore it is not necessary to inquire further what pleases him. For we know that if we do this we shall obey his will, and if not, he will not be pleased at all. Here, then, you have the rule of human actions: the Word of God revealed to us. Let us rest in this, without evasion or calumny.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: In Deo non sunt duae contrariae voluntates.
units.tr: In God there are not two contrary wills.

units.la: ET si voluntas Dei, si ipsam voiendi facultatem, ejusq; simplicem actum, simplexque objectum in ipso Deo, & constantem de re quavis extra Deum existente sententiam spectemus, una sit & simplex; tamen pro vario agendi modo rebus ipsis diuersissimis sapienter accommodato, ipsa quoque volendi actio, quam seu volitionem appellant, varie distingui potest & soleat. Quemadmodum enim Dei sapientia, licet in se sit simplex, tamen ab apostolo πολυποίκιλος, id est, multiformis appellatur. Ephef. 3. 10. ita & voluntas ipsius varie dicitur. Est enim ea interua aucex-terna. terna. 2* præcipiens aut efficiens, 3* per- ficiens aut permittens. 4* revelata aut oc- culta, five signi aut beneplaciti, r. absoluta aut conditionalis. 6* efficax autinefficax.7* antecedens aut consequens. 8* ordinaria aut extraordinaria. Internam dicimus, qua Deus seipsum, & quæ sibi simpliciter natu- ralia sunt intelligenter appetit: externam vero, qua omnia quod non est Deus, natu- ræ suæ convenienter vult. Illa est prorsus necessaria: hæc libera, & omnis contingen- tiæ in rerum universitate radix. Præcipue- tem dicimus, quæ jus morale præscribit, & per se nihil foris in nobis physicè agit, fedtâ- tùm quid a nobis fieri velit tum apud fe de- cernit, tum signo aliquo declarat. Efficien- tem, five agentem cum Junio de peccato primo Adami q. 2. c, 3. ex Augustino & aliis non contemnendis theologis (quanquam fateamur hanc appellationem non satis esse commodam, quam nobis idonei vocabuli, quo oppositam speciem voluntatis præcipi- entis satis exprimam) defectus peperit) cō- sideramus vel ut perficientem, quæ quod in- tusapud fe constituit, foris efficit, fi sui ope- ris sit: aut ad finem bonum etiam ordinat, quod sui operis non est: vel ut permittentem, quæ intus statuit foris operari hoc est, sinere viam creaturæ suæ in manu ipsius & actione pecpeccantis non impedire. Revelatam dicimus voluptatem, quatenus nobis in verbo vel in eventu est manifestata: occultam, quatenus ea nobis est abscondita, liberrimaeque Dei potestati relinquitur, dum vel ex oraculo vel ex eventu innotescat. Eodem sensu dicimus voluntatem Dei esse signi, nempe quia signo aliquo nobis innotescit, vel beneplaciti, qua Deus in rem aliquam sibi inclinat. Absolutam voluntatem Dei nuncupamus, qua ipse absolute, sine respectu ad inferiores causas quaedam vult facere, aut a nobis vult fieri. Conditionalem, qua Deus quaedam vult facere certa conditione interveniente, aut a nobis quaedam vult fieri, ita ut aliter eadem fieri possint. vide Zanch. lib. 3. de nat. Dei c. 4. q. 3. p. 310. Efficacem appellamus, quae effectum suum in creaturis consequitur: inefficacem, quae quoniam ex certa conditione pendet, effectum suum non sortitur, eo quod conditio deficiat. Antecedentem Dei voluntatem vocamus, qua sine omni circumstantiarum respectu ex ordine bonitatis & sapientiae suae creaturis suis bene vult. Consequentem, qua ratione circumstantiarum aliis quidem per se vult salutem, aliis vero per accidens condemnationem. Ordinariam dicimus, qua Deus ordinem naturae & gratiae semel sancitum perpetuo
units.tr: Even if we consider the will of God (the faculty of willing itself, its simple act, its simple object in God himself, and his constant judgement about anything existing outside God) as one and simple, nevertheless the act of willing itself, which they call volition, can be and commonly is distinguished in various ways, according to the varied manner of acting that is wisely suited to very diverse things. For just as the wisdom of God, though simple in itself, is called by the apostle *polypoikilos* [πολυποίκιλος], that is, multiform (Ephes. 3. 10), so his will is also said to be varied. For it is: (1) internal or external; (2) preceptive or efficient; (3) perfective or permissive; (4) revealed or hidden, that is, of sign or of good pleasure; (5) absolute or conditional; (6) efficacious or inefficacious; (7) antecedent or consequent; (8) ordinary or extraordinary. We call it internal by which God freely desires himself and what is simply natural to himself, and external by which he wills everything that is not God, in agreement with its nature. The former is wholly necessary; the latter is free, and is the root of all contingency in the universe. We call it preceptive which prescribes what is morally right, and which does not of itself physically work anything outside us, but only decides within itself what it wills us to do, and declares it by some sign. We consider it efficient, or agent (with Junius, on the sin of the first Adam, q. 2, c. 3, following Augustine and other theologians not to be despised, although we admit this name is not very suitable, since we lack a fitting word by which to express adequately the opposed kind of preceptive will), as perfective, when it effects outwardly what it has determined inwardly within itself, if the work is its own; or when it also orders to a good end what is not its own work. Or we consider it as permissive, which determines within and acts outwardly, that is, allows the course of its creature to proceed in its own hand and does not hinder the action of the sinner. We call the will revealed insofar as it is made manifest to us in the word or in the event; hidden insofar as it is concealed from us and left to the most free power of God, until it becomes known either from an oracle or from an event. In the same sense we say the will of God is of sign, namely because it becomes known to us by some sign, or of good pleasure, by which God inclines himself to some matter. We call the will of God absolute by which he wills to do certain things, or wills that they be done by us, absolutely, without respect to inferior causes. Conditional is that by which God wills to do certain things when a certain condition intervenes, or wills certain things to be done by us, in such a way that they could be otherwise. See Zanchius, book 3 on the nature of God, c. 4, q. 3, p. 310. We call it efficacious which attains its effect in creatures; inefficacious, which, since it depends on a certain condition, does not obtain its effect because the condition fails. We call the will of God antecedent by which, without any respect to circumstances, he wills well to his creatures out of the order of his goodness and wisdom. Consequent is that by which, in view of circumstances, he wills salvation to some through themselves, but condemnation to others by accident. We call it ordinary by which God constantly preserves the order of nature and grace once established;

units.la: petuò seruat: extraordinariam, qua ab ordine illo, quoties ita collibitum est, aliquatenus recedit. Quinquam verò hæc distinſte devoluntate Dei tradamus, tamen diligenter cautum volumus, ne quis propterea in deo duas verè contrarias voluntates ejusſ dem rei respectu statuat. Quicquid enim Deus in verbo suo præcipit aut interdicit, promittit aut minatur aut alia quavis ratione velle se testatur, id verè & sciò ipsum velle ex animo credimus ac docemus. Hincemergit meram calumniam esse, nos docere quod Deus voluntate revelata nolit & arcana velit peccata: neque nos attingere, quæ thesi 8. scribis: Docent ergo, inquiens, arcanam quandam esse in Deo voluntatem, quæ etsi interdum cum ea quæ verbo externo revelata est, conveniat, tamen sæpenumero ab ea differt multa ut velit Deus secundum illam, quæ verbo externo vetat: multa ut nolit, quæ tamen verbo mandat atque imperat. Multa promittat, quæ non statuerit præstare; minetur, quæ nunquam facere decreverit. Non mirum si hæc nobis non salivam, sed stomachum movear. Sunt enim crudæ ac prope dixerim crudelia. Quis, amabo te, ita insaniat, ut de optimo Deo nostro, qui veritas & justitia est ipsissima, tam profana cogitare audeat? Ergo Deus singulare aliquod judicium exercitu-
units.tr: ...preserves constantly: extraordinary, by which he somewhat departs from that order whenever it pleases him. Although we set out these distinctions about the will of God clearly, we want it carefully guarded that no one therefore posits in God two truly contrary wills concerning the same thing. For whatever God commands or forbids in his word, promises or threatens, or declares by any other means that he wills, we believe and teach from the heart that he truly and knowingly wills. Hence it follows that it is pure calumny to say that we teach that God by his revealed will does not will something while by a hidden will he wills sins. Nor do they touch what you write in thesis 8: Docent ergo, you say, "they teach that there is a certain hidden will in God, which, although it sometimes agrees with that which is revealed in the external word, yet very often differs from it: that God wills many things according to that hidden will which the external word forbids; that he does not will many things which yet he commands and enjoins by the word. He promises many things which he has not decided to perform; he threatens what he has never decided to do." It is no wonder if these things stir in us not spit but nausea. For they are crude, and I might almost say cruel. Who, I beg you, is so mad as to dare to think such profane things of our best God, who is truth and justice itself? Therefore God, exercising some singular judgment,

units.la: tus rus soleat quaedam praecipere, quae vel non statim vel non ita absolute, ut verba praesferunt, fieri vult: tamen minime omnium Deo opt. max. tribuenda est de re eadem prorsus contraria voluntas. Quod si apud theologos tale quippiam de voluntate Dei occurrere videatur, id ex allegatis divinae voluntatis distinctionibus facillime conciliabitur: Imprimis si diligenter notemus voluntatis divinae conditiones in scripturis aliis exprimi, aliàs suppriml, quae ubi rerum eventus cernuntur, demum sepe innotescant. Noli igitur horridioribus doctorum phrasibus inhaerere, sed ad publicas ecclesiarum confessiones animi oculos convertere, quae si quid forte disputationis calor incommodi dictum imprudentibus extorsit, ex verbo Dei ad commodum sensum perducunt; pretium quum noris hos ipsos illarum auctores esse, atque ab hominibus perturbatis ad sedatos provocare non modo licere, sed & decere. Quorsum vero istud caffers, Berti? Faciunt igitur duplicem theologiam unam occultam, alteram revelatam, atque illam quidem vocant, hanc ... sive verbo declaratam: non quod haec ex illa expressa sit tanquam signum ex suo prototypo, eoque cum ipsa semper consentiat; sed quod putent plerunque haec diversi esse generis. Unde consequens est, vera
units.tr: Therefore God is accustomed to enjoin certain things that he does not wish to be done immediately, or not so absolutely as the words express. Yet a contrary will concerning the same matter is by no means to be attributed to God, most good and great. But if something of this sort seems to occur among theologians concerning the will of God, it will very easily be reconciled by the distinctions of the divine will mentioned above. Chiefly, if we carefully note that the conditions of the divine will are expressed in some Scriptures and suppressed in others, and these conditions are often at last made known when the outcome of events is seen. Do not therefore cling to the rougher phrases of the teachers, but turn the eyes of your mind to the public confessions of the Churches. If the heat of disputation has perhaps wrung some incorrect statement from the imprudent, these confessions bring it back to a sound sense from the Word of God. Since you know these very men are the authors of those confessions, it is not only lawful but also fitting to call the agitated back to the calm. But to what end is this quibbling, Berti? They therefore make a twofold theology, one hidden and the other revealed, and they call the former ... and the latter ... declared by the Word. Not that the latter is expressed from the former as a sign from its prototype, and therefore always agrees with it, but because they think these are for the most part of different kinds. Whence it follows that true

units.la: multa esse in theologia revelata, quae in occulta falsa sint: multa falsa in illa, quae vera sint in ista. Quis theologorum hujus distinctionis tanquam est abusor, quantus tu existis accusator, prope scripsisse calumniator? Ut ista quidem distinctio, at nusquam ab orthodoxis tam fide atque tu fingis, quod sciam, detorta legitur. Enoftris, qui schola-ticam theologiam felicissime tractavit. F. Junius ea utitur libro suo de theologia cap. 3. Archetypam is theologiam definit divinarum rerum divinam sapientiam. Et hanc, inquit, nos adoramus, ac non investigamus, cap. 4.
units.tr: many things are in revealed theology that are false in the hidden, and many things are false in that which are true in this. Which of the theologians is an abuser of this distinction, and how great an accuser, or almost a calumniator in writing, are you? As for this distinction itself, nowhere among the orthodox, as far as I know, is it read twisted in the way you pretend. Among our own, F. Junius, who handled scholastic theology most happily, uses it in his book on theology, chap. 3. He defines archetypal theology as the divine wisdom of divine things. And this, he says, we adore and do not investigate, chap. 4.

units.la: Theologiae vero, quam vocat, latissimum uberrimumque campum, quam brevissime fieri potest, circumdatis certis decurrit & sic commode definit: Theologia ... five simpliciter (ut vocat) five secundum quid considerata, est sapientia divinarum rerum a Deo ex archetypo ipsius in-formata per communicationem gratiae ad gloriam ipsius. cap. 5. Hujus vestigia sequuntur Polanus, Trelcatius, alii, ille vero patru & magni istius Germaniae nostrae luminis, Philippi Melanchthonis, qui in definitione legis id pulcherrime ostendit, dum docet quam rationem illa habeat in mente divina, secundum quam omnes divinae leges cocipiuntur & nobis promulgantur. Quid vero clarius dici poterat ad diluendam ob-jectæ calumniæ iabem? Junius sane, à quo alii non dissentiunt, theologiam ἐκ(Greek) sive revelatam ex θεοῦ(Greek) tanquam signū ex suo prototypo, tanquam rivulum ex fonte derivat liberalissime. At quoniam à lectoribus hujus rei fidem postulas, age produc in medium ipsorum auctorum tabulas ut fidei tuæ testes; aliter enim nemo quod dicis credit. Opponemus, inquis, quoque prophylactici loco divina oracula, ut ita appareat quantum theologia in verbo revelata ab humanis commentis differt. Sed quorsum oppones prophylactica ista? Cur illa nobis opponeres, qui commenta hominum damnamus, qui theologiam in verbo revelatam colimus, à quibus contagium non sit metuendum, quippe qui ab ista peste fumus liberi, sani, integri? Nulla igitur tibi opus est theriaca, nulla urina, lixivio nullo, & si quid aliud suadent medici in pestis prophylacticis. Ne nos infectos suspiceris, Berti, quum pestis venenum permaneat in personis per bimestre, nos ne intra annum quidem, forte & quinquennium totum homines illa correptos vidisse scias. Sed tamen quæ prophylactica ex Dei verbo depromis, ea omnia recipimus. Sunt enim causæ nostræ totidem contra malam doctrinā amuleta.
units.tr: Of theology, which he calls ... he runs through the broad and fruitful field, marking its boundaries as briefly as possible, and defines it thus aptly: Theology ... whether considered simply (as he calls it) or in some respect, is the wisdom of divine things, informed by God from his archetype through the communication of grace to his glory. Chap. 5. Polanus, Trelcatius and others follow his footsteps, and so does that great man and light of our Germany, Philip Melanchthon, who shows this most beautifully in his definition of law, while teaching what relation it has in the divine mind, according to which all divine laws are conceived and promulgated to us. What could be said more clearly to wash away the stain of the objected calumny? Junius, whom others do not dissent from, derives theology, which is from God [ἐκ θεοῦ] or revealed, as a stream from its spring, most freely. But since you demand from your readers faith in this matter, come, produce before us the tablets of the authors themselves as witnesses of your claim; for otherwise no one believes what you say. We will oppose, you say, also as a prophylactic, the divine oracles, so that it may appear how far theology revealed in the Word differs from human inventions. But why would you oppose those prophylactics? Why would you oppose them to us, who condemn the inventions of men and cultivate theology revealed in the Word, from whom no contagion is to be feared, since we are free, sound and whole from that plague? So you have no need of theriac, no urine, no lye, and whatever else physicians advise as prophylactics against plague. Do not suspect us of being infected, Berti. The poison of plague remains in persons for two months, and you know that we have not seen people seized by it within a year, perhaps not even in five whole years. Nevertheless, whatever prophylactics you draw from the Word of God, we accept them all, for our arguments are so many amulets against bad doctrine.

units.la: Quæ verò illa? Num. 23, 19. Deus fortis non est qui mentiatur, aut filius hominis quem pœniteat. {a}Ipse dixerit & non faciet, {a}An locutus fuerit & non præstabit illud? Bene! Moses negat Deum mentiri posse aut pœnitudine duci in statu hominis in eius pœnitentia cum naturali imperfectione, moralis vitiositas sæpe concurrit. Idem & nos ex animo negamus, quia mendacium omne pugnat cum perfectissima Dei natura & veracitate: pœnitentiæ verò imperfectiones sunt contrariæ exquisitissimæ ipsius sapientiæ atque omnipotentiæ. An Piscator hoc affirmat? Ita tu affirmas: Deus interdum verbo significat id, absque mendacio & hypocrisi pro summa sua agendi libertate, sed vel le, quod revera non vult, aut nolle quod revera vult. Pisc. adversus Schmiff. thes. 45. pag. 88. Piscator, qua est pietate Mosi contradictoresse noluit, dum ait Deum sine mendacio & hypocrisi verbo significare se velle quod revera non vult: id circo si quid durum in illius phrasi est, id malleo & igne verbi, quod ille pari nobis cum affectu revereatur & amplectitur, sapienter est emolliendum. Ergo igitur sensus verborum. Sæpe Deum aliquid præcipere in verbo, quod tamen aliter evenire posse non modo sciat, sed & velit permittere, ut aliter eveniat. Omnia
units.tr: But what are those things? Num. 23, 19: "God is not a man that he should lie, nor the son of man that he should repent. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not make it good?" Well said! Moses denies that God can lie, or be moved to repentance as a man is, in whom repentance comes with natural imperfection, and often moral vitiosity as well. We too deny this from our hearts, because every lie is utterly opposed to the most perfect nature and truthfulness of God, while the imperfections of repentance are the exact contraries of his wisdom and omnipotence. Does Piscator affirm this? You affirm the opposite: that God sometimes signifies in his Word, without lying or hypocrisy, and by his supreme freedom of action, that he wills what in truth he does not will, or is unwilling what in truth he wills. Piscator, Against Schmiff, thesis 45, p. 88. Piscator, with what piety I do not know, was unwilling to contradict Moses when he says that God by his Word signifies, without lying or hypocrisy, that he wills what in truth he does not will. Therefore, if anything in that phrasing is harsh, it must be wisely softened with the hammer and fire of the Word, which Piscator reveres and embraces with the same feeling as we do. So then, the sense of the words is this: God often commands something in his Word, which nonetheless he not only knows may come about otherwise, but also wills to permit, so that it does come about otherwise. All

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Omnia quidem Dei praecepta sunt seria & vera: at quis ea nos Deo prorsus invito ac transgressionem non permittente aut impedire non valente transgredi dixerit? Ita igitur Deus sine mendacio & hypocrisi in verbo suo significat se velle, quod tamen aliter evenire posse, nonnunquam etiam evenire sciat & quo dictum est modo ut eveniret permittere velit: velit, in quam, non voluntate approbante ac jubente, sed permittente, quae jubenti non est contraria. Ita etiam deveneranda sunt nobis d'icta Deut. 32. v. 4. Rupis illius opus perfectum: omnes enim viae illius sunt jus. Deus fortis fidelis, & expers iniquitatis, justus & rectus est. Psal. 11. vel potius 11. vers. 3. & 4. si illa verba in psalmorum numeratione, quam a te allegatam video: Vana loquuntur sunt unusquisque ad proximum suum labia dolosa, in corde & corde loquuntur. Disperdat Dominus universa labia dolosa. Jof. 24. v. 14. Servite Jehovae perfecte & vere. 1. Reg. 2. 4. Ambula coram me in omni veritate, in omni corde tuo & in omni anima tua: velut melior habet versio: Si observaveris filii tui viam suam, ambulando coram me in fide: ex toto corde suo & ex toto animo suo &c. Haec & similia, quibus veritatis studium Deus commendat, cujus modi & sunt Sir.2.v.14. Jac.4. 8. Jer.9. 8.psal. 28.v.3. 2.Tim.2. v.13. Job 10.35. quis in dubium vocat? An Zanchius? At ille lib. 3.de nat.Dei.c.4.pag.368. iis ipsis verbis, quae citas significat voluntatem Dei totam non semper verbo significari, sed ex parte reticeri & occultari, donec ex eventu cognoscatur. Quid autem hac doctrina est planius? quid verius? An vero Beza hic est reus? Is in colloq.Momp.p.174, Deus, ait, saepe non vult facere, quod factum sed dixit? An ideo Deus argutitur mendacii? Minime. Deus enim saepe sub conditione aliquid se facturum dicit, quod absolute dictum videtur. Unde & explicandum est quod hic Beza docet. Res liquida est ex historia Jonae. Iterum ne ad partes vocatur Zanchius? Nempe quia de natura Dei lib.3.c.4.q.3.pa. 310. Non semper, ait, vult Deus quod mandat & promittit. Hic tu corrumpis & mutilas verba meremq; Zanchii, uti ex integre ascriptis constabit. Altera dicitur voluntas signi: quod scilicet praecepta & promissiones cum conditione praeceptorum servandorum signa sint Deum sic velle: quanquam NON SEMPER, ET IN OMNIBUS SIMPLICITER vult quod mandat, aut promittit: ut in Abrahamo primum, deinde in Pharaone liquido apparet. Illi enim mandat ut filium
units.tr: All of God's precepts are serious and true. But who would say that we transgress them while God is utterly unwilling, or while he is unable to prevent the transgression? So God, without lying or pretence, signifies in his word that he wills something which can nevertheless turn out otherwise, and which he knows sometimes does turn out otherwise, and which he is willing to permit to happen in the way it is said to happen. He wills it by permitting, not by approving and commanding, and this permission is not contrary to his command. Thus we must also receive reverently the words of Deut. 32.4: The work of that Rock is perfect, for all his ways are judgment. God is faithful and without iniquity, just and right. Ps. 11, or rather Ps. 11.3 and 4, if those words are in the numbering of the Psalms that you cite: They speak vanity every one with his neighbour; with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak. May the Lord cut off all flattering lips. Josh. 24.14: Serve Jehovah perfectly and truly. 1 Kings 2.4: Walk before me in all truth, with all your heart and with all your soul; as the better version has it: If your sons take heed to their way, walking before me in faithfulness, with their whole heart and their whole soul, etc. These and similar passages, in which God commends the pursuit of truth, of which kind are also Sir. 2.14, Jas. 4.8, Jer. 9.8, Ps. 28.3, 2 Tim. 2.13, Job 10.35: who calls them into doubt? Does Zanchius? But he, in book 3 of On the Nature of God, chapter 4, page 368, in the very words you cite, says that the whole will of God is not always signified in the word, but is partly withheld and hidden, until it is known from the outcome. But what is plainer or truer than this doctrine? Or is Beza the guilty one here? He, in the Colloquy at Montbéliard, page 174, says: God, he says, often does not will to do what he has said he would do. Does God therefore fall into the charge of lying? Not at all. For God often says that he will do something under a condition, which seems to be said absolutely. And so what Beza teaches here must be explained in that way. The matter is clear from the story of Jonah. Again, is Zanchius called to account? Indeed, because in On the Nature of God, book 3, chapter 4, question 3, page 310, he says: God does not always will what he commands and promises. Here you corrupt and mutilate the words of Zanchius, as will be clear from the whole passage that I transcribe. The other is called the will of sign: namely, that precepts and promises, with the condition of keeping the precepts, are signs that God wills thus. Yet NOT ALWAYS, AND NOT SIMPLY IN ALL CASES, does he will what he commands or promises, as is plain first in Abraham and then in Pharaoh. For he commands Abraham that he kill his son.

units.la: non sit ... lium occidat: fuit igitur voluntas signi. nec ta-men volebat Deus simpliciter, ut Abrahamus fi-lium occideret: sicut & prohibitio addita, et eve-tus declaravit. Fuit igitur haec altera voluntas beneplaciti. &c. Ex his vel Homero liqueat Zanchium non simpliciter negare, Deum velle quae mandat aut promittit, sed docere Deum non omnia talia velle simpliciter & absolute: quoniam absoluta Dei voluntas semper impletur. Si autem haec falsa sunt dum scribuntur a Zanchio, quaero ex te, Berti, an vera fiant, si scribantur a Vorstio? Ita ille disp. 6. de voluntate Dei p. 63. thes. 30.
units.tr: ...lium occidat [i.e. his son]: there was therefore a will of sign. Yet God did not simply will that Abraham should kill his son; just as the added prohibition and the outcome showed. There was therefore this second will, the will of good pleasure, etc. From these things it will be clear even to a blind man that Zanchius does not simply deny that God wills what he commands or promises, but teaches that God does not will all such things simply and absolutely, since God's absolute will is always fulfilled. But if these statements are false when written by Zanchius, I ask you, Berti, whether they become true when written by Vorstius? So he writes in Disputation 6, on the will of God, page 63, thesis 30:

units.la: Extra ordinem tamen quum singulare aliquod judicium exercere vult, solet DEUS quadam praecipere, quae vel non statim, vel non ita absolute, ut verba praeferunt fieri vult. v gr. quum Abrahamus ab ipso jussus est, filium suum immolare, quod tamen Deus non ita absolute, ut verba innuebant, fieri volebat: sicut ex eo, quod ipse Deus eventum postea impedivit, apparet, Gen. 22. &c. Item quum Pharao populum Israelis dimittere jussus est, quod tamen non statim fieri Deus volebat; sicut ex eo, quod Deus ipse praedixerat se Pharaonis animum indurraturum, apparet, Exod. 4. v. 21. & 8. 15. 19. Et thes. 31. Sed voluntas speciālis inabsoluta seu conditionata non semper impletur. Nam nec praecepta Dei semper a nobis observantur, quae tamen ipse vult, seu potius vellet ac cuperet, à nobis observari: nec promissa semper illis, quibus alioqui Deus ea præstare cuperet, reipsa præstantur, vide Esa. 1. 19. 20. & 15. 1. &c. & 48. 18. & 65. 2. Matth. 23. 37. Luc. 7. 30. Act. 13. 40. 2. Pet. 3. 9. & alibi passim. Hæc ita similia sunt ut Vorstius è Zanchio transcripsisse videri possit, si locus allegatus cum Vorstii disputationib⁹ diligenter comparetur. Eodem modo explicandus est Piscator qui p. 68. Voluntas Dei, inquit, interdum pugnat cum præcepto. Non pugnat simpliciter, & in se sed in specie & humano judicio id est, non eadem cum præcepto est, vide Calvinum de prædestinatione contra Castell. p. 1015. quis enim dixerit voluntatem, qua Deus permittit peccatum fieri, esse eandem cum præcepto? Procul sit profanum istud delirium. In hunc sensum trahe quod p. 15. Non oportet, inquit, præcepta Dei cum ipsius voluntate confundere. Tremque illud Lutheri de servo arbitrio ita defendendum: Multa Deus vult (nempe voluntate consequente aut conditionata) quæ verbo suo ostendit se non velle. Sic non vult mortem peccatoris verbo se. Vult autem illam voluntate sua imperscrutabili, hoc est, Deus non vult mortem peccatoris si pœnitentiam agat, vult mortem peccatoris, si non agat. Quæ voluntatis divinæ oc-cultacultatio miranda potius, quam rimanda est. Denique vellicas illa Sturmii de præd. pag. 117. Duplex est voluntas Dei una arcana, altera revelata, quæ nobis sequenda est. Quum dicitur: Qui facit voluntatem Dei is non peccat, id intelligendum est de voluntate revelata, quæ nobis sequenda est. Quum dicitur peccantes facere voluntatem Dei, intelligendum id est de arcana Dei voluntate, quia nobis non est invecтiganda. Quid inde efficis? An Deum vel approbare, vel jubere, vel perficere peccata? Absit. Non enim Sturmius vult peccatores facere voluntatem Dei approbantem aut jubentem. Ea enim ex verbo liquet. Nec perficientem. Ea enim voluntas Dei est actio, non hominis. Peccatores autem faciunt voluntatem Dei permittente non quòd eam facere debeant aut etiam velint (Idenim nec a Deo jubentur, neque ipsi sciunt, aut volunt) seu faciunt malum, quod Deus dum ab ipsis fit non impedit nec vult impedire. Quâ distinctionem ex præceptore suo Zanchio de nat. Dei p. 310 haurire potuit. Alio enim, inquit, modo vult (Deus) bona, nempe per se: alio mala; nempe propter aliud, id est, propter bonum: & idcirco fit, ut alia dicatur esse voluntas Dei, quæ vult bona, & alia illa, quæ vult mala. Illa dicitur voluntas bona, complacens: hæc permissiva seu permissio volun-
units.tr: Yet when God wishes to exercise some singular judgment outside the ordinary course, he is accustomed to command certain things which he does not wish to be done at once, or not in the absolute way that the words express. For example, when Abraham was commanded by him to sacrifice his son, God did not will that this be done absolutely, as the words suggested; as is evident from the fact that God himself afterwards prevented the outcome, Gen. 22, etc. Likewise, when Pharaoh was ordered to let the people of Israel go, which God did not will to be done at once; as is evident from the fact that God himself had foretold that he would harden Pharaoh's heart, Exod. 4.21, and 8.15, 19. And thesis 31. But a special will that is not absolute, or is conditional, is not always fulfilled. For neither are God's precepts always observed by us, which he nevertheless wills, or rather would wish and desire, to be observed by us; nor are his promises always actually performed for those to whom otherwise God would desire to perform them. See Isa. 1.19, 20, and 15.1, etc., and 48.18, and 65.2; Matt. 23.37; Luke 7.30; Acts 13.40; 2 Pet. 3.9; and elsewhere passim. These statements are so similar that Vorstius might seem to have copied them from Zanchius, if the cited passage is carefully compared with Vorstius's disputations. In the same way Piscator must be explained, who says on page 68: The will of God, he says, sometimes fights against the precept. It does not fight absolutely and in itself, but in its aspect and in human judgment; that is, it is not the same as the precept. See Calvin on predestination against Castellio, page 1015. For who would say that the will by which God permits sin to happen is the same as the precept? Far be that profane madness. In this sense also must be taken what he says on page 15: It is not right, he says, to confuse the precepts of God with his will itself. And Luther's statement in On the Bondage of the Will* must be defended in the same way: God wills many things (namely by a consequent or conditional will) which by his word he shows that he does not will. Thus he does not will the death of a sinner by his word. But he wills it by his inscrutable will; that is, God does not will the death of a sinner if he repents; he wills the death of a sinner if he does not repent. This hidden knowledge of the divine will is to be wondered at rather than searched into. Finally, you pick at that passage of Sturm on predestination, page 117: The will of God is twofold: one hidden, the other revealed, which we must follow. When it is said, "He who does the will of God does not sin," this must be understood of the revealed will, which we must follow. When it is said that sinners do the will of God, this must be understood of the hidden will of God, because we must not investigate it. What do you infer from this? That God approves, commands, or performs sins? Far from it. For Sturm does not mean that sinners do the will of God approving or commanding it. That is clear from the word. Nor that he performs it, for that will of God is his action, not man's. Sinners do the will of God by permission, not because they ought to do it or even wish to (for they are neither commanded by God to do it, nor do they know or wish it themselves); rather they do the evil which God, while it is being done by them, does not hinder nor wish to hinder. Zanchius, his teacher, in On the Nature of God, page 310, could have drawn this distinction from him: For God wills good things in one way, namely for their own sake; and evil things in another way, namely for the sake of something else, that is, for the sake of good. And so it comes about that one will of God is said to be that which wills good things, and another that which wills evil. The former is called the good, well-pleasing will; the latter is the permissive will or the permission of the voluntary.

units.la: (Sturmius = Sturmii; reference "117." as printed in text.) voluntaria. Quid? quod ipse tu, Berti, i- dem fateris & doces thesis. Nimirum eo, ais, recurrendum est, quo nos ducunt scriptura & ratio & experientia, ut, posito extra Deum alio quodam actionum principio, cogitemus, non omnia Deum agere neque vero agere decrevisse, sed permittere multa, & quidem volentem, quamvis ipse non probat. Nimirum hoc idem est quod sentiunt doctores, quando dicunt peccantes facere voluntatem Dei occultam, quae pervestiganda non sit, qua Deus peccata non probet, non jubeat, non faciat, sed fieri sancte permittat, & permissa gubernate & ad finem sibi quidem gloriosum ecclesiae vero salutarem ordinare decreverit.
units.tr: voluntary. What then? Do you not yourself, Berti, hold and teach the same thesis? Certainly, you say, we must return to the point to which Scripture, reason and experience lead us: namely, that, positing some other principle of actions outside God, we should think that God does not do all things, nor indeed has decreed to do so, but permits many things, and indeed willingly, although he himself does not approve. Certainly this is the same thing the teachers mean when they say that sinners do the hidden will of God, which is not to be searched out, by which God does not approve sins, does not command them, does not effect them, but holily permits them to happen, and, having permitted them, has decreed to govern and order them to an end that is indeed glorious to himself but salutary to the Church.

units.la: CAP. III. Duae in Deo voluntates facile conciliari possunt.
units.tr: CAP. III. Two wills in God can easily be reconciled.

units.la: OPrimè in Deo conciliatae sunt voluntates. Quum enim voluntas Dei in & per se una duntaxat sit & simplex, tamen multiplex esse dicitur tum propter diversa rerum genera, quae ipse vult: tum propter volendi rationem, prout antegresso cap.explicatum est, in quo contrarias voluntates ejus.
units.tr: First, the wills in God are reconciled. For although the will of God is in itself and by its nature one only and simple, yet it is said to be manifold, both on account of the diverse kinds of things which he wills, and on account of the manner of willing, as was explained in the preceding chapter, in which his contrary wills were set out.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: ejusdem rei eodem respectu nullas Deo tribui posse aut debere pertendimus. Quapropter etiam nihil attinet eas excusare, ob summam Dei in agendo libertatem. Quid enim? Dei libertas nullius mendacii aut hypocrisis est principium. Naturalis enim Dei bonitas & Justitia liberum voluntatis actum semper antecedit, eúq; moderatur & quasi format. Hoc etiam D. Piscator, què hic notas, facile, opinor, nobiscum dixerit. Bucanus contrarias in Deo voluntates non agnoscit. Non igitur eas conciliare studet. Id liquidum est ex institutionibus theologicis l. 14. de Dei providentia, q. 15. An duæ constituuntur contrariæ in Deo voluntates, quæ arcano suo consilio decernere & regere dicitur, quæ tamen palam lege sua prohibet? Mihi-me: sed quum una sit & simplex Dei voluntas, multiplex nobis apparet; quia pro imbecillitate mentis nostræ non posumus capere quomodo Deus idem non eodem modo & sine (sic enim sibi contradiceret) sed diverso modo vult & nolit fieri: est enim sapientia ejus Ephes. 3. v. 10. Quam ille responsionem ex lib. 1. inst. c. 18. §. 3. totidem pene verbis exscripsit. Quid tu ad ista? Profecto, ais, necesse est ferreum esse illi intellectum, qui conciliaturus sit, Nolo, Volo, dere eadem. At etiam Vorstius tam (ex te loquor) ferreo C intellectu ista sic videtur conciliare, disp. 6. de voluntate Dei, thes. 36. Non quicquid Deus vult ab aeterno in aeternum vult. Nam ut quaedam vult tantum ad tempus, quaedam vero in perpetuum: sic quaedam in tempore reipsa vult, quae antea sic nominatim atque in specie noluit, vel definite vult aut non vult, quae antea definite nec voluit, nec noluit. Nunc enim non vult eum cultum, quem voluit olim in veteri testamento. Vides quomodo Deus diverso modo quaedam velit ac nolit? Et mirum est te notas oppositionis leges aut dissimulare posse, aut omnes ad unam rescindere vel restringere velle. Et quid? annon tu ipse fateris Deum permittere multa & quidem volentem? Vult ergo rem unam & non vult. Vult permittere, non vult agere seu efficere. An non ita tu conciliias Volo, Nolo de re eadem? Hinc jam judicare licet: utrum intellectus, qui nobis tantas hic difficultates fingit, ferreus sit an terreus. Porro Zanchii mentem non attingis, dum patefactae & occultae voluntatis distinctionem sic ab illo vis conciliatam, ut occulta voluntas sit beneplaciti, quasi aliud Deus verbo significet quam ipsi placet. Plane contrarium docet Zanchius de natura Dei pag. 314. his verbis: Quod vero etiam multa jubeat fieri quae non fiunt: non inde tamen sequitur, aut impotentem tentem esse: quasi non possit efficere, ut, qua jubet fiant: aut revera multiplicem esse in Deo voluntatem, unam, quam per verbum significet, alteram, qua apud se nolit fieri, quod jubet.
units.tr: We maintain that contrary things cannot and must not be ascribed to God in the same matter and in the same respect. For this reason there is no point in excusing them, given God's supreme freedom in acting. For what? The freedom of God is the source of no lie or hypocrisy. God's natural goodness and justice always precede his free act, govern it, and, as it were, shape it. Our Piscator, whom you note here, will, I think, readily say this with us. Bucanus does not acknowledge contrary wills in God, and so he does not strive to reconcile them. This is clear from his theological institutions, book 1, on the providence of God, question 15: Are two contrary wills said to be established in God, which he is said to decree and govern by his secret counsel, yet which he openly forbids by his law? By no means: but since the will of God is one and simple, it appears to us manifold, because in our weak minds we cannot grasp how God wills and does not will the same thing, not in the same way and not without contradicting himself, but in different ways: for his wisdom is manifold, Ephes. 3. v. 10. He copied this answer almost word for word from book 1 of the Institutes, chapter 18, section 3. What do you say to this? Surely, you say, the mind must be iron that is going to reconcile "I do not will" and "I will" about the same thing. Yet Vorstius too, to speak of you, seems to reconcile these things with an iron intellect, disp. 6, on the will of God, thes. 36: Not whatever God wills from eternity, he wills for eternity. For as he wills some things only for a time, and others forever, so he really wills some things in time which he previously did not will by name and in particular, or he now definitely wills or does not will what he previously neither willed nor did not will definitely. For now he does not will that worship which he once willed in the Old Testament. Do you see how God wills and does not will certain things in different ways? And it is strange that you can either ignore the laws of opposition or wish to abolish or restrict them all at once. And what? Do you not yourself admit that God permits many things, and indeed while willing them? Therefore he wills one thing and does not will it. He wills to permit it, and does not will to act or bring it about. Do you not in this way reconcile "I will" and "I do not will" about the same thing? From this one may now judge whether the intellect that invents such great difficulties for us here is iron or earthen. Furthermore, you do not grasp Zanchius's mind when you want the distinction between revealed and hidden will to be reconciled by him in such a way that the hidden will is that of good pleasure, as if God by his word signified something other than what pleases him.
