Zanchius teaches the very opposite in his book on the nature of God, page 314, in these words: That he commands many things to be done which are not done does not, however, follow from this, either that he is powerless, as if he could not bring it about that what he commands should come to pass, or that in God there is truly a manifold will, one which he signifies by the word, and another by which he is unwilling for what he commands to be done.

units.la: Duo enim sunt praeceptorum Dei genera: quaedam simpliciter absoluta, & sine ulla omnino conditione vel expressa vel tacita. Haec sunt certissima, absoluta & simplicis divina voluntatis, quae beneplacitum dicitur, testimonium. Quale illud fuit ad Mosen, fac omnia secundum exemplar, quod vidisti in monte. Item, sic dices filiis Israel; vade in Aegyptum: & alia id genus multa tum ad ipsum Mosen, tum ad prophetas facta mandata. &c. Alia sunt praecepta quae cum conditione, si non expressa, saltem tacita promulgarit: uti sunt, quaecunque habemus in lege. Ita Zanchius, quam illi tribuis opinionem, refutat. Adhaec objicis simplicitatem Dei & ab hominibus requisitam, quam sententia nostra non laedit. Pugnantes enim aut simulatas in Deo voluntates non agnoscimus. Ideo etiam non opus est <bl>κεφαλαίως</bl> quo nonnullos uti doces; videlicet revelatam DEI voluntatem nobis duntaxat esse sequendam. Equidem hanc solam sequendam judicamus, non tamen illo fine, ut pugnantes in Deo voluntates conciliemus, quia nullas tales agnoscimus: sed quia tam diu eam voluntatem, quam
units.tr: For there are two kinds of God's precepts. Some are absolute in themselves, without any condition at all, either expressed or tacit. These are the most certain testimony of the absolute and simple divine will, which is called good pleasure. Such was that to Moses: "Make all things according to the pattern which you saw on the mountain." Likewise: "Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: go into Egypt," and many other commands of this kind given both to Moses himself and to the prophets, and so on. Other precepts he has promulgated with a condition, if not expressed, at least tacit: such as all those we have in the law. Thus Zanchius refutes the opinion you attribute to him. Besides, you object to the simplicity of God, which is also required of men, and which our view does not harm. For we do not acknowledge conflicting or feigned wills in God. Therefore there is also no need for the [κεφαλαίως] which you say some use, namely that only the revealed will of God is to be followed by us. Indeed we judge this alone to be followed, yet not with that aim, that we reconcile conflicting wills in God, since we acknowledge no such; but because for as long as

units.la: Deus verbo expressit, beneplaciti esse credendum est, donec D. eus pleniùs, definitiùs ac clariùs, quid velit, nobis aperiat. Et plus quam diabolicum cavillandi cacoëthes in thef. 12. delitescit, quo quidem verbo divino sua auctoritas, fidei omnis certitudo, ac precibus religio derogatur, erras enim Berti, fi fallax signu voluntatis divinæ verbu Dei esse à nobis dici existimas. Erras, fi voluntatem signi improprie id est, falsò voluntatem Dei esse nos dicere putas. Proprium enim hic non est idem quod verum & improprium idem quod falsum: sed improprium est quod tropicum seu figuratum: proprium quod simplex & non figuratum. Acyrologiam esse in vocibus signi & beneplaciti ex ipso Vorstio discere potuisses, qui eam ex Thoma Aquinate annotat disp. 6. de voluntate Dei, thes. 21. Et nos hanc distinctionem ex animo detestamur, crede hoc mihi ferio dicenti, mi clarissime Berti, si hoc trahatur, quasi voluntas signi non bene Deo placeat, aut quasi cum Dei beneplacito pugnet: quia sic sanctissimo Deo simulationem cum deceptione conjunctam, imò mendacium & iniquitatem aperte tribuit, asserendo, eum non vere id velle, quod jubet aut vetat aut promittit aut minatur, sed id duntaxat quod evenire videmus. De modo loquendi lis est, non de re, Nemo enim negat voluntatem signi esse veram Dei voluntatem: at nihilominus improprie voluntatem dici Zanchius contendit quoniam signum non est reipsa idem quod res signata & quoniam nō est ita plene voluntas, ut voluntas bene placiti. Id enim magis proprie Deus velle dicitur quod magis vult. Id autem magis vult quod vult ipse efficere & contra quod nihil vult permittere. Voluntas signi est signum voluntatis divinæ: signum non fallax, sed certum: non mendax, sed verum. Similiter ludunt hodierni Lutherani qui cavillantur de tropico & improprio corpore Christi in cœna, quando cum orthodoxis de modo loquendi disputant. Quòdsi incommoda vox exciderit theologo, boni viri erit non sugillare vocem sed mentem attendere, quæ publicis explanata est confessionibus.
units.tr: God has expressed in his word, it is to be believed to be his good pleasure, until God more fully, definitely, and clearly reveals to us what he wills. And more than diabolical itch for quibbling lurks in thesis 12, by which the authority of the divine word, all certainty of faith, and the religion of prayer are undermined. For you are mistaken, Berti, if you think we call the Word of God a deceptive sign of the divine will. You are mistaken if you think we say that the will of the sign is improperly, that is, falsely, the will of God. For here proper is not the same as true, and improper the same as false: rather, improper is what is tropical or figurative, and proper what is simple and not figurative. You could have learned from Vorstius himself that there is an acyrology in the words "sign" and "good pleasure," which he notes from Thomas Aquinas, disp. 6, on the will of God, thes. 21. We detest this distinction from our heart; believe me, I say this in earnest, most distinguished Berti, if it is pressed as if the will of the sign does not please God well, or as if it conflicts with God's good pleasure. For thus you openly attribute to the most holy God a simulation joined with deception, indeed lying and iniquity, asserting that he does not truly will what he commands, forbids, promises, or threatens, but only what we see come to pass. The dispute is about the manner of speaking, not the thing itself. For no one denies that the will of the sign is the true will of God; yet Zanchius nonetheless contends that it is improperly called will, since the sign is not in reality the same as the thing signified, and since it is not fully a will in the way that the will of good pleasure is. For that is more properly said to be willed by God which he wills more. And he wills more that which he himself wills to bring about, and against which he wills to permit nothing. The will of the sign is a sign of the divine will: a sign that is not deceptive but certain, not lying but true. Similarly the modern Lutherans play tricks, who cavil about the tropical and improper body of Christ in the Supper, when they dispute with the orthodox about the manner of speaking. But if an unsuitable word has slipped from a theologian, it is the part of a good man not to sneer at the word but to attend to the mind, which has been explained in the public confessions.

units.la: Cap. IV. Deus non vult peccata, neque ipsa per se decrevit.
units.tr: Chapter IV. God does not will sins, nor has he decreed them in themselves.

units.la: DEUM nolle peccata ex Scriptura est manifestissimum. Psal. 5. v. 5, 6. Non Deus volens iniquitatem tu es. Neque habitabit juxta malignus, neque permanebunt injusti ante oculos tuos. Psal. 45. v. 8. Dilexisti justitiam, et odisti iniquitatem. Idem de Christo dicitur ad Heb. 1, v. 9. Sunt autem qui contrariam opinionem ex iisdem literis probare conantur, & allegant Exod. 9. v. 7. Jes. 9. v. 10. Rom. 1. v. 28. 2. Thess. 2. v. 11. Matth. 6. v. 13.
units.tr: That God does not will sins is most plainly taught in Scripture. Ps. 5:5, 6: "For thou art not a God who willeth iniquity; neither shall the wicked dwell with thee; neither shall the foolish stand in thy sight." Ps. 45:8: "Thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity." The same is said of Christ in Heb. 1:9. Yet there are those who try to prove the opposite opinion from the same writings, and they cite Exod. 9:7; Isa. 9:10; Rom. 1:28; 2 Thess. 2:11; Matt. 6:13.

units.la: Quapropter praestantissimi theologi utiliter distinxerunt, quae in hac thesi ambigua sunt, ne contradictionem aliquam in scripturis inesse cogantur asserere. Zanchius lib. 3, de natura Dei c. 4. q. 4. ita distinguit.
units.tr: Therefore the most excellent theologians have usefully distinguished what is ambiguous in this thesis, so that they are not forced to assert any contradiction in the Scriptures. Zanchius (De natura Dei, book 3, ch. 4, q. 4) distinguishes it thus.

units.la: Malum culpa trifariam consideratur: Primum, uti est peccatum pugnans cum lege Dei: atque ita duntaxat est malum culpae.
units.tr: Evil considered as fault may be viewed in three ways. First, as it is sin, conflicting with the law of God; and in this way it is only the evil of fault.

units.la: Deinde uti est poena praecedentis peccati.
units.tr: Second, as it is the punishment of a preceding sin.

units.la: Tertio uti est causa subsequentis peccati. Est haec distinctio cognitu necessaria: qua ostendimus Deum velle peccatum non quatenus peccatum est, aut causa peccati: sed quatenus poena peccati est. Unde intelligitur Deum nolle peccatum quatenus ipsum, velle autem aliquid peccato cuidam conjunctum, nempe alterius peccati poenam.
units.tr: Third, as it is the cause of a subsequent sin. This distinction is necessary to know, for by it we show that God wills sin not insofar as it is sin, or the cause of sin, but insofar as it is the punishment of sin. Hence it is understood that God does not will sin as such, but wills something conjoined with a certain sin, namely the punishment of another sin.

units.la: In peccato tria sunt, primum quidem actio. Deinde deformitas actionis, quae a Johanne ἀνομία dicitur. Postremo reatus seu obligatio
units.tr: In sin there are three things. First, the action itself. Second, the deformity of the action, which John calls lawlessness [ἀνομία]. Lastly, guilt or obligation

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: tio ad poenam, Deum actionem, quae bo-na est velle, ut & obligationem ad poenam concedunt docti: de actionis deformitate pernegant. 3 Aliquid velle dicimur bifariâ, aut proprie & per se: quia appetibile est sua natura. hoc modo bonum duntaxat appre-hensum, vel verum vel apparens volumus: aut improprie & propter aliud id est, propter bonum, quod inde sequitur (h e, ut clarius dicam, quod virtute ordinantis inde pro-ducitur, quum ex malo alioquin per se nihil boni oriatur aut sequatur.) non autem quod per se illud appetibile sit, hoc modo dici-mur velle malum, &c. Quanto minus igi-tur dici potest Deus proprie velle malum? Proinde potius dicendus est permittere. Sed volens non autem invitus: proprie autem velle id quod ex malo consequitur bonum. 4 Duo scopuli sunt vitandi. Unum, ne fa-ciamus Deum peccati auctorem & causam: quum nullo modo sit aut esse possit. Ta-lem autem esse omnino doceremus: si do-ceremus Deum proprie loquendo, velle peccatum, seu velle fieri peccatum. Alter scopulus nobis vitandus est, ne statuamus a-liquid mali in mundo fieri, Deo aut infscio aut invito, (ita ut veluti coactus permittat) hoc enim esset negare ipsius Dei omnipo-tentiam: eoq; ipsius Deitatem. Utantem
units.tr: ...tion to punishment, and God's act, which is good to will; learned men concede both this and the obligation to punishment, but they deny that the act is deformed. We are said to will something in two ways: either properly and in itself, because it is desirable by its nature (in this way we will only the good as apprehended, whether true or apparent), or improperly and on account of something else, that is, on account of the good that follows from it (or, to put it more clearly, the good that is brought about from it by the power of the one ordaining, since otherwise nothing good arises or follows from evil in itself). We are not saying that the evil itself is desirable in itself when we say in this way that we will evil, and so on. How much less, then, can it be said that God properly wills evil? Rather, it should be said that he permits it. He wills it, not unwillingly, but properly he wills what good follows from evil. Two rocks must be avoided. The first is that we make God the author and cause of sin, since this is in no way and cannot be so. We would teach that he is exactly this if we taught that God, speaking properly, wills sin, or wills that sin be done. The other rock we must avoid is the claim that some evil happens in the world either without God's knowledge or against his will, so that he permits it as if compelled; for this would deny the omnipotence of God himself, and thus his deity. To explain the matter briefly, it stands thus.

units.la: rem paucis expediamus, ita habe. Deus peccatum nullo modo vult seu approbat: quædam tamen permittit sapienti consilio. Optimè enim Augustinus ex Davidis verbis in enchir. ad Laurentium c.95. Nonfit aliquid nisi omnipotens fieri velit vel sinendo ut fiat, vel ipse faciendo. Deus decernit se peccata permissurum esse & ordinaturū. Ordinat enim ille non solùm quicquid bonum est & abipso est, verùm etiam quicquid malum est, & non est ab ipso, sed permittit ab ipso tantùm. Etsi enim malum non est bonum, bona tamen est mali permissio & ad bonum ordinatio. Nam rectè Fulgentius lib. 1 ad Monimum: Deus, ait, licet auctor non sit malarum cogitationum, ordinator tamen est malarum voluntatum; & de malo opere cuiuslibet mali non definit ipse bonum operari. Et Augustinus scite libr. 1. de genesi ad literam c.5. Species naturasq; ipsas & facit & ordinat: privationes autem species, defectusq; naturarum non facit, sed ordinat tantum. Quædam ergo & facit Deus & ordinat: quædam vero tantum ordinat. Iustos & facit & ordinat: peccatores autem, inquantum peccatores sunt, non facit: sed ordinat tantum: quippe quum illos ad dexteram, hos ad sinistram constituit. Ex Vorstio eandem potes sententiam haurire. Ita enim ille disp. 6. de volunvoluntate Dei thef. 16. Malum morale seu peccatum neque efficit, neque approbat, neque præcipit neque suadet, hoc est, nullo modo ipse facere aut ab aliis fieri vult Deus: sed odit, prohibet, dissuadet, punit ac sæpe etiam inhibet, juxta illud psalmi 5.5. Non es Deus volens impietatem, & illud Zachar. 8. 17. Hæc sunt (peccata) quæ odit, inquit Deus, & illud Ephes. 5.6. Propter hæc venit ira Dei super incredulos. Interim volens, hoc est, non invitus aut coactus, sed iciens, prudens, ex certo consilio ea fieri finit, & quum fiunt, in bonum finem ordinat: videlicet propter certas causas satius esse judicans ea permittere, quam impedire. Etsi enim mala quatenus mala, non sunt bona, tamen ut non solum bona, sed & mala sint, bonum est: ut recte inquit Aug. in enchir. ad Laur. c. 96. Ex eadem disputatione Vorstii confícitur, Deum aliquo modo velle peccata fieri.
units.tr: God in no way wills or approves sin, yet by wise counsel he permits certain things. For Augustine rightly says, drawing on the words of David, in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 95: Nothing happens unless the Almighty wills it to happen, either by permitting it to happen or by doing it himself. God decrees that he will permit sins and order them. For he orders not only whatever is good and is from him, but also whatever is evil and is not from him, but which he only permits. For although evil is not good, the permission of evil is nevertheless good, and its ordering to good is good. Indeed Fulgentius rightly says in the first book to Monimus: God, he says, although he is not the author of evil thoughts, is nevertheless the orderer of evil wills; and he does not cease himself to work good out of any evil work. And Augustine aptly says in the first book of the literal commentary on Genesis, chapter 5: He both makes and orders the species and the natures themselves; but privations, the defects of natures, he does not make, but only orders. So God both makes and orders some things, but only orders others. He both makes and orders the just; but sinners, insofar as they are sinners, he does not make, but only orders, since he places the former at his right hand and the latter at his left. You can draw the same view from Vorstius, who in disputation 6, on the will of God, thesis 16, writes as follows: Moral evil, or sin, neither does God effect, nor approve, nor command, nor persuade; that is, God in no way wills to do it himself or to have it done by others. But he hates it, forbids it, dissuades from it, punishes it, and often even restrains it, according to the psalm: You are not a God who wills wickedness (Ps. 5.5), and that of Zechariah: These are the things (sins) that God says he hates (Zech. 8.17), and that of Ephesians: Because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the unbelievers (Eph. 5.6). Meanwhile he wills, that is, not unwillingly or under compulsion, but knowingly, prudently, and by a certain counsel, allows them to happen, and when they happen, he orders them to a good end, judging that for certain reasons it is better to permit them than to prevent them. For although evil things, insofar as they are evil, are not good, yet it is good that they should be not only good but also evil, as Augustine rightly says in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 96. From the same disputation of Vorstius it follows that God in some way wills sins to happen.

units.la: Nihil fieri potest quod omnipotens Deus simpliciter fieri nolit. Atqui peccata fiunt. Ergo peccata non simpliciter Deus fieri non vult; ac per consequens aliquo modo vult.
units.tr: Nothing can happen which almighty God simply does not will to happen. But sins do happen. Therefore God does not simply not will that sins happen; and consequently in some way he wills it.

units.la: Majoreft i).Vorftii thef.7.scribentis: In omnibus rebus quacunque sunt aut fiunt, alia quaineft boni ratio, fi non per fe, saltem per accidens: & sic aliquam Dei voluntatem eius intervenire necesse est: quum nihil fieri possit, quod omnipotens Deus simpliciter fieri nolit: cuiquam facile est, quicquid vult facere, tam non difficile est, quicquid non vult impedire. Ita etiam interpretaberis quae ab aliis forte duriuscule dicta sunt, in quem tu censum refers istud: Certum est omnia fieri in mundo ex decreto Dei, ergo etiam peccata: nam fi Deus non decrevit absolute ut peccata fiant, decrevit igitur sub conditione, sed sub qua? Decretum hic ne aliud cogita, quàm συγχωρησις, quo Deus peccata quaedam non impedit: alioqui verba illa odimus, fi ad aliam decretorum divinorum speciem referantur. Sequitur enim theologiam revelatam, ex qua tu ipse citas Jerem. 19. verf. 5. Ædificarunt excelsa Baalim, quae non praecepi nec loquutus sum, nec ascendit in cor meum. Et cap. 31. verf. 35. Non praecepi hoc eis, nec venit in cor meum ut facerent abominationem hanc, ut ad peccandum adducerem Judam. Hactenus videsq, quo sensu a quibusdam doceatur, Deum aliquo modo velle peccata h.e. ea non approbare aut jubere aut suadere aut efficere, sed permittere seu non impedire & ordinare re in bonum finem: nullo autem modo eorum auctorem ac procuratorem esse. Si autem & hoc à nonnullis dicatur, id non de peccatis, quatenus talia sunt & proprie dicuntur, sed qua vel actiones vel pænæ sunt, intelligendum est. Fere enim fit ut, quæ arctissimè conjuncta sunt eadem dicamus in populari sermonis usu. Citas in hunc sensum Calvini institutionem lib. 1. c. 18. & c. 4. §. 4. & 5. Zwinglii librum de providentia c. 6. &c. Egregiè ille se & alios fratres à calumniis Castellionis vindicavit, ut mirandum sit esse hoc ævo qui de mente illius in hoc argumento dubitare audeat. Et tu quoque rectius faceres, mi Berti, si in apologia illius potius acquiesceres, quàm duriora illius dicta hinc inde corraderes, de gluberes & siniistrè acciperes, quod ut pace tua dicam patieris. Sic enim te moneri interest justitiæ.
units.tr: The major premise is from Vorstius, thesis 7, writing: In all things that are or happen, there is some reason of good, if not in itself, at least by accident; and so it is necessary that some will of God intervene: since nothing can happen that almighty God simply does not will to happen; it is easy for anyone to do whatever he wills, and not difficult to hinder whatever he does not will. In the same way you will interpret what others have perhaps said rather harshly, and which you refer to that opinion: It is certain that all things happen in the world by the decree of God, therefore also sins: for if God has not decreed absolutely that sins should happen, then he has decreed it under a condition; but under what condition? Here do not think of any decree other than [συγχώρησις] permission, by which God does not hinder certain sins; otherwise we would dislike those words if they were referred to another kind of divine decree. For this follows from revealed theology, from which you yourself cite Jeremiah 19:5: They have built the high places of Baal, which I did not command, nor did I speak it, nor did it come into my heart. And chapter 31, verse 35: I did not command them this, nor did it come into my heart that they should do this abomination, so as to lead Judah into sin. Thus far you see in what sense some teach that God in some way wills sins, that is, does not approve, command, persuade, or effect them, but permits them or does not hinder them and orders them to a good end; yet in no way is he their author or manager. But if some also say this, it is to be understood not of sins as such, and as they are properly called, but insofar as they are either actions or punishments. For it commonly happens that we speak in ordinary usage of things that are most closely joined as the same. You cite in this sense Calvin's Institutes, book 1, chapter 18, and chapter 4, sections 4 and 5, and Zwingli's book on providence, chapter 6, etc. He vindicated himself and his other brethren most nobly from the calumnies of Castellio, so that it is to be wondered at that in this age there are some who dare to doubt his mind on this question. And you too, my Berti, would do better to rest satisfied with his apology, rather than to gather together his harsher sayings from here and there, to twist them and to take them in a bad sense, which, with your leave, I say you have suffered. For it is in your interest, as a matter of justice, to be warned thus.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAP. V.

units.la: Deus non ordinavit, decrevit & voluit efficaciter ut Adam laberetur.
units.tr: God did not ordain, decree, or efficaciously will that Adam should fall.

units.la: EX iis, quæ hactenus diximus manifestè constare arbitror nequeefficacem Dei ordinationem, neque efficax decretum aut voluntas... voluntatem causam necessitatis fuisse, ob q; Adam peccaverit. Contingens enim fuit lapsus Adami, non necessarius, à voluntate libera non à causa ulla externa voluntatem adigente. Nam non ideo peccavit Adam, quia Deus hoc futurum noverat, sed praescivit Deus quasi Deus quod ille erat propria voluntate fa-cturus, teste Hieronymo dial. 3, adversus Pelagianos. Etsi enim Deus sapiente consilio decrevetit & voluerit, ante quam Adamus laberetur, se lapsum illius non impeditu-rum & in bonum finem ordinaturum, si laberetur: tamen nullatenus ei causa fuit, qua in lapsum invitus aut divinitus persuasus propelleretur. Ita docemur à sacris literis, quae Deum vetuisse lapsum clare ostendunt Gen. 2. v. 16. & punivisse, c. 3. v. 17. Jam Deus non est ultor, cujus est auctor, uti ex Fulgentio, Irenaeo, Eusebio, Chrysostomo, Basilio, Ambrosio, Augustino & aliis constat. Sed interim offendunt te verba Calvini lib. 1. inst. c. 18, §. 4. Non debet absurdum videri, quod dico Deum non modo primi hominis casum & in eo ruinam posterorum praevidisse, sed arbitrio quoque suo dispensasse. Haec quidem illo in loco quem citasti non leguntur sed lib. 3. c. 23. §. 7: attamen nihil à vero alienum habent si recte accipiantur. Quando enim Deus dicitur lapsum primi ho-minis minis arbitrio suo dispensasie, negatur de Deo quòd ipso vel inscio vel coacto aut negligente homo ceciderit. Id luculenter & continenter per verba malè à te omissa declarat. Ut enim ad ejus sapientiam pertinet omnium quæ futura sunt esse præscium, sic ad potentiam omnia manu sua regere ac moderari. Amplius ex Augustino declarat ibidem & confirmat: Et hanc quoque, dicës quæstionem Augustinus, ut alias scite expedit, Salu-berrimè confitemur quod rectissime credimus, Deum Dominumq; rerum omnium, qui creavit omnia bona valde & mala ex bonis oritura præscivit, & scivit magis ad suam omnipotentissimam bonitatem pertinere etiam de malis benefacere, quàm mala esse nò sinere: sic ordinasse angelorum et hominum vitam, ut in ea primus ostenderet quid posset liberum arbitrium, deinde quid posset gratia sua beneficium justitiaq; judicium. Secundum hæc intellige quod de ordinatione & dispensatione Calvinus dixit: ut & ista: Decretum quidem horribile, fateor: inficiari tamen nemo potest quin præsciverit Deus, &c. quem exitum esset habiturus homo antequam ipsum coderet & ideo præsciverit, quia decreto suo sic ordinarat. Ea quidem inibi exstant, quæ proximè addis: Homo justo Dei impulsu agit, quod sibi non licet. At plenius exscribere illa decuisset, ne verbamur. ba mutilata lectoris pravū progigneret sen-sum. Sic integrē sonant: Si quos autem, ma-gis impediat quod nunc dicimus, nullū esse Dei eum homine consensum, ubi hic justo illius im-pulsu agit quod sibi non licet: succurrat quod alibi admonet idem Augustinus, Quis non ad ista judicia contremiscat, ubi agit Deus etiam in cordibus malorum quicquid vult, reddens eis tamen secundum eorum merita? Epist. 48. ad Vincentium. Haec docet postquam li-quido explicuit, quomodo in eodem ope-ratam se prodat hominis crimen, quàm re-fulgeat Dei justitia. Praeterea in toto isto passagio nullum verbum exstat de lapsu Adami, de quo hic disputamus: sed oftentitur Deum non esse auctorem scelerum 1. ex-emplis ex Davidis historia depromtis 2. ex apostasia Israelitarum 3. ex Achabi & Jehu historia 4. ex confessione Augustini & historia mortis Christi. Huc etiam spectat, quod thes. 24. ais: Coguntur etiam docere, Deum non permittere mala, sed facere. A quo cogun-tur? Anne id probare potes? Id tentas proba-re ex lib. 1. instit. cap. 18. §. 1. Calvini, ubi ille ita scribit: Tergiversando effugiunt, quārunt; Dei tantum permissu, non etiam vo-luntate peccata fieri. Ipse vero palam se facere pronuncians, effugium illud repudiat. At quae hic impietas est? Calvinus rejicit per-misionem
units.tr: From what we have said so far, I think it is plainly clear that neither God's efficacious ordination nor an efficacious decree or will was the cause of necessity by which Adam sinned. The fall of Adam was contingent, not necessary, and came from his free will, not from any external cause compelling the will. For Adam did not sin because God knew that this would happen, but God foreknew, as God, that he was going to act by his own will, as Jerome states in the third dialogue against the Pelagians. For although God, by wise counsel, decreed and willed, before Adam fell, not to hinder his fall and to order it to a good end if he should fall, yet in no way was he the cause by which Adam was driven into the fall, unwilling or divinely persuaded. We are taught this by the sacred letters, which clearly show that God forbade the fall (Gen. 2. v. 16) and punished it (c. 3. v. 17). Now God is not the avenger of that whose author he is, as is established from Fulgentius, Irenaeus, Eusebius, Chrysostom, Basil, Ambrose, Augustine and others. But meanwhile the words of Calvin in Institutes book 1, chapter 18, section 4 trouble you: It ought not to seem absurd that I say God not only foresaw the fall of the first man and the ruin of his posterity in him, but also arranged it by his own decision. These words are not read in the place you cited, but in book 3, chapter 23, section 7; nevertheless they contain nothing foreign to the truth if they are rightly understood. For when God is said to have arranged the fall of the first man by his own decision, it is denied that God's man fell without God's knowledge, against his will, or through negligence. Calvin declares this clearly and consistently in the words you wrongly omitted: For just as it belongs to his wisdom to foreknow all that is going to be, so it belongs to his power to rule and govern all things by his hand. Calvin further declares and confirms this from Augustine in the same place: And this question too, as Augustine elsewhere skilfully explains, we most healthily confess, and believe most rightly, that God, the Lord of all things, who created all things very good, foreknew the evils that would arise from good things, and knew that it pertains more to his most almighty goodness to bring good even out of evils than to suffer evils not to be. So he ordained the life of angels and men, that in it he might first show what free will could do, and then what his grace could confer by way of benefit, and his justice by way of judgment. Understand in accordance with this what Calvin said about ordination and arrangement, and likewise this: I admit the decree is indeed horrible; yet no one can deny that God foreknew what end man would have before he created him, and therefore foreknew it because he had so ordained by his decree. These words are indeed there, as you add next: Man acts by God's just impulse what is not permitted to him. But it would have been proper to copy them out more fully, lest the mutilated words produce a wrong sense in the reader. They sound complete as follows: But if what we now say troubles some people, namely that there is no agreement of God with man where man acts, by God's just impulse, what is not permitted to him, let them recall what Augustine warns elsewhere: Who does not tremble at those judgments, where God works even in the hearts of the wicked whatever he wills, yet rendering to them according to their merits? Letter 48 to Vincentius. Calvin teaches this after he has clearly explained how the crime of man, in the same work, displays itself, and how the justice of God shines forth. Moreover, in the whole of that passage there is not one word about the fall of Adam, which is what we are discussing here; rather, he shows that God is not the author of sins: (1) by examples drawn from the history of David; (2) from the apostasy of the Israelites; (3) from the history of Ahab and Jehu; (4) from the confession of Augustine and the history of Christ's death. To this also belongs what you say in thesis 24: They are also compelled to teach that God does not permit evils but does them. By whom are they compelled? Can you prove that? You try to prove it from Calvin's Institutes book 1, chapter 18, section 1, where he writes thus: By shifting their ground they escape, and ask: sins happen only by God's permission, not also by his will. But he himself, openly declaring that he does them, rejects that escape. But what impiety is there here? Calvin rejects mere permission

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: missionem à voluntate separatam. An tu talem probas? Tu ipse dicis Deum voluntem permittere mala quæ diximus. Calvinus ociosam permissionem repudiat, quam Epicurei fingunt. Id patet ex §. 2. ubi ait: Isti cesfores volunt ipsius ociofo tantum permissu contingere. Et quomodo peccata voluntate Dei eveniant jam ante explicatum est satis. Quanquam vero hanc blasphemiam omnibus operibus à se amoliantur theologi, tamen id nec credis nec pateris, sed pro virili tua improperas, & nunc Pharaonis nunc aliorum exempla objectas, quibus Deum auctorem & procuratorem peccatorum faciat. Cur ita offirmas, Berti? Quomodo in Deo non sint contrariæ voluntates jam supra satis explicatum puto. Quomodo Zanchius & Piscator intelligi possint, quando Deum aliud mandare, aliud velle dicunt, ex iisdem quæ diximus, sciri potest. Sed tu duriter tractas fratres tuos, omnem illis amorem, omnem fidem derogas. Ita enim scribis: Quum ergo hæc ita ab ipsis asserantur & defendantur, imò & dici debeant, si candide agere cupiant & principia sua servare & congruaiis dicere, quæ de occulta Dei voluntate prodiderunt; admit, tendæ non sunt contestationes eorum, qui post ista adhuc negant se docere, Deum ipsum ...
units.tr: a permission separated from the will? Do you approve of such a one? You yourself say that God wills to permit the evils we have mentioned. Calvin rejects an idle permission, such as the Epicureans invent. This is clear from §2, where he says: These cutthroats want sins to happen only by his idle permission. And how sins happen by the will of God has already been explained sufficiently. Although theologians keep this blasphemy far from all their works, you neither believe nor allow it, but to the best of your ability you heap reproaches, and now you bring forward the examples of Pharaoh, now of others, by which you make God the author and procurer of sins. Why do you so assert, Berti? I think it has been explained sufficiently above how there are not contrary wills in God. From the same things we have said, it can be known how Zanchius and Piscator may be understood, when they say that God commands one thing and wills another. But you treat your brothers harshly and deprive them of all love and all faith. For you write thus: Since these things are asserted and defended by them, and indeed ought to be said, if they wish to act candidly, keep their principles, and speak consistently with what they have published concerning the hidden will of God, the protestations of those are not to be admitted who, after these things, still deny that they teach that God himself ...

units.la: CAP. V. DE ESSE AUCTORUM PECCATORUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. ON WHETHER GOD IS THE AUTHOR OF SIN.

units.la: Contestationes Libertinorum non admisit Calvinus, & inerito, ficergo scribit epistola ad Rhotomagenfes de Francifcano quodam: Deum peccati auctorem facere nolle affirmat: camus & nos idem de istis: negant enim fe dicere, id quod dicunt; ἀλλὰ τὸ ταφεῖ Bo ... Ubi est frons tua, Berti? Quò abiit mens tua? fortassis convivatum ad Æthiopas? Ubi est amor tuus? Ubi φιλαδελφία, quam alibi jactas? Hæccine tu scriberes in fratres? imò in patres optimè meritos de te, de republica, de ecclesia Dei? in Deifervos & amicos Hiccine est spiritus ille πνεῦμα, man-suetudinis & charitatis, quo aguntur fratres Arminiani, quemque à multis contri-stari publicè lamentantur? Nulla, nulla ti-bi justa causa est eos errores hujus & blas-phemiæ incusandi, qui eam animitus ab-horrent, & publicitus editis scriptis refu-tant, condemnant, execrantur. Quid jut-vat illas tam charas Deo animas cum Lige-bertinis contendere? Iniquissima est con-tentio. Quod enim hi nequiter & blas-phemè astruunt, id illæ religiosè piéque destruunt, & quando in hac cum istis vefa-nia consentient.
units.tr: Calvin did not accept the protestations of the Libertines, and rightly so. In his letter to the people of Rouen about a certain Franciscan he writes that he is unwilling to make God the author of sin. We say the same of these men: they deny that they teach what they teach. ἀλλὰ τὸ ταφεῖ [but the ...] Bo ... Where is your forehead, Bertius? Where has your mind gone? Perhaps you have gone to dine with the Ethiopians? Where is your love? Where is that brotherly love (φιλαδελφία) which you boast of elsewhere? Would you write such things against brethren? Nay, against fathers who have deserved so well of you, of the commonwealth, and of the Church of God, against the servants and friends of God? Is this that spirit (πνεῦμα) of gentleness and charity by which the Arminian brethren are moved, and which many publicly lament to be grieved? You have no just cause at all to accuse of these errors and blasphemy those who inwardly abhor it and, by published writings, refute, condemn and execrate it. What good does it do you to contend with the Libertines on behalf of souls so dear to God? The contention is most unjust. For what these men wickedly and blasphemously assert, those men religiously and piously overthrow, and they do so when they agree with these madmen on this point.

units.la: Adfontem Xanthi versa recurret aqua.
units.tr: Back to the source of Xanthus the water will run.

units.la: Quodsi fi insanis consequentiis aliorum innocentiam tibi libet obruere, quid nos prohibebit fanis ratiocinationibus vos urgere & ad incitas Pelagianorum redigere? Damnata Pelagianorum hæresis est, Nos ESSE AUCTORES SALUTIS NOSTRÆ, Damnata est no modo a prisca ecclesia, verum etiam decreto illustrisf. ac potentisf. Hollandiæ ac Westfrisiæ ordinum recens vetita. Ita enim illi salubèrrimè decreverunt: Rebus diu multumque perpensis, religioseque & circumspecte examinatis singulis, quæ in colloquio duodecim pastorum Anno 1611. nostro conventu ore primum perata, mox etiam cum ipsorum consiliis perscripta, nobisque tradita fuere: usi ea auctoritate, quæ nobis, ut summis legitimis potestatibus juxta sanctum Dei verbum eorumque Regum, principum, ac civitatum quæ reformationem religionis amplexa sunt, exempla, competit, imperavimus atque etiamnum imperamus, ut in memoratis modo interpretationibus diligenter quisque attendat ad sancti Pauli apostoli monitum, docentis, ne quis supra modum sapiat ultra quam oportet sapere, sed sapiat ad sobrietatem, prout cuique Deus partitus est mensuram fidei: & id quod passim tradunt sacra litera, salutem quidem nostram ex Deo solo esse, at nos
units.tr: But if you wish to overwhelm the innocence of others with your insane consequences, what will prevent us from pressing you with sound reasoning and driving you back into the camp of the Pelagians? The heresy of the Pelagians is condemned, the one that says that WE ARE THE AUTHORS OF OUR OWN SALVATION. It has been condemned not only by the ancient Church but also recently forbidden by the decree of the most illustrious and powerful Lords States of Holland and West Friesland. For they decided most wholesomely as follows: Having long and carefully weighed, and religiously and circumspectly examined, each of the points which were first spoken at the conference of twelve ministers in our assembly in the year 1611, then also written out with their counsel and handed to us, we, using that authority which belongs to us as the supreme lawful powers according to the holy Word of God and the examples of their kings, princes and cities which have embraced the reformation of religion, have commanded and still command that everyone diligently attend, in the aforesaid interpretations, to the admonition of the holy apostle Paul, who teaches that no one should think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but should think soberly, as God has dealt to each the measure of faith; and that what the holy Scriptures everywhere teach, namely that our salvation is indeed from God alone, but we

units.la: D. 2 nobis
units.tr: D. 2 nobis

units.la: § 1. Cap. V.
units.tr: § 1. Chapter V.

units.la: nobis ipsis perniciem accerserte at proinde inex, plicandis sacris literis quoties ita feret occasio, pastores infigent populo singulorumque sub no- stro imperio habitantium animis principium, progressum ac finem humanae salutis atque ita- pfam adeo fidem non nativis hominum viribus aut factis, sed sola promerita Dei in re- Christo servatore nostro gratia accepta ferri debere. &c. Contra hoc sapientissimum il- luftrium ordinum decretum docetis homi- nem esse auctorem suae salutis, si consequē- tiis res fit agenda, ex quibus, quum id mihi non fit propositum, duxit unam hicap- pono:
units.tr: ...to bring destruction upon themselves. But therefore, whenever the occasion requires in expounding the sacred letters, ministers shall fix in the minds of the people, and of all who live under our rule, that the beginning, progress and end of human salvation, and faith itself, are to be ascribed not to natural human powers or works, but to the sole merit of God and the grace received in Christ our Saviour. etc. Against this most wise decree of the illustrious orders, you teach that man is the author of his own salvation, if the matter is to be treated by consequences. Since that is not my purpose here, I set down just one such argument:

units.la: Quirem aliquam procurat, is rei est auctor & causa.
units.tr: Whoever procures something is the author and cause of that thing.

units.la: Atqui homo procurat salutem suam.
units.tr: But man procures his own salvation.

units.la: Ergo homo est auctor salutis suae.
units.tr: Therefore man is the author of his salvation.

units.la: Hinc alia nascitur consequentia.
units.tr: From this another consequence arises.

units.la: Si homo est auctor salutis suae, falsum est quod decreverit ordines Hollandiae & Weft- frifiae, solum Deum esse au- &torem salutis humanae.
units.tr: If man is the author of his salvation, then it is false that the orders of Holland and West Friesland have decreed that God alone is the author of human salvation.

units.la: Atqui abfurdifimum est post erius, nec di- &edum, Ergo & prius, quod ex vestris principiis sequitur. Nam utraq; praemissa prio-ris syllogismi est D. Vorstii. Major quidem exstat in amica illius collatione cum D. Piscatore Herbornae edita sect. 68. pagin. 123 Sane, inquit, quisquis rem aliquam procurat (& sic quidem, ut ipsa res tandem infallibiliter fiat; imo non fieri non possit) ii rei procurata auctor & causa, nō immerito vocatur. Nam quid aliud reipsa est, rem aliquam procurare, quam curare ac studere, sive operam dare ut res fiat. Et post pauca: Quid fictitium discrimen inter rei procuratorem & auctorem hic prodesse potest? Minor vero etiam legitur apud eundem in eadem amica collatione p. 193. Sed alia, inquit, est ratio eorum, quae ipse sic in nobis efficere vult, ut simul a nobis libere aliquid fieri postulet: sive ita ut liberem assensionem, ac cooperationem nostram simul requirat. Cujusmodi est fides & conversio nostra, & denique tota salutis aeternae in nobis procuratio.
units.tr: But the latter is most absurd and must not be said; therefore the former too, which follows from your principles. For both premises of the first syllogism are from Vorstius. The major indeed stands in his friendly conference with Piscator, published at Herborn, sect. 68, p. 123: "Surely," he says, "whoever procures something (and indeed in such a way that the thing itself is at last infallibly done, indeed cannot fail to be done) is rightly called the author and cause of what is procured. For what else is procuring a thing in fact, than caring for and striving after it, or giving effort that the thing may come about." And after a few words: "What fictitious distinction between the procurer of a thing and its author can help here?" The minor is read in the same friendly conference, p. 193: "But another," he says, "is the case of those things which he wishes to effect in us in such a way that at the same time he requires something to be done freely by us: namely, that he requires our free assent and cooperation together. Of this kind are faith and our conversion, and finally the whole procuring of eternal salvation in us."

units.la: Quam belle haec cum illustrium ordinum decreto conveniant, judicet lector qui videt ad procurationem salutis nostrae requiri nostram cooperationem. Quanquam nos non negemus hominem regeneratum simul agere actum a spiritu Dei. Sed quid opus est consequentia & iis, quae ante decretum hoc edita sunt? Annon tu ipse postilla audacissime dispescis humanam salu-tem temin inter Deum & hominem ? verba tua sunt. Ipse etiam Tu culpans id quod dixeram, non oportere nos comminisci fedus eusmodi in quo solus Deus agat omnia, ita scribis. Hoc vero redolet ignorantiam discriminis ejus quod est inter fœdus naturæ & gratiæ. Qua-sificilicet naturæ fœdus sit. Ego hæc a vobis exi-go ut faciatis, & permitto facientibus præmium. Gratia vero fœdus sit, Ego a vobis nihil exigo, sed ipse vobis dabo atque instillabo, principium progressum, finem, i. e. præmium, eaque omnia quæ ad præmium pertinent, quorum nihil habet rationem causæ: sunt enim omnia consata-lia : & vos ad illa quum plane mortui sitis, nihil potestis. Quædam hic agnosco veris-sima, quædam tanquam tua καταλλαγὴ re-seco. Vere enim hæc est distinctio fœderis naturæ & gratiæ, quod illud promittat vi-tam, si legem propriis naturæ nostræ viribus præstemus: hoc vero eandem polliceatur, si evangelio credamus, non fide ex nostris viribus suscitata, sed ex sola Dei gratia con-cepta. Fidem enim Dei donum esse nosti, & quidem non ex morali suasione, ut col-latio Hagensis vult, aut Spiritus Casistentia, ut placet Arnoldo, sed, ut recte fatetur in declaratione sententiæ suæ de prædestina-tione Arminius, ex infusione, & hujus prin-cipium, progressum ac finem non nobis sed sola Deo, rectissimè ascribunt illustrissimi ordines. Tuum verò & frivolum est quod eorum nihil quæ ad primum pertinent, habeat rationem causæ, sed omnia sint confatalia. Etenim scimus mortem & passionem Christi esse causam meritoriam præmii, fidem vero nostram esse quidè ejus causam ut instrumentalem. Verum de his alibi plenius agendi locus erit: tu verò interea neminem condemna, te qui nondum vidit
units.tr: How well these agree with the decree of the illustrious orders, let the reader judge, who sees that for the procuring of our salvation our cooperation is required. Yet we do not deny that the regenerate man at the same time acts, moved by the Spirit of God. But why do we need consequences and things published before this decree? Do you not yourself, in your Postil, most boldly divide human salvation between God and man? Those are your words. You yourself, blaming what I had said, that we ought not to devise a covenant of this kind in which God alone works all things, write thus: "This smells of ignorance of the distinction between the covenant of nature and that of grace. As if, forsooth, the covenant of nature were this: I demand these things from you, and I grant a reward to those who do them. But the covenant of grace is this: I demand nothing from you, but I myself will give and instil into you the beginning, progress and end, that is, the reward, and all those things which pertain to the reward, none of which has the character of a cause, for they are all fated together (confatalia); and you, since you are wholly dead to them, can do nothing." Some things here I acknowledge as most true, and some I cut away as your reconciliation [καταλλαγή]. For it is true that this is the distinction between the covenant of nature and that of grace: the former promises life if we perform the law by the powers of our nature; the latter promises the same if we believe the gospel, not with faith raised up by our own powers, but conceived from the sole grace of God. For you know that faith is the gift of God, and indeed not from moral persuasion, as the Hague collation wants, nor from the presence of the Spirit, as Arnoldus pleases, but, as Arminius rightly confesses in his declaration of opinion on predestination, from infusion. The illustrious orders most rightly ascribe its beginning, progress and end not to us but to God alone. Your claim that none of those things which pertain to the first has the character of a cause, but all are confatalia, is both trifling and vain. For we know that the death and passion of Christ are the meritorious cause of the reward, and our faith is indeed its instrumental cause. But there will be a place to treat these matters more fully elsewhere. Meanwhile you, condemn no one, you who have not yet seen yourself...

units.la: Pratorem in curribus altis Exstantem, et medio sublimem in pulvere circi Iuvenica Iovis, & pictâ serrana ferentem Ex humeris aulaea toga, magnaque corona Tantum orbem, quanto cervix non sufficit ulla.
units.tr: The praetor standing aloft in high chariots, raised in the middle of the dust of the circus, like Jove's bull-calf, bearing on his shoulders a toga embroidered with pictures and a great crown, a sphere so vast that no neck is strong enough to bear it.

units.la: CAP. VI. Quod non omnia absoluta necessitate gerantur.
units.tr: CHAP. VI. That not all things happen by absolute necessity.

units.la: INter scholasticos doctores Johannes Duns Scotus, quem divinus Scaliger lumen veritatis appellat, exerc. 224. sapienter pronunciavit, eos qui negant contingentiam & clamant omnia necessariò fieri, tormentis esse exponendos, & tandiu cruciandos, donec concedant possibile esse, se non torqueri, lib. 1. sent. dist. 39. Qui enim negat ens rectè dividi in necessarium & contingens, is non tantùm sacræ scripturæ & & recte rationi, sed & communi hominum sensui & experientiae adversatur. Ideo & Scaliger Cardanum id non advertentē mes rito ridet, exerc. 39. Distinguuntur, inquiens, esse ntiis integris contingens & necessariis, Sicut per se & per accidens & ab alio. Quae sunt primaria notiones entis apud divinam philosophum: cuius te nugarum (hic enim vocas) si alumnus esse, tuus iste fastidii plenissimus contemtus non peperisset tam monstrosam sententiam. Sed & tu, doctissime Berti, doctrina ecclesiae de voluntate Dei notas, quod omnem tollat libertatem & contingentiam.
units.tr: Among the scholastic teachers, John Duns Scotus, whom the divine Scaliger calls the light of truth, wisely declared (Exerc. 224) that those who deny contingency and cry out that everything happens of necessity should be put to the torture, and tortured until they concede that it is possible that they themselves are not being tortured (Lib. 1, Sent. dist. 39). For whoever denies that being is rightly divided into the necessary and the contingent opposes not only Holy Scripture and sound reason but also the common sense and experience of mankind. So Scaliger rightly mocks Cardan for not noticing this: Exerc. 39. "Contingent and necessary," he says, "are distinguished by integral notions, as through itself, through accident, and from another. These are the primary notions of being among the divine philosophers. If you were a pupil of this nugatory (for so you call it) philosophy, your disdainful and utterly contemptuous attitude would not have produced such a monstrous opinion." But you too, most learned Bertius, notice that the doctrine of the Church concerning the will of God removes all freedom and contingency.

units.la: At fructra. Etsi enim Deus omnia praescit, quae in mundo bona & mala geruntur, & quidem infallibiliter; tamen falsum est omniageri ex divina & fatali necessitate five coactione, qua omnis proxerefis & libertas creaturis eripiatur. Quid enim hoc aliud esset quam ordinem rerum evertere? Et verò quemadmodum supra de voluntate Dei disputatum est, nihil libertati aut contingentiae five mutabilitati rerum creatarum decedit, quae quum habent causas liberas & contingentes, liberae sunt & contingentes, quum vero habent causas necessarias sunt necessariae. Utraque autem divinae gubernationi subjacent. Necessariae, ut liquet ex Job. 5, v. 10, & 37, v. 5. Psal. 104. Contingentes.
units.tr: But this is false. For although God foreknows infallibly all the good and evil things that are done in the world, it is nonetheless false that everything happens from divine and fatal necessity or compulsion, by which all free choice [προαίρεσις] and liberty would be snatched from creatures. For what would this be other than overturning the order of things? Indeed, as was argued above concerning the will of God, nothing is taken from the liberty, contingency, or mutability of created things. Things that have free and contingent causes are free and contingent; things that have necessary causes are necessary. Both, however, are subject to divine government. The necessary ones, as is clear from Job 5:10 and 37:5, and Psalm 104. Contingent ones.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: tes ac liberæ, ut patet, Job. 1. v. 21. Prov. 16. 1. 33. Matth. 19. 29. 30. Gen. 45. 8. & 50. 20: Esa. 10. v. 5. Thren. 3. 37. & alibi passim. Quod de libero arbitrio obiicis ex Luthero, id non valet contra nos, sed contra pontificios, & synergistas, qui in primo momento conversionis salutaris liberi arbitrii cooperationem asserunt, contra quos Lutherus emphaticè disputat, licet alicubi hyperbolicè, ut fit in calore, animi sensa elo-quatur, & omne in universum creaturis arbitrium adimere videatur. Decet autem fratres ad interpretationem scriptorum a fratribus editorum optimâ interpretandi ma‐giftram charitatem afferre & æquitate cum studio veritatis conjungere. Hæc jubet nos modestè considerare quod de veteribus scribit Sixtus Senensis in præfatio lib. 5. bibliothecæ: Veteres dum unum errorem omnium vitium conatu destruere annituntur, sape in alterum errorem vel deciderunt vel quodammodo decidisse videntur agricolarum more, qui incurvum tenera arboris stipitem corrigere nolentes, immodica nonnunquam attractione modum excedunt, plantamque in contrariam diversamque deducunt formam. Ea in his moderatione opus est, quam nos Anselmus docet in 2. ad Corinth. In libris sanctorum doctorum, quos authentice legit ecclesia, nonnunquam inveniunveniuntur prava vel haeretica; non tamen pro his vel libri vel auctores damnantur. Dictum Calvini, quod ex lib. 3. inst. cap. 23. §. 6. citas, ibi nō legitur, attamen facilem & commodam admittit interpretationem secundum ea, quae supra diximus. Omnia quae fiunt, inquit, Dei voluntate fiunt et decreto. An tu hoc negare nō erubescis? Certe quidem de voluntate ac decreto peccata vel approbante, vel efficiente, vel jubente vel quocunq; modo suadente id non affirmo: at de permittente peccata, & res omnes ordinante ac gubernante ne tu quidem ipse alibi negasti, nec D. Vorstius negat, qui parefactionem divinae gloriae fundat in decreto peccatum permittendi, in amica collatione sect. 65. Quid ergo impietatis est in dicto? ex bernante ejusd. 2 capitis 55,8. notas quod Calvinus cum Augustino asserit, voluntatem Dei esse rerum necessitatem. Id commode explanat idem verbis continenter adjectis.
units.tr: ...contingent and free, as is evident from Job 1:21, Prov. 16:1, 33, Matt. 19:29–30, Gen. 45:8 and 50:20, Isa. 10:5, Lam. 3:37, and passim elsewhere. What you object from Luther about free will does not tell against us, but against the Papists and the synergists, who assert the cooperation of free will in the first moment of saving conversion. Luther disputes emphatically against them, although sometimes hyperbolically, as happens when, in the heat of feeling, he expresses his sentiments, and he seems to take away all will from creatures altogether. Yet brothers, in interpreting writings edited by brothers, ought to bring charity, the best guide to interpretation, and join fairness to zeal for the truth. This bids us consider modestly what Sixtus of Siena writes about the ancients in the preface to book 5 of his Bibliotheca: The ancients, while they strive to destroy one error with the effort of opposing every fault, have often either fallen into another error or seem in some way to have fallen into it, like farmers who, unwilling to straighten a crooked stem of a young tree, sometimes pull too hard, exceed the proper measure, and bend the plant into a contrary and different shape. In this matter moderation is needed, which Anselm teaches us on 2 Corinthians: In the books of the holy doctors, which the Church reads as authentic, things that are false or heretical are sometimes found; yet neither the books nor their authors are condemned on account of these. The saying of Calvin that you cite from Institutes 3.23.6 is not read there, yet it admits an easy and convenient interpretation in line with what we said above. "All things that come to pass," he says, "come to pass by the will and decree of God. Do you not blush to deny this?" Certainly I do not affirm that sins are approved, effected, commanded or urged by God's will and decree in any way; but as for God permitting sins and ordering and governing all things, you yourself have nowhere denied it, nor does Vorstius deny it, who founds the manifestation of the divine glory on the decree to permit sin, in the friendly conference, section 65. What, then, is impious in the saying? From the discussion of governance (book 2, chapter 5, §8) you may note that Calvin, with Augustine, asserts that the will of God is the necessity of things. He explains this aptly in the words that follow immediately.

units.la: Non dubitabo igitur cum Augustino simpliciter fateri, voluntatem Dei esse rerum necessitatem, atque id necessario futurum esse quod ille voluerit: quaecunque ea vere futura sunt, quae praviderit. Haec puto omnibus cordatis viris dicenda & concedenda esse.
units.tr: I will not hesitate, therefore, to confess simply with Augustine that the will of God is the necessity of things, and that whatever he has willed will necessarily come to pass, whatever those things are that he has foreseen will truly be. I think this must be said and conceded by all men of sound judgment.

units.la: Quemadmodum enim rerum contingentia praecipue est ab indeterminata atque indifferendifferente voluntaris divinæ libertate, ita & omnium rerum creatarum necessitatem quam in incomplexis hypotheticam, in complexis vero alias absolutam, alias hypotheticam deprehendimus, a sapiente ac justa ejusdem determinatione dependere judico.
units.tr: For just as the contingency of things arises chiefly from the undetermined and indifferent liberty of the divine will, so I judge that the necessity of all created things, which we find in incomplex propositions as hypothetical, and in complex propositions sometimes absolute and sometimes hypothetical, depends on his wise and just determination.

units.la: Tentabo an clarius possim per exempla hoc eloqui. Mundum creari erat contingens, quia Deus esset in se beatissimus, licet mundum non creasset. Deus enim creationem ita libere voluit, ut potuerit etiam nolle per voluntatis suæ indifferentiam.
units.tr: I shall try whether I can express this more clearly through examples. That the world was created was contingent, because God was most blessed in himself even if he had not created the world. For God willed creation so freely that, through the indifference of his will, he could also have been unwilling.

units.la: Mundum creatum esse, Christum esse missum mundi redemptorem, Deum pœnitentium peccatorum misereri, necessarium est ex hypothesi, quia sapiente consilio Deus hæc libera voluntate sua decreminavit. Homo est animal rationale, est propositio absolutè necessaria, quia hominem esse, qui aut non sit animal, aut non sit rationalis implicat contradictionem, quæ in sinu Dei nec est necesse potest. Hæc necessitas non est ex eo, quod vel subjectum sit ens necessarium, vel prædicatum, vel utrumque, sed ex eo quod perpetua et necessaria est connexio aut disjunctio inter subjectum et prædicatum, secundum omnes temporis differentias, nempe præsens, præteritum et futurum. Ab aliis vocatur necessitas connexonis rerum enunciativæ. Omnia quidé entia necessitatis hypotheticæ excepto Deo in entibus incomplexis quantum ad essentiam attinet, quæ ex absoluta naturæ suæ necessitate agit, hæc tamen enunciata, quæ absolutè necessaria dicimus necessitatem hypotheticam non admittunt, quia necessitas absoluta in ente complexo seu enunciato excludit omnem contingentiam; quam tamen necessitas hypothetica includit, & oritur vel ex principio externo, quod est finis aut efficiens, vel accidens quoddam entis separabile &c. Ita necessariæ sunt propositiones. ¹ Omnes mortui resurgent. Deus enim sic decrevit. ² Quidam homines servantur. Nam credunt in Christum. ³ Quidam homines damnantur. Nam non credunt in Christum. ⁴ Homines credunt in Christum. Voluntatem enim servari. ⁵ Homines Deo puniuntur. Quotidie enim peccant. ⁶ Homines discunt. Volunt enim evadere docti. &c. Idem Calvinus cum Augustino etiam voluisse videtur. Quod denique ex Zuinglii libro de providentia dicitur, solum Deum agere et caussare reliqua omnia esse duntaxat instrumenta agentis, Id licet de actionibus bonis creaturarum assereretur (de peccatis enim proprie dictis aliter judicandum est) tamen libertas & contin-
units.tr: That the world has been created, that Christ has been sent as the Redeemer of the world, and that God shows mercy to repentant sinners, is necessary by hypothesis, because God, by his wise counsel, decreed these things by his free will. "Man is a rational animal" is an absolutely necessary proposition, because for a man to be either not an animal or not rational implies a contradiction, which cannot even exist in the bosom of God. This necessity does not arise from the subject being a necessary being, or from the predicate, or from both, but from the fact that the connection or disjunction between subject and predicate is perpetual and necessary, across all differences of time, namely present, past and future. By others it is called the necessity of the enunciative connection of things. Indeed, all beings except God have hypothetical necessity in their incomplex essence, since God acts from the absolute necessity of his own nature; yet these enunciations, which we call absolutely necessary, do not admit hypothetical necessity, because absolute necessity in a complex being or enunciated proposition excludes all contingency, whereas hypothetical necessity includes it, and arises either from an external principle, which is an end or an efficient cause, or from some separable accident of the being, and so on. Thus the following propositions are necessary: (1) All the dead will rise, for God has so decreed. (2) Some men are saved, for they believe in Christ. (3) Some men are damned, for they do not believe in Christ. (4) Men believe in Christ, for they will to be saved. (5) Men are punished by God, for they sin every day. (6) Men learn, for they wish to become learned, and so on. Calvin seems also to have held the same as Augustine. As for what is said from Zwingli's book on providence, that God alone acts and causes all things, and that all the rest are merely instruments of the agent: although this is asserted of the good actions of creatures (for sins, properly so called, must be judged otherwise), nevertheless liberty and contingency

units.la: contingentia rerum obtineretur, quoniam vos ipsi asseritis, Deum nihil extra se agere ex absoluta natura necessitate, sed omnia libere, quae de re vide disputationes D. Vorstii de Deo, notas, exegeses, amicam collationem & alia scripta. Praeterea quod Zuinglius de creaturis docet eas agere tanquam instrumenta Dei, id commode explicare potes cum Beza de praedeft. contra Castellionem p. 374. Nos vero, inquit ille, contra, ne vel Deo infi-nitam et immensam potestatem eripiamus et cum Epicureis sententiamus, dicimus, quod res est, Deus nihil nisi volente vel agere per instrumenta, vel permittere instrumentis utagunt, ita tamen ut justissime agat quicquid agit & justissime permittat, quicquid permittit. Sed de his satis, ubi prius in signem locum Philippi Melanchthonis de libertate humani arbitrii appoluerimus, quem D. Pezelius in loco de viribus liberi arbitrii ex libello de formandis concionibus allegavit pag. 311.
units.tr: …the contingency of things would be preserved, since you yourselves assert that God does nothing outside himself from absolute natural necessity, but all things freely. On this matter see the disputations of Dr. Vorstius on God, his notes, exegeses, friendly conference and other writings. Further, what Zwingli teaches about creatures, that they act as instruments of God, you can conveniently explain with Beza, On Predestination, against Castellio, p. 374: "We, however," he says, "on the contrary, lest we snatch from God his infinite and immense power and side with the Epicureans, say that the case is this: God does nothing except by willing it, either to act through instruments, or to permit the instruments to act as they do, yet so that he most justly does whatever he does and most justly permits whatever he permits." But enough of these things. Let us first set down the following passage of Philip Melanchthon on the liberty of the human will, which Dr. Pezel cited in his locus on the powers of free will from his little book on forming sermons, p. 311.

units.la: Magna quaestio est: Num sit in homine liberum arbitrium, quo se comparat ad gratiam? Verum nos sic sentimus: fidem non nostris viribus parari, sed esse summum & maximum Spiritus opus & donum, neque posse ita omnibus Dei verbis assentiri cor, nisi divina vi excitetur. Sic David orat: Crea in me Deus cor mundum. Spiritus sancti.
units.tr: There is a great question: whether there is in man a free will by which he prepares himself for grace. But we think thus: faith is not prepared by our own powers, but is the highest and greatest work and gift of the Holy Spirit, nor can the heart assent in this way to all the words of God unless it is stirred by divine power. Thus David prays: "Create in me a clean heart, O God." Of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: hæc sine verbo statueret Ezechias, insanus merito videri queat. Et apparet mundum nihil aliud judicare fidem, quàm insaniam & furorem ex vino conceptum. Habet autem Ezechias verbum, illi inniti tur contra omnem rationem & sensum, adeo prorsus immutatur & novatur cor. Neq; est quod putemus nostris viribus effici fidem, quum ea omnes nostras vires & excellentissima in homine dona vincat & mutet. Spiritus sanctus primò cognitione peccati terret atque timnos; post cum desperatione luctantibus verbum aliquod offert, quod ita animis imprimit, ut ceu in lapides impressæ notæ, evelli denuò non possint. Illud verbum sic est in corde efficax, ut Satanam, peccatum, mortem, & quicquid malorum est, vincat. In hac Melanchtoniana, imò divina simplicitate lubens acquiesco: arbitrium humanum, sic assero, ut gratiam non deseram; gratiæ sic omnia tribuo, ut arbitrio nec nimium nec parum. Utinam in hac acquiesavisset cum Arminio Arnoldus, utiq; contra Tilenum non scripsisset p. 337. Arminii sententia est: Gratiam non ita instruere hominem novis viribus, quin semper maneat in hominis potestate ut uti vel non uti. Utinam in hac acquievisent Remonstrantes, & non scripsissent in collatione Hagensi p.
units.tr: Ezekiah, if he established these things without the Word, could rightly seem mad, and it appears that the world judges faith to be nothing but madness and frenzy born of wine. But Ezekiah has the Word, and he leans on it against all reason and sense, so completely is the heart changed and renewed. Nor have we reason to think that faith is brought about by our own powers, since it overcomes and transforms all our powers and the most excellent gifts found in man. The Holy Spirit first terrifies and frightens with the knowledge of sin; then, to those struggling in despair, He offers some word which so imprints itself on the minds that, like marks pressed into stones, it cannot be torn out again. That word is so effective in the heart that it conquers Satan, sin, death, and whatever evil there is. I gladly rest in this Melanchthonian, or rather divine, simplicity: I so assert the human will that I do not desert grace, and I so ascribe all things to grace that I give nothing too much or too little to the will. Would that Arnoldus had rested in this with Arminius, and had not written against Tilenus at p. 337. The opinion of Arminius is this: that grace does not so furnish man with new powers that it always remains in man's power to use or not to use it. Would that the Remonstrants had rested in this, and not written in the Hague conference at p.

units.la: Etiamsi credere Dei donum appelletur, nihil hoc ad praesente materiam facit, nisi probetur omne donum dari per infusionem & irrefragabiliter, quod res ipsa docet esse absurdum, & cum experientia pugnat. Nam praeceptor dat discipulo scientiam linguarum, discipulus eam accipit, verum non irrefragabiliter: dat aliquis eleemosynam, quam tamen amicus renuit accipere. Quanto melius ipse Arminius in declaratione sententiae suae de providentia, de libero arbitrio, de quo gratia Dei judicat? pag. 205, 206. Utinam tu ipse in ea tandem acquiesceres, & forte cessares imitari Democritum, qui perpetuo risu pulmonem agitare solebat, atque irridere, quod alicubi scripsit: Quod in ista admirabilitate non capit ratio, capiat fides. Sed de hoc alias: nunc corollarii vice quaedam hic adjiciam, ex Calvini, Bezae & aliorum Dei fervorum sententia, ut perspicue intelligas quid sit permissione etiam circa peccata ociosam esse negant, quae negatio illis duplicem apud incompositae mentis homines calumniam peperisse videtur; alteram, quod Deum auctorem peccatorum asserant: alteram quod humanam suam libertatem & ad oppositam indifferentiam eripiant. Quae utraque calumnia est calumniosissima et vanissima, ut patebit lectori ex sequentibus observa-tionibus.
units.tr: Even if faith is called a gift of God, this does nothing for the present matter, unless it is proved that every gift is given by infusion and irrefutably, which the thing itself shows to be absurd and at odds with experience. For a teacher gives a pupil knowledge of languages, and the pupil receives it, but not irrefutably; someone gives alms, which nevertheless a friend refuses to accept. How much better would Arminius himself have done in his declaration of his opinion on providence and free will, concerning which the grace of God judges! See pp. 205, 206. Would that you yourself at last rested in that, and perhaps ceased to imitate Democritus, who used to shake his lungs with perpetual laughter and to mock what he wrote somewhere: "What reason does not grasp in this wonder, let faith grasp." But of this elsewhere. Now, by way of a corollary, I shall add here some points from the opinion of Calvin, Beza and other zealous servants of God, so that you may clearly understand what they deny: that permission is idle even with regard to sins. This denial seems to have brought them a double slander among men of unsettled mind: first, that they assert God to be the author of sins; second, that they snatch away human freedom and the indifference to the opposite. Both of these slanders are most calumnious and most empty, as will be clear to the reader from the observations that follow.

units.la: VOLVNTAS DIVINA NON est prorsus ociosa in actionibus peccantium, sed per has quoq; ostendit testimonia sua.
units.tr: The divine will is not entirely idle in the actions of sinners, but through these also it shows its evidences.

units.la: SAPIENTIÆ.
units.tr: Of Wisdom.

units.la: 1. Malis enim voluntatibus impiorum bene utitur.
units.tr: 1. For he makes good use of the evil wills of the impious.

units.la: 2. Mala quæ ipsi faciunt male, ad optimos fines convertit servientes suæ gloriæ & electorum saluti atque ita ostendens se per contraria, & ubi minimè cogitare potest sapientia aut ratio humana, sua opera perficit.
units.tr: 2. The evils they themselves do, he turns to the best ends, serving his own glory and the salvation of the elect. Thus he shows himself through contraries, and accomplishes his work where human wisdom or reason can least expect it.

units.la: BONITATIS.
units.tr: Of Goodness.

units.la: 1. Sustentat enim impiorum substantiam sive essentiam.
units.tr: 1. For he sustains the substance or essence of the impious.

units.la: 2. Servat potentiam & modum agendi in creatione ipsis attributum, quo differt creatura rationalis à natura bruta; ut videlicet quicquid agant, etiam dum maximè peccant, spontaneo tamen ac libero motu sine coactione agant & volentes peccata agant, iisque sponte indulgeant.
units.tr: 2. He preserves the power and mode of acting given to them in creation, by which a rational creature differs from brute nature. So whatever they do, even while sinning most grievously, they act by a spontaneous and free motion, without compulsion, and they commit sins willingly and indulge in them of their own accord.

units.la: 3. Concurrit ad actiones malas, at concursus ille est ad actum, quà talis, non quà peccatum. quia peccatum est. Etsi autem hic concur-sus fit positus in miro Dei arbitrio: tamen illam nunquam denegat creaturæ rationali & liberę, quando ejus potentiæ & voluntatiactum permisit.
units.tr: 3. He concurs in evil actions, but that concurrence is to the act as such, not as sin, because it is sin. Although this concurrence is placed in God's wondrous decree, he never denies it to the rational and free creature when he has permitted the act to its power and will.

units.la: Justitiæ ac severitatis.
units.tr: Of Justice and Severity.

units.la: 1. Impedimentum enim ponit vel potestati per legislationem, vel potentiæ per essentiæ & vitæ ablationem aut per potentiæ majoris vel saltem æqualis oppositionem, aut per objecti subductionem aut per potentiæ ablationem seu diminutionem: vel denique voluntati per divinam persuasionem & spiritus sui illuminationem.
units.tr: 1. For he places an impediment either to the faculty, through law; or to the power, by taking away life and being, or by opposing a greater or at least equal power, or by withdrawing the object, or by removing or diminishing the power; or finally to the will, through divine persuasion and the illumination of his Spirit.

units.la: 2. Permittit quamdiu vult voluntates impiorum malas esse, id est, non convertit voluntates impiorum, ut velint bonum seu Deo placens, sed omnia impedimenta quæ potentiæ aut voluntati objici possunt, suspendit.
units.tr: 2. He permits the wills of the impious to remain evil for as long as he wills. That is, he does not convert their wills so that they will the good, or what is pleasing to God, but he suspends all the hindrances that can be set against their power or will.

units.la: 3. Permittit i.e. non impedit malos perseverare in sua malicia.
units.tr: 3. He permits, that is, he does not prevent the wicked from persisting in their malice.

units.la: 4. Tradit suis cupiditatibus in ignominiam ipsorum, id est, ut magis magisque confirmentur in sua malicia & ex peccatis in peccata ruant.
units.tr: 4. He hands them over to their lusts, to their own shame; that is, so that they are more and more confirmed in their malice and fall from sins into sins.

units.la: 4. Tradit diabolo impellendos qui est efficax in filiis incredulitatis. 5. Etiam tum quàdo per ipsos sua opera peragit non ostendit eis voluntatem suam, neq; flectit voluntates ipsorum ad obtem-perandum ipsi.
units.tr: 4. He hands over to the devil those who are to be driven on, the devil being effective in the sons of unbelief. 5. Even when through them he carries out his works, he does not reveal his will to them, nor does he bend their wills to obey him.

units.la: MISERICORDIÆ.
units.tr: Of Mercy

units.la: 1. Inhibet enim malorum conatus quæ-retium <bl>πανοληπτων</bl> piorum, servat ecclesiam & mirabiliter ducit per mala sanctos suos.
units.tr: 1. For he restrains the schemes of the wicked [πανούργων] against the godly, preserves the Church, and wonderfully leads his holy ones through evils.

units.la: 2. Quosdam ex impiis in medio cursu impietatis vocat ad poenitentiam & efficaciter convertit, ut Nabuchodonosorum, Paulum, alios.
units.tr: 2. He calls some of the ungodly, in the midst of their course of impiety, to repentance and effectively converts them, as he did Nebuchadnezzar, Paul, and others.

units.la: 3. Sanctos etiam lapsos castigat & erudit malis.
units.tr: 3. He also chastises and instructs fallen saints with afflictions.

units.la: POTENTIÆ.
units.tr: POTENTIA.

units.la: 1. Ponit enim metas malitiæ & furoribus malorum.
units.tr: 1. For he sets limits to wickedness and to the rage of the wicked.

units.la: 2. Arcana seu occulta gubernatione sua dirigit etiam malas ipsorum voluntates, non inferens novam malitiam, non cogens, sed inclinas ut hoc potius quàm alio loco, tempore & modo & in hanc potius quàm in illam personam aut rem libere feruntur, & in deliberatione de suis factis hanc potius quàm alteram partem eligant.
units.tr: 2. By his hidden or secret government he also directs their evil wills, not by inferring new malice and not by compelling them, but by inclining them so that they freely turn to this place rather than another, to this time and manner, and to this person or thing rather than that, and in deliberating about their deeds they choose this side rather than the other.

units.la: 3. Præbet occasiones & objecta vel appetenda vel fugienda, quæ eo pertinent, ut Deus suum opus etiam per impios efficiat.
units.tr: 3. He presents occasions and objects, either to be sought or to be avoided, which serve to bring about that God accomplishes his work even through the impious.

units.la: 4. Reprimit poenitentiam ubi vult reprimere, & memorabilibus exemplis vindictae suę ipsorum scelera ulciscitur.
units.tr: 4. He restrains repentance where he wills to restrain it, and by memorable examples he avenges their crimes by his own vengeance.

units.la: Haec fere sunt illa, Berti, quae Dei voluntatem circa peccata creaturarum non sint ut plane ociosam fingere. Ex his tamen omnibus nulla peccati culpa Deo tribui potest: sed Deus in his ostendit testimonia suę sapientiae malis instrumentis bene utendo & mala convertendo in bonum. Ita enim ostendit se sapientiorem hostibus suis, qui contra ipsorum consilia suos servat, atque iis ipsis medius quibus se munire & Dei gloriam impedire conabuntur ipsos perdet, atque ex tenebris lucem producere possit. Bonitatis in sustentatione etiam impiorum, in quibus servat suum opus, quatenus ex creatione est reliquum. Et servat ad optimos fines, ut spatium poenitentiae impiis concedat: ut pertinaces severe puniat, idque eo justius, quod impii spontaneo suo & voluntario motu peccata appetant & admittant: ut per ignavos denique aut etiam invitos opera sua in genere humano nonnunquam peragat. 3 Iustitiae gratiam suam subtrahens, id est, ex malis voluntatibus non faciens bonas: sed quales ex corruptione naturae sunt tales relinquens: item non dirigens cogitationes & voluntates impiorum ut hoc spectent.
units.tr: These, Berti, are roughly those things which we should not imagine as God's will concerning the sins of creatures as wholly idle. Yet from all these things no guilt of sin can be attributed to God; rather, in these things God shows the evidence of his wisdom, in using evil instruments well and turning evil into good. For thus he shows himself wiser than his enemies: he preserves his own people against their counsels, and by the very means through which they try to fortify themselves and hinder the glory of God, he destroys them, and he is able to bring light out of darkness. Goodness: in the sustaining even of the impious, in whom he preserves his work insofar as what remains from creation. And he preserves them for the best ends: that he may grant the impious a space for repentance; that he may severely punish the obstinate, and that all the more justly, because the impious desire and commit sins by their own spontaneous and voluntary motion; and finally, that he may at times carry out his work in the human race through the slothful or even the unwilling. 3 Justice: by withdrawing his grace, that is, by not making evil wills good, but leaving them such as they are from the corruption of nature; likewise by not directing the thoughts and wills of the impious toward this end.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAP. VI.
