units.la: spectent, quod Deo est propositum, quum per eos bonum suum opus vult peragere: interea etiam tradens eos suis ipsorum cupiditatibus & satanæ, hoc est, non modo sinens seu non prohibens ipsos ruere ex uno delicto in aliud, nec impediens diaboli conatus impellentis eos subinde in atrociora peccata: sed his etiam quasi mancipio addicens suo imperio & mandato, ut fit efficacia erroris, asi mari non tantum adimat ventos, sed etiam immittat ventos, ut fluctus immanes tollant (Lasst sie nicht allein hin fahren, sondern stößt sie von sich und über gibt sie über) Atque ita partim ostendit se misereri cujus vult misereri, partim punit præcedentia ipsorum peccata: & viam parat ostendendæ suæ potentiæ in molitionibus ipsorum disjipandis. 4 Misericordia, dum ecclesiam suam conservat in atrocissimis malorum persequutionibus, convertit aliquos ex hostib. castigat sanctos, illustrat regulas misericordiæ Domini, quod non consumti simus gratia exuberante supra peccatum. 5 Potentia, Metas præfigendo quantum & quousque sit toleraturus impios: & reprimens tandem: facit id bono ecclesiæ & ostendit se potentiorem satana & impiis: inclinans ad objecta profutura suæ gloriæ & electorum saluti, non inserit novum
units.tr: that it is God's purpose to carry out his good work through them. Meanwhile he also delivers them over to their own lusts and to Satan. That is, he not only permits or does not prevent them from rushing from one sin into another, nor hinders the devil's attempts, which keep driving them into more atrocious sins. He also hands them over, as if sold into slavery, to his own command and mandate, so that the effect of error follows. It is as if he not only took the winds from the sea but also sent winds to raise huge waves (Lasst sie nicht allein hin fahren, sondern stößt sie von sich und über gibt sie über; he does not merely let them go, but thrusts them away from himself and gives them over). And so, partly he shows that he has mercy on whom he wills to have mercy, and partly he punishes their earlier sins, and he prepares the way to display his power in dissolving their schemes. 4 Mercy: while he preserves his Church amid the most savage persecutions of the wicked, he turns some of its enemies, chastens the saints, and illustrates the rules of the Lord's mercy, that we are not consumed, since grace abounds beyond sin. 5 Power: by setting limits on how much and how far he will allow the wicked to go, and by finally restraining them, he does this for the good of the Church and shows himself more powerful than Satan and the wicked, inclining them to objects that will serve his glory and the salvation of the elect. He does not implant a new

units.la: {4} Misericordia.
units.tr: {4} Mercy.

units.la: {5} Potentia. novam malitiam ipsorum voluntatib, ne-que malitiam priorem ipse auget: sed voluntates per se malas sic flectit, ut licet liberè semper agant, tamen in deliberatione hoc potius quam illud eligant, gubernat item ac dirigit ad personas, loca, tempora: aliud ipse spectat, aliud impii eo ipso peccantes quod ignari consilii divini & injusti contra expressam legem appetunt objecta illa: ut quum fratres Joseph fratrem vendunt in Ægyptum. Quo divinius inclinabantur voluntates ipsorum, Deo ante reprimente conatum interficiendi Josephi: ipsi autem malum scopum sibi praefigentes peccant, non obediunt.
units.tr: {5} Power. new wickedness in their wills, nor does he himself increase their former malice. Rather, he so bends wills that are evil in themselves that, although they always act freely, in their deliberation they choose this rather than that. He also governs and directs them with regard to persons, places and times. He has one aim, and the wicked have another; in that very act of sinning, they are ignorant of the divine counsel and unjustly desire those objects against the express law. So it was when Joseph's brothers sold their brother into Egypt. The more divinely their wills were inclined, while God restrained beforehand their attempt to kill Joseph, the more they sinned by setting before themselves an evil goal; they did not obey.

units.la: Hæc proculdubio recte accipies, eoque etiam lubentius si talia excellentissimum sanctæ memoriæ theologum D. Christophorum Pezelium, scholæ atque ecclesiæ nostræ immortale decus, quod tibi in pretio fuisse, quæ Leydæ esse m, recordari possum, bene multa ex Calvino, Bezâ & aliis observata, excerpta, & ad calcem tractationum theologicarum D. Bezæ ... olim adiecta & proprio calculo approbata, si forte id tehactenus latet, nunc ex me audias. Illecta enim tibi esse possunt, quia edita non sunt. Quanquam ipse D. Arminius in disputatione sua de iustitia & efficacia proviprovidentiae Dei in malo eadem erudite tractat, inter publicas IX & X. pag. 87. & 105. Eum si malis hac in parte sequi, per me licet. Eum vero in modum, clarisf. Berti, ut difficiliora, obscuriora aut implicatiora theologorum dicta & scripta interpretemur, aequitas suadet, charitas iubet, candor postulat: nihilque interpretamentorum malignitate in odium apud imperitos adducamus, quod ullo pacto ad verum & pium sensum trahi potest, maxime ubi in publico nota & grata sunt merita, fides, pietas & studia auctorum sua redimentium vitia (si quibus tamen ut homines urgentur) virtutibus, & plus habentium quod laudares, quam quod ignosceres. Facesat ergo omnis morosa & iniqua interpretatio. De verborum sententia lis est non de veritate.
units.tr: Doubtless you will understand these things rightly, and all the more gladly if you hear them from me now, since I can recall that they were esteemed by you at Leiden. They are the words of the most distinguished theologian of holy memory, Doctor Christoph Pezel, the immortal ornament of our school and church, who gathered and excerpted many things observed in Calvin, Beza and others, and approved them with his own judgment. These he added long ago to the end of Doctor Beza's theological tractates. Perhaps this has remained hidden from you until now, so I tell you now. Those writings may be unfamiliar to you because they have not been published. Yet the same learned points are treated by Doctor Arminius himself in his disputation on the justice and efficacy of God's providence in evil, among the public disputations IX and X, pages 87 and 105. If you prefer to follow him in this matter, I have no objection. But fairness urges, charity commands, and candour requires that, as the most distinguished Bertius put it, we interpret the more difficult, obscure or intricate sayings and writings of theologians in such a way that we do not stir up hatred among the unlearned by malicious interpretation, when something can in any way be drawn to a true and pious sense. This is especially so where the merits, faith, piety and zeal of the authors are well known and welcome, and where their virtues outweigh their faults (if they are pressed by any faults, as men are), so that there is more to praise than to pardon. Let every peevish and unfair interpretation therefore be set aside. The dispute is about the sense of words, not about the truth.

units.la: Docent & fatentur theologi: Deum non esse auctorem peccati: Libertatem a voluntate tolli non posse, nec verti vel in naturalem necessitatem aut externam victoriam. Haec moderatis ingeniis sufficere possunt.
units.tr: Theologians teach and confess that God is not the author of sin, and that freedom cannot be taken away from the will, nor turned into natural necessity or external compulsion. These points should be enough for moderate minds.

units.la: Sed quid? Magna pars querelas manu facit, aut falsa suspicando, aut levia aggravando. Ideo Calvini & Bezae ipsissima verba hac repono, qualia posteritati voluerunt esse certissima suae pietatis ac sententiae testimonia. Ea, benevole lector, ita habe & cum iudicio translege.
units.tr: But what then? A large part of people make complaints with their hands, either by suspecting falsely or by magnifying trifles. Therefore I set before you here the very words of Calvin and Beza, such as they wished to be the most certain testimonies of their piety and opinion for posterity. Take them thus, kind reader, and read them through with judgment.

units.la: 1. Primum articulum arripis quod Deus nudo puroque voluntatis suæ arbitrio maximam mundi partem creaverit ad perditionem. Atqui totum illud de maxima parte mundi, & de nudo puroque Dei arbitrio fictitium est, atque ex malitiæ tuæ officina productum. Calvinus de occulta Dei providentia contra Castell. p. 1012. n. 50.
units.tr: 1. You seize on the first article, that God by the bare and pure decision of his will created the greatest part of the world for destruction. But all that talk of "the greatest part of the world" and of "the bare and pure decision of God" is fictitious, and has been produced from the workshop of your malice. Calvin, On God's Hidden Providence, against Castellio, p. 1012, n. 50.

units.la: 2. Quanquam mihi Dei voluntas summa est causa, ubique tamen doceo, ubi in ejus consiliis & operibus causa nō apparet, apud eum tamen esse absconditam, ut nihil nisi juste & sapienter decreverit: Ibid. p. 1013. n. 5.
units.tr: 2. Although for me the will of God is the supreme cause, I nevertheless teach everywhere that where the cause does not appear in his counsels and works, it is nonetheless hidden with him, so that he has decreed nothing except justly and wisely. Ibid., p. 1013, n. 5.

units.la: 3. Quam vis natura bonus fuerit homo, hanc rectitudinem, quę fluxa & caduca erat cum Dei prædestinatione non pugnare, qua factum est ut sua culpa periret, qui purę naturę, imo ejus qua ornatus erat præstantiæ intuitu ad salutem creatus erat: ideoque perpetua & stulte infers suisse creatū ut bonus periret, quum sua infirmitate cecidisse palam sit, ut non nisi juste damnationi obnoxius periret. Ibid. p. 1015. n. 5.
units.tr: 3. Although man was good by nature, this uprightness, which was frail and perishable, did not conflict with God's predestination. By it, it came about that he perished through his own fault, though he had been created for salvation, looking to the pure nature and the excellence with which he was adorned. Therefore it is foolish to infer that he was created to perish as a good man, since it is plain that he fell through his own weakness, so that he perished as one liable to nothing but just damnation. Ibid., p. 1015, n. 5.

units.la: 4. Proferlocum ex scriptis meis, ubi doceam lapsus causa propositum fuisse pomū Adæ. Ibid. p. 1016.
units.tr: 4. Produce a passage from my writings where I teach that the cause of the fall was God's purpose concerning Adam's apple. Ibid., p. 1016.

units.la: 5. Voluntas Dei etsi neque aliunde pendet, nec aliam habet priorem causam, in optima tamen ratione, summaque æquitate sunt data. data est. Nam quum legis fi eno indigeat humana intemperies, alia est Dei ratio, qui sibi ipse lex est, & cujus voluntas regula est optimæ rectitudinis. Ibid.p. 1017.
units.tr: 5. The will of God, although it depends on nothing else and has no prior cause, has nonetheless been given in the best reason and the highest equity. It has been given. For since human intemperance needs the rule of law, God's reason is different, for he is a law to himself, and his will is the rule of the best rectitude. Ibid., p. 1017.

units.la: 6. Si tibi tantopere arridet verbum permittedi, respode volens ne permittatan nolens Huic secundo membro reclamat quod legitur in psalmo, Deum facere quacunque vult. Si autem volens permittit, ociolum fingere nefas erit. Ibid.p. 1020.
units.tr: 6. If the word permits pleases you so greatly, answer whether he permits willing or unwilling. Against this second member there cries out what is read in the Psalm, that God does whatever he wills. But if he permits willing, it will be wrong to invent idleness. Ibid., p. 1020.

units.la: 7. Perinde mecum litigas ac si dixissem peccatum esse justum Dei opus: quod in omnibus scriptis meis passim detestor.Ib.p.1021.
units.tr: 7. You quarrel with me just as if I had said that sin is the just work of God, which I detest everywhere in all my writings. Ibid., p. 1021.

units.la: 8. Egone qui tam reverenter ubiq; praedico quoties peccati fit mentio procul removendum esse Dei nomen, usquam dixerim maleficia nō tantum eo volente, sed etiam authore perpetrari? Certè ut quidvis contra tam prodigiosam blasphemiam dicatur, liberter patiar, modò ne immerito admisceatur nomen meum. Ibid.p.1022.
units.tr: 8. Would I, who so reverently proclaim everywhere that whenever mention of sin is made, the name of God must be kept far away, ever have said that wicked deeds are committed not only with his will but also with him as author? Certainly, let whatever you like be said against such a monstrous blasphemy; I will gladly bear it, provided my name is not unjustly mixed in. Ibid., p. 1022.

units.la: 9. Hæc summa est; quum peccati causa sit in hominibus mala voluntas, Deum recta sua judicia per eorum manus exercendo, adeo culpa non involvi, ut mirabiliter lucem gloriæ suæ ex tenebris eliciat. Et quidem in eo libello, qui furias istas ex profundis inferis contra me excitavit, subinde occurrit ælaia illa distinctio, nihil esse iniquius, vel magis magis praepositerum, quam Deum trahere in societatem reatus, dum per manus diaboli & impiorum judicio sua exsequitur, quum in ratione agendi nulla sit affinitas. Ibid.
units.tr: 9. This is the sum: since the cause of sin is an evil will in men, God, by carrying out his righteous judgments through their hands, is so far from being involved in guilt that he wonderfully draws the light of his glory out of darkness. Indeed, in that little book which stirred up those furies from the depths of hell against me, that distinction keeps recurring, that nothing is more unjust, or rather more absurd, than to drag God into fellowship of guilt when he carries out his judgments through the hands of the devil and of the wicked, since there is no affinity in the manner of acting. Ibid.

units.la: 10. Caeterum, jam ante annos duodecim editu a me opus est, quod me a putidis illis calumniis satis superque vindicat, ab omni autem molestia debebat immunem reddere, si qua inte, ac similibus esset humanitas guttura: delirium enim illud quo jam multos fascinaverant Libertini, moštrosum hominum genus, quam dextre refutaverim non jacto. Certe ex profeso causam illam agendam suscepi, & luculete exposui Dei peccati non esse auctorem. Ib. p. 1022.
units.tr: 10. Besides, I published a work twelve years ago which vindicates me sufficiently and more than sufficiently from those foul calumnies. It ought to have made me free from all annoyance, if there were any humanity in such throats as theirs and those like them. For I do not boast of how skilfully I refuted that madness by which the Libertines, a monstrous breed of men, had already bewitched many. Certainly I took up that cause on purpose and set out clearly that God is not the author of sin. Ibid., p. 1022.

units.la: 11. Profer locum ubi dixerim fapiffime pugnare Dei voluntatem cum praecepto: mihi enim ne per somnium quidem id unquam in mentem venit. Cum potius interalia sideliter exposui quomodo simplex & unica Dei voluntas, quamvis inter arcanum ejus consilium & doctrinam quaedam appareat disfidiifpecies. Ibid. p. 1023. n. 13.
units.tr: 11. Cite the passage where I said that the will of God very often fights against the precept: the idea never once entered my mind, not even in a dream. Rather, among other things, I faithfully explained how the simple and single will of God appears, although between his secret counsel and the doctrine there is some appearance of conflict. Ibid. p. 1023. n. 13.

units.la: 12. Ergo ne quid mihi maculae asspergat mendaciorum tuorum spurcities breviter hoc testatum fit leftoribus, quod velut ex me profectum ostendis de contrariis Dei voluntatibus, improbissime esse abs te confi- dum, quando ubique a me optimus inter abscon-
units.tr: 12. Therefore, lest the filth of your lies stain me, let this be briefly attested to the readers: what you present as coming from me, about God's contrary wills, is shamelessly invented by you, since everywhere I most clearly

units.la: Deo non sunt contrarii voluntatis ... (marginal reference) absconditum Dei consilium, & externam doctrinæ vocem consensus prædicatur. Ibi-dem. n. 20.
units.tr: ...God is not contrary to himself in his will... (marginal reference) the hidden counsel of God and the outward voice of the doctrine are proclaimed to be in agreement. Ibidem. n. 20.

units.la: 13. Subtilis tibi videtur captio, dum quæ-ris, ex quo Deus adulterium committere voluit, velitne omnes esse adulteros, an partem. Nam si de parte respondeo, infers Deum sibi esse contrarium. Atqui jam certum respōsum tenet, Deum ab omnibus exi-gere castitatem, quia eam in omnibus amat; diversas tamen volendi rationes ipsa experientia, me tacente, ostendit. Nam si æque efficaciter vellet omnes esse castos, haud du-bie castos omnes redderet. Nunc quum sin-gulare ejus donū sit castitas, colligere prom-tū est, aliter velle quod verbo præcipit, quàm quod spiritus regenerationis implet. Ibid. p. 1023. n. 5e.
units.tr: 13. The trap you set seems subtle to you, when you ask at what point God wished adultery to be committed, and whether he wills that all men be adulterers or only some. For if I answer about some, you infer that God is contrary to himself. Yet the true answer is already at hand: God requires chastity from all, because he loves it in all; but the different ways of willing are shown by experience itself, even without my saying so. For if he willed with equal efficacy that all be chaste, he would without doubt make all chaste. Now, since chastity is his singular gift, it is easy to gather that he wills one thing in a different way when he commands it by the word, and another when his Spirit of regeneration fulfils it. Ibid. p. 1023. n. 5e.

units.la: 14. Hac ratione non est cur impudica rua lingua hypocrisin Deo exprobret, ac si mel in ore haberet, sel autem in corde. Neq; enim si quicquam simulat Deus jubendo aut vetando: sed naturam suam sincere patefacit. In occulta autem voluntate, qua dirigit cunctas homi-num actiones, nihil huic justitia contrarium reperies. Ibid. p. 1014.
units.tr: 14. For this reason your shameless tongue has no cause to charge God with hypocrisy, as if he had honey in his mouth and gall in his heart. For God does not feign anything in commanding or forbidding, but sincerely reveals his own nature. In his hidden will, however, by which he directs all human actions, you will find nothing contrary to justice. Ibid. p. 1014.

units.la: 15. Si te impedit tua cæcitas, vident omnes oculati consentaneum esse ut Deus, qui scortationem & cades, quatenus peccata sunt, fanc, id (quod eodem redit) peccatum, legis suae transgressionem, in scortatione caedi-busq; odit, idem & per cades & per alia quae-vis maleficia, justus de hominum peccatis poenas exigens, judicia sua exerceat. Ibid. pa. 1024. n. 10.
units.tr: 15. If your blindness hinders you, let all who have eyes see that it is fitting that God, who hates fornication and murder insofar as they are sins, that is (which comes to the same thing) a transgression of his law, and who as a just judge exacts punishment for men's sins, should execute his judgements through murders and through every other kind of wrongdoing. Ibid. p. 1024. n. 10.

units.la: 16. Quum bona sit Dei voluntas quam in lege prodidit, quicquid contrarium est, cöcedo malum esse, sed occultam illam voluntatem, qua Deus vasa misericordiae, a vasis irae discernens, pro suo arbitrio utrisque libere utitur, contrariam esse blaterans, commentum non minus detestabile quam falsum exhalas ex foetida ignorantiae tuae lacuna. Ibidem.
units.tr: 16. Since God's will, which he has revealed in the law, is good, whatever is contrary to it is, I grant, evil. But when you prattle that his hidden will, by which God, separating the vessels of mercy from the vessels of wrath, uses both freely according to his own decision, is contrary to it, you breathe out a fiction no less detestable than false from the foul pit of your ignorance. Ibidem.

units.la: 17. Christum de aperta voluntate loqui fateor, ubi dicit, Jerusalem, Jerusalem, quoties Volui congregare pullos tuos, & noluisti. Idem enim Judaeis exprobrat quod in cantico Moisis. Et iane reipsa Deum praestituisse scimus quod verba illa sonant: quando & legis doctrina & pietatis exercitia & tot beneficia quibus sibi Deus populum illum devinxerit, non secus atque alarum expansio fuerunt ad eos protegendos, nisi alioqui eos rapuisset indomita sua feritas. Ib. p. 1024.
units.tr: 17. I admit that Christ speaks of his revealed will when he says, "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered your chicks, and you would not." For he reproaches the Jews with the same thing as in the song of Moses. And indeed we know that God actually intended what those words say: since both the teaching of the law, the exercises of piety, and the many benefits by which God bound that people to himself were, as the spreading of wings, meant to protect them; unless, that is, their own untamed savagery had carried them off. Ibid. p. 1024.

units.la: 18. Neque longa refutatione incurrile dicterium dignabor, ubi Deum iniustum fore arguis, si barbatos punit, eo quod barbam gestant quam ipse creavit. Quis enim un-quam dixit, creatam esse a Deo iniquitatem, quamvis incomprehensibili ejus consilio ad justos rectosque fines ordinetur? Apage ergo cum tua ista insulsitate, qua barbam, quæ naturaliter dormientibus provenit, cum voluntariis sceleribus permisces. Nobis quamvis insanias fixum hoc manebit, quorum pravos affectus ad exsequenda sua judicia destinat & regit Deus, eosdem jure punire quia reos sua ipsorum conscientia peragit. Ac vide quomodo te implices: ubi enim confessus es ignota nobis esse Dei arcana, contra excipis Dei justitiam nobis esse cognitam. Verum si quis an aliqua sit in Dei arcanis justitia necne, ex te quærat, an negabis? Justitiam porro illam quomodo notam esse dices, quam David & Paulus, quia sensus eorum fugit, cum admiratione suscipiunt? Abyssus multa & dives altitudo sapientiæ in Dei judiciis annon justitiam in se continent? Cur ergo justum esse Deum negabis quoties te latebit operum ejus ratio? Sicuti in libro Job distinctio notatu digna statuitur inter sapientiam Dei impervestigabilem, a qua arcetur humanum genus, & eam quæ in lege nobis tradita est; sic te quoque, nisi omnia confunderes, potius distinguere oportuerat inter profundâ illam.
units.tr: 18. I will not waste a long refutation on the taunt that you raise, where you claim that God would be unjust if he punished bearded men because they wear the beard which he himself created. For who has ever said that iniquity was created by God, although it is ordained by his incomprehensible counsel to just and right ends? Away, then, with your silly nonsense, by which you confuse the beard that naturally grows on men in their sleep with voluntary crimes. Though you rave, this will remain fixed for us: that God directs and governs the wicked affections of those whose judgements he executes, and rightly punishes those same men, since their own conscience convicts them as guilty. And see how you entangle yourself: for when you confessed that the secrets of God are unknown to us, you then objected that God's justice is known to us. But if someone asks you whether there is any justice in God's secrets or not, will you deny it? Again, how will you say that justice is known, when David and Paul, because it escapes their understanding, receive it with wonder? "O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how unsearchable are his judgements!" Do not his judgements, then, contain justice within them? Why, then, will you deny that God is just whenever the reason of his works is hidden from you? Just as in the book of Job a distinction worth noting is drawn between the unsearchable wisdom of God, from which the human race is shut out, and that which has been delivered to us in the law; so you too, unless you confused everything, ought rather to have distinguished between that deep wisdom and the other.

units.la: Sapientia & justitia Dei partim est occulta, partim revelata. illam justitiam & admirabilem quæ humanis mentibus non capitur, & justitia regula quæ regenda hominum vita in lege præscripta est. Secundum apertam illam euangelii doctrinam fateor, judicabit Deus mundū: sed arcana suæ providentiæ æquitatem simul contra omnes rabulas asserret. Ib. p. 1028.
units.tr: The wisdom and justice of God are partly hidden and partly revealed: the justice that is admirable and not grasped by human minds, and the justice which is the rule for regulating human life and is prescribed in the law. According to that plain teaching of the gospel, I admit, God will judge the world; yet the hidden things of his providence will at the same time vindicate his equity against all the wranglers. Ib. p. 1028.

units.la: 19. Frustra necessitatis clypeus obtenditur, ubi suā quemq; conscientia voluntariæ malitiæ convincit. Ib. p. 1030.
units.tr: 19. The shield of necessity is held up in vain, when each man's own conscience convicts him of voluntary malice. Ib. p. 1030.

units.la: 20. Neque ego sane ad arcanam Dei electionem nem homines ablego, ut inde salutem hiantes exspectent; sed recta ad Christum pergere justo, in quo nobis propositā est salus: quæ a lioquiin Deo abscondita lateret. Nam quisquis plana fidei via non ingreditur, illi Dei electio nihil quàm exitialis erit labyrinthus. Itaque ut certa sit nobis peccatorum remissio, ut in vitæ æternæ fiducia conscientiæ nostræ acquiescant, ut Deum intrepidè patrem invocemus, hinc minime faciendum est exordium, quid de nobis ante mundum conditum Deus statuerit: sed quid de paterno ejus amore nobis in Christo fit patefactum, & quotidie per euangelium Christus ipse prædicet. Nihil altius nobis quæren-dum, quàm ut filii Dei simus. De æterna Dei præde[s]tinatione, p. 975.
units.tr: 20. Indeed, I do not send men away to God's secret election so that, gaping for salvation, they wait for it from there; rather, one should go straight to Christ, in whom salvation is set before us, which otherwise would lie hidden from God. For whoever does not enter the plain way of faith, for him God's election will be nothing but a deadly labyrinth. Therefore, so that the forgiveness of sins may be certain for us, so that our consciences may rest in the confidence of eternal life, and that we may boldly call upon God as Father, we must by no means begin here, with what God decided about us before the world was made; rather, we must begin with what of his fatherly love has been revealed to us in Christ, and what Christ himself proclaims daily through the gospel. We have nothing higher to seek than that we be sons of God. On the eternal predestination of God, p. 975.

units.la: 21. Porrò sicuti hæc hæreditas & Christi sanguine parta est semel & sacris euangelii tabulis consignata: ita ejus possessio non aliter quàm fide adiri potest.Ibid.
units.tr: 21. Moreover, just as this inheritance was won once for all by the blood of Christ and sealed in the sacred tablets of the gospel, so its possession can be approached in no other way than by faith. Ibid.

units.la: 22. Denique nō tantum libenter fateor, sed passim in scriptis meis inculco & fidei alligatam esse hominum salutem & Christum unicam esse januam, qua in regnum cœlorum omnes ingredi oportet, nec alibi tranquillā pacem quam in euangelio inveniri: quicunq; inde vel nimium deflectunt, nihil quàm per flexuosas ambages errare: & quo quisque in profunda illa divini consilii adyta confidentius irrumpere & penetrare conatur, eò longius à Deo recedere. Ergo quin per fidei viam ambulandum sit non nego. Ibidem.
units.tr: 22. Finally, I not only gladly admit, but everywhere in my writings I insist, that men's salvation is bound to faith, and that Christ is the only door by which all must enter the kingdom of heaven, nor is peaceful tranquillity to be found anywhere else than in the gospel: whoever strays too far from this wanders only through winding detours; and the more confidently anyone tries to rush into and penetrate those deep sanctuaries of the divine counsel, the farther he withdraws from God. Therefore I do not deny that we must walk the way of faith. Ibidem.

units.la: 23. Quod Deus sciens ac volens hominem ipsum cadere passus est: occulta ratio esse potest: injusta non potest. Hoc quidem absque controversia tenendum: semper illi peccatum odio fuisse. Nam verè elogiū hoc quo ornatur à Davide, in eum competit: Quod Deus sit iniquitatem nō volens. Quum potius in ordinando hominis lapsu finem habuit optimum & rectissimum, à quo abhorret peccati nomen. Quanquam sic ordinasse dico, ut eum proprie auctorem fuisse non concedam. Ibid p. 979.
units.tr: 23. That God, knowing and willing it, allowed man himself to fall may have a hidden reason; it cannot be an unjust one. This must certainly be held without controversy: sin was always hateful to him. For that praise which David gives him truly applies to him: that God is not willing iniquity. Rather, in ordaining the fall of man he had the best and most upright end, from which the very name of sin shrinks. Although I say he so ordained it, I will not concede that he was properly the author of it. Ibid. p. 979.

units.la: 24. Naturam hominis ideo rectam primò conditam fuisse ubique assero, ne pravitas, quam sibi defectione contraxit, Deo possit asscribi: mortem cui se mancipavit, qui ante compos vitæ erat, sic profectam esse ab ejus culpa, ne Deus auctor censeatur. Ibid. p. 979.
units.tr: 24. I assert everywhere that man's nature was first created upright, lest the depravity which he contracted for himself by defection be ascribed to God; likewise, the death to which he sold himself, although he had been master of life before, I assert arose thus from his own fault, lest God be judged the author. Ibid. p. 979.

units.la: 25. Denique in hac Augustini sententia non minus tranquille quam libenter acquiesco: Deum qui creavit omnia bona valde, & mala ex bonis exoritura præscivit, & scivit magis ad suam omnipotentissimam bonitatem pertinere, etiam de malis benefacere, quam mala esse non sinere: sic ordinasse angelorum & hominum vitam, ut in ea prius offenderet, quid posset liberum eorum arbitrium, deinde quid posset gratiæ suæ beneficium, justitiaque judicium. pag. 980.
units.tr: 25. Finally, I acquiesce no less calmly than gladly in this sentiment of Augustine: God, who created all things very good, and foreknew that evils would arise from good things, and knew that it pertained more to his most omnipotent goodness to bring good even out of evils than to not allow evils to exist; so he ordained the life of angels and men, that in it he might first test what their free will could do, and then what the benefit of his grace and the judgment of his justice could do.

units.la: 26. Quanquam interim quæ Augustinus libro de Genesi ad literam undecimo disseruit, quum ad Dei timorem & reverentiam omnia temperet, minime improbo. Altera autem pars, quod ex damnata Adæ sobole, Deus quos visum est, eligit, quos vult, reprobat, sicuti ad fidem exercendam longe aptior est, ita majore fructu tractatur. In hac igitur doctrina, qua humana natura et corruptionem & reatum in se continet, libentius insistit: sicuti non solum ad pietatem propius conducit, sed magis mihi videtur theologica. Meminerimus tamen in ea quoque sobrie. brie modestéque philosophandum; ne ulterius progredi tentemus, quàm Dominus nos verbo suo deducit. Ibid.
units.tr: 26. Yet meanwhile I by no means condemn what Augustine discussed in the eleventh book of his literal commentary on Genesis, since he tempers everything to the fear and reverence of God. The other part, that from the damned offspring of Adam God chooses whom he pleases and reprobates whom he wills, is as much more suited to exercising faith, and so is handled with greater fruit. In this doctrine, which contains in itself both the corruption and the guilt of human nature, he dwells more willingly: for it not only leads more closely to piety, but seems to me more theological. Yet let us remember to philosophize soberly and modestly here too, and not try to advance further than the Lord leads us by his word. Ibid.

units.la: 17. Quod Deus arcano spiritus afflatu ad se homines trahat vel quotidianæ preces nostræ testes sunt: nam quum pro perse-quutoribus oramus, quid petimus aliud, quàm ut fiant ex nolentibus, volentes ex repu-gnantibus consentientes, ex oppugnantibus amantes? Atqui palam constat non omnibus indifferenter hoc dari, ut centies exitiü meritos Deus repente vitâ dignetur. Quomodo hanc gratiam dispenset, inquit Augustinus, alios secundum meritum faciens vasa ira, secundum gratiam alios vasa misericordiæ: quis cognovit sensum Domini? p. 980.
units.tr: 17. That God draws men to himself by a secret inspiration of the Spirit is witnessed by our daily prayers. For when we pray for our persecutors, what else do we ask but that they may become willing from unwilling, consenting from resisting, lovers from opponents? Yet it is plain that this is not given indifferently to all, that God should suddenly deign to give life to those who have deserved death a hundred times. How he dispenses this grace, says Augustine, making some vessels of wrath according to merit and others vessels of mercy according to grace: who has known the mind of the Lord? p. 980.

units.la: 18. Statuendum procul dubio est, eligi à Deo, quos fide donare apud se decrevit. p. 988.
units.tr: 18. Undoubtedly it must be held that those are chosen by God whom he has decided to endow with faith, to have with himself. p. 988.

units.la: 19. Quis n. nisi persuasionem hanc peni-tus animo infixam habeat, justum esse Deũ & recta ejus opera: in solo ejus placito acquiescet? Itaq; Sorbonicum illud dogma, in quo sibi plaudunt papales theologastri detestor; quod potentiam absolutam Deo affingit. Solis enim lucem à calore avellere, imo suum ab igne calorem facilius erit, quàm Dei potentiam separare à justitia. Faciant ergo procul à piis mentibus monitrum, sæ illæ speculationes: plus aliquid Deũ posse quàm separari.
units.tr: 19. For who, unless he has this conviction deeply fixed in his mind, that God is just and his works are right, will rest content in his pleasure alone? Therefore I detest that Sorbonne dogma, in which the papal theologasters flatter themselves, which ascribes to God an absolute power. For it will be easier to tear the light of the sun from its heat, or indeed the heat from fire, than to separate God's power from his justice. Let them therefore keep far from pious minds those monstrous speculations: that God can do something beyond being separated from justice.

units.la: F quam conveniat: veleum sine modo & ratione quicquam agere. Ib. p. 1002.
units.tr: F how fitting it is, or that he should do anything without measure and reason. Ib. p. 1002.

units.la: 30. Nec verò commentum illud recipio, Deum, quia lege solutus sit, quicquid agat, reprehensione vacare. Deum enim exlegem qui facit, maxima eum gloriae suae parte spoliat, quia rectitudinem ejus ac justitiam sepelit. Non quod legi subjectus sit Deus, nisi quatenus ipse sibi lex est. Talis enim est inter potentiam ejus ac justitiam symmetria & consensus, ut nihil ab ipso nisi moderatum, legitimum, & regulare prodeat. Et certè quem omnipotentem praedicant fideles, eundem simul mundi judicem agnoscant necesse est, ut potetiam sensu suo apprehendant, justitia & aequitate temperatam. Ibid.
units.tr: 30. Nor do I accept that fiction, that God, because he is loosed from law, is free from blame whatever he does. For whoever makes God lawless strips him of the greatest part of his glory, since he buries his uprightness and justice. Not that God is subject to law, except insofar as he is law to himself. For between his power and his justice there is such a symmetry and harmony that nothing proceeds from him except what is moderate, lawful and regular. And certainly, whom the faithful proclaim as omnipotent, they must at the same time acknowledge as judge of the world, so that they may grasp his power, by their understanding, as tempered by justice and equity. Ibid.

units.la: 31. Quu justa de causa licet nobis ignota, à Domino procedant, quae celeriter ab hominibus maleficia perpetrantur: etiamsi rerum omnium prima causa sit ejus voluntas, peccati tamen eum esse auctorem negó. pag. 1003.
units.tr: 31. Although the things that the Lord brings about, for reasons just though unknown to us, are not the same as the wicked deeds quickly committed by men, and although his will is the first cause of all things, I deny that he is the author of sin. p. 1003.

units.la: 32. Quod habetur in psalmo verisfimū est: quod Deus non in iniquitate voluit. Nec verò illic Davidis testatur aliud, quā ipsa quotidie probat, dum poenam de hominum peccatis sumit. Neque enim impunitum est, nisi odisset. Ulterius videt approbatores non esse statuendum est: sed in eo fallùtur multi, quòd Deum juste velle non reputât, quæ homines peccando faciunt. Quomodo, inquies, adulteria incestosque coitus abominatur? Quod Absolom patris concubinas coram populo constuprat, an fit Deo nolente? Atqui hoc se facturū ipse per servum suum Nathan prædixerat: Tollam uxores tuas in oculis tuis: & dabo proximo tuo, qui dormiet cum illis in conspectu solis hujus. Tu fecisti occulte ego autem coram toto populo & coràm sole facturus sum. Plena est talibus exemplis scriptura. Ibid.
units.tr: 32. What is found in the Psalm is most true: that God does not will iniquity. Nor does David there testify anything other than what he himself proves every day while he exacts punishment for men's sins. For it is not left unpunished unless he hated it. It must not be held that he approves further; but many are deceived in this, that they do not reckon that God justly wills what men do by sinning. How, you will ask, does he abominate adulteries and incestuous unions? Does it happen against his will that Absalom debauched his father's concubines before the people? Yet he himself had foretold that he would do this through his servant Nathan: "I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbour, who shall lie with them in the sight of this sun. You did it in secret, but I will do it before the whole people and before the sun." Scripture is full of such examples. Ibid.

units.la: 33. An ideo vel peccati culpam Deo imputabimus, vel duplicem in eo voluntatem fabricabimus, ut secum ipse dissideat? verum sicut jam ostendi, idem eum velle cum sceleratis & improbis, sed diverso modo: ita nunc tenendum est, quæ in specie diversa sunt, eodem modo eum velle: Ut in ista, quæ mentibus nostris occurrit, varietate optimè temperata sit symphonia. Quatenus immanis adversus patrem impietas, perfida conjugii violatio, fœda etiam ordinis naturæ profanatio est, Absolomi facinus displicere Deo certum est, cui placet honestas, pudicitia, fides, modestia, qui legitimum quem prescripsit, ordinem coli & integrum servari vult inter homines; quia tamen ille placet, hoc mo-
units.tr: 33. Shall we then either impute the guilt of sin to God, or fabricate in him a double will, so that he disagrees with himself? But as I have already shown, he wills the same thing as the wicked and the evil, but in a different way. So now we must hold that things which are different in kind he wills in the same way, so that in that variety which presents itself to our minds there may be a well-tempered harmony. Insofar as the monstrous impiety against a father, the treacherous violation of marriage and the foul profanation of the natural order are concerned, it is certain that Absalom's deed displeases God, to whom honesty, chastity, faith and modesty please, and who wills the lawful order he has prescribed to be cultivated and kept whole among men. Yet although that pleases him, in this way

units.la: F 2 do addo ulterium Davidis ulcisci, quae diversa non bis videntur, eodem modo vult. Una enim & simplex est voluntas, qua praecipit quid fieri debeat, & qua legis suae transgressiones ulciscitur. Haec ibidem eius finem tractatus de aeterna Dei praedestinatione Calvinus, quae uti & antegressa vel infinities ingeminat in fuia Christiana institutione & commentariis in scriptu-ram editis, ut suspiciosis contradictoribus ostenderet videatur. Sed audiamus plura ex Beza.
units.tr: F 2 I add further that he takes vengeance for David's sin, which seem to us different, he wills in the same way. For his will is one and simple, by which he commands what ought to be done, and by which he avenges the transgressions of his law. This is the end of Calvin's treatise on the eternal predestination of God; as he repeats this, and what went before, countless times in his Christian Institutes and in his published commentaries on Scripture, so that he might show it to suspicious opponents. But let us hear more from Beza.

units.la: 34. Ego vero miror tantam cujusquam esse impudentiam, posse ut invidiosum illud fatinomen Calvino audeat objicere, de quo quid jam olim scripserit, non pigebit ipsius verbis referre, ut ab ipso statim initio quilibet animadvertat quem animum ad hanc agendam causam attulerit. Sic ergo Calvinus calumniantur esse Stoicorum dogma de fato, qui hujus doctrinae invidiam facere volunt; quod & exprobratum Augustino aliquando fuit. Nos etsi de verbis invitiliti-gamus, Fati vocabulum non recipimus, tum quia est ex eorum genere quorum novitates refugere nos Paulus docet, tum quia ejus odio conantur gravare Dei veritatem. Beza de aeterna Dei praedestinatione p. 338.
units.tr: 34. Indeed I marvel that anyone has such impudence as to dare to throw at Calvin that invidious name "fatalist". Concerning this, I will not hesitate to report his own words on what he once wrote, so that anyone may notice from the very beginning what spirit he brought to this business. Thus Calvin's calumniators say that the Stoic dogma of fate is his, since they wish to stir up hatred of this doctrine; which was once also thrown in Augustine's face. We, although we quarrel over words, do not accept the word "Fate", both because it belongs to that class of novelties which Paul bids us shun, and because they seek to weigh down God's truth with hatred of it. Beza, on the eternal predestination of God, p. 338.

units.la: 35. Dices fatum ab eo tolli verbo, re constitui. ftitui, Audi igitur quid eo ipso loco subji-ciat: Dogma ipsum Stoicorum inquit.falso nobis ac malitiose objicitur. Non enim cum Stoicis necessitatem cōminiscimur ex per-petuò causarum nexu & implicita quadam serie quæ in natura contineatur: sed Deum constituimus arbitrum ac moderatorem omnium, qui pro sua sapientia ab ultima æter-nitate decreverit q; factypus esset, & nunc sua potetia, quod decrevit, exsequatur. Un-de ejus providentia non cœlum modò ac terram ac creaturas inanimatas sed homi-num etiam consilia & voluntates guberna-ri sic asserimus, ut ad destinatum ab easco-pam deducantur. Beza ibid.
units.tr: 35. You will say that he removes fate by word but establishes it in fact. Hear then what he adds in that very place: The Stoics' own dogma, he says, is falsely and maliciously thrown at us. For we do not devise with the Stoics a necessity arising from the perpetual chain of causes and a certain intertwined series contained in nature; but we establish God as the arbiter and governor of all, who from eternity decreed by his wisdom what would be, and now carries out by his power what he has decreed. Hence we assert that his providence governs not only heaven and earth and inanimate creatures, but also the counsels and wills of men, so that they are led to the goal he has set. Beza, ibid.

units.la: 36. Prima Castellionis calumnia est: Deum maximam mundi partem nudo puroque voluntatis suæ arbitrio creasse ad perditionem. Eam refutat Calvinus Inst. Christ. lib. 3. c. 23. s. 5. et c. 21. s. 7. & libro de æterna Dei præde stinatione. Beza contra Castell. p. 339.
units.tr: 36. Castellio's first calumny is this: that God created the greater part of the world by the bare and pure arbitrary will of his own, for destruction. Calvin refutes this in his Institutes, book 3, chapter 23, section 5, and chapter 21, section 7, and in his book on the eternal predestination of God. Beza against Castellio, p. 339.

units.la: 37. Dicimus quadruplici modo consilia Dei à nobis intelligi. Unum est ex revelatione per prophetas, cujus exempla passim exstant, in scripturis. Alter est ex peculiari revelatione Spiritus, ut de Simeone legimus, atque etiam de fidelibus omnib. quorum spiritui testificatur spiritus Dei quæ sint ipsis à Christo donata. Id enim est quod fidem & ΣΥΝΕΦΕΙΑ vocamus, quae facit ut Pauli exemplo tam certi simus nos à Deo gratis electos in Christo, quàm si prae-sentes æterno ipsius cõsilio interfuissemus. Tertium est ex causarum naturalium consi-quutione à nobis observata, quomodo sa-pe physici & prudentes, peritique rerum humanarum homines multa vaticinantur. Sed fallax est & incerta multis in rebus ista conjectura, propterea quod causas inter-medias Dominus pro occulta sua voluntate sæpe inflectit. Quartum autè modus cer-tissimus, qui à posteriore, quod ajunt, judicat. Beza ibid. p. 350.
units.tr: 37. We say that the counsels of God are understood by us in four ways. The first is from revelation through the prophets, of which examples are found everywhere in the Scriptures. The second is from a special revelation of the Spirit, as we read of Simeon, and also of all the faithful, to whose spirit the Spirit of God bears witness what things have been given to them by Christ. This is what we call faith and assurance [ΣΥΝΕΦΕΙΑ], which makes us, following Paul's example, as certain that we have been freely elected by God in Christ as if we had been present at his eternal counsel. The third is from our observation of the sequence of natural causes, as physicians and prudent men, skilled in human affairs, often foretell many things. But this conjecture is deceptive and uncertain in many matters, because the Lord, by his hidden will, often bends the intermediate causes. The fourth, however, is the most certain way, which judges from the outcome, as they say, from the after-effect. Beza, ibid., p. 350.

units.la: 38. Dico igitur duo esse quae non modò verbum Dei, sed sensus etiam ipse commu-nis nobis dictat. Unum est; Deum nunquam posse mutari, itaque id ipsum quod res as-pissime mutetur æterno & immutabili Dei consilio fieri. &c. Alterum autem hoc est, quod ipse quoque sensus communis dictat, Deo vel ignorante, vel invito vel ocioso ni-hil fieri: quia nec ignorantia, nec imbecilli-tas in Dei naturam cadit, nec ociosa præsci-entia ei tribui potest, præsertim in tam ex-cellētis opificii, i.e. hominis gubernatione, quia maxima ex parte confirmetur impium Epicurei dogma, mortales Deo curæ non esse. Beza ibidem.
units.tr: 38. I say, therefore, that there are two things which not only the word of God but also common sense itself teaches us. The first is that God can never be changed, and so whatever things change most often are done by the eternal and unchangeable counsel of God, etc. The second is what common sense itself also teaches: that nothing is done by God either in ignorance, or against his will, or in idleness; for neither ignorance nor weakness can fall upon the nature of God, nor can an idle foreknowledge be ascribed to him, especially in the governing of so excellent a work as man, since to a great extent the impious dogma of the Epicureans, that mortals are of no concern to God, would thereby be confirmed. Beza, ibid.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: 39. Calumnia secunda est, Deum non solum praedestinasse ad damnationem, sed & ad causas damnationis Adamum, cujus nō modò lapsum praeviderit, sed voluerit decreto aeterno & occulto, ordinaritque ut laberetur: quod ut suo tempore fieret, lapsus causa pomū propositum fuisse. Eam ex Calvino refutat Beza ibid. p. 357. &c.
units.tr: 39. The second calumny is that God has not only predestined men to damnation, but has also predestined Adam to be the cause of their damnation. God not only foresaw Adam's fall but willed it by an eternal and hidden decree, and ordained that he should fall, and that the apple was set before him so that the fall would happen at the appointed time. Beza refutes this from Calvin, ibid. p. 357 etc.

units.la: 40. Tertia calumnia est, peccata quae remittuntur non solum permissione, verum etiam voluntate Dei committuntur. Nam frivolum esse assignare discrimen inter permissionem & voluntatem Dei, quod ad peccatum attinet. Eam confutat Beza ibidem p. 362. &c. ex Calvino contra Libertinos probatissime.
units.tr: 40. The third calumny is that sins which are forgiven are committed not only by God's permission but also by his will. For it is said to be a trivial thing to draw a distinction between God's permission and his will where sin is concerned. Beza refutes this very thoroughly, ibid. p. 362 etc., from Calvin against the Libertines.

units.la: 41. Quarta calumnia est, omnia quae à quovis homine perpetrantur facinora, bona esse justaque Dei opera. Eam refellit Beza ibid. p. 388. &c.
units.tr: 41. The fourth calumny is that all the crimes committed by any man are good and just works of God. Beza refutes this, ibid. p. 388 etc.

units.la: 42. Quinta calumnia est, Nullum adulterium, furtum, homicidium comitti, quin Dei voluntas intercedat. Inst. lib. 1. c. 17. f. 5. Eam Beza ita refutat. Non simpliciter dicimus voluntatem Dei intervenire iis quae mala sunt, sed duo adjicimus. Unum, ita intervenire Dei voluntatem in his etiam rebus, ut tamē eas minimē velit aut agat quatenus sunt aliorum malorum poenae, aut per eas Dominus occulta quidem interdum, sed tamen semper iusta sua iudicia exsequitur. Alterum, sic Dominum uti, ut quoties libuit, malis etiam instrumetis ad iusta sua opera peragenda, ut ipsa interim Dei voluntati minime pareant, imo vero ex diametro repugnent. Ibid. p. 390.
units.tr: 42. The fifth calumny is that no adultery, theft or murder is committed without the will of God intervening. Institutes, bk. 1, ch. 17, sec. 5. Beza refutes it thus: "We do not simply say that God's will intervenes in those things which are evil, but we add two points. First, that God's will so intervenes even in these matters that yet he by no means wills or does them as far as they are punishments of other evils, or that through them the Lord, though sometimes in hidden ways, always carries out his just judgments. Second, that the Lord so uses evil instruments, as often as he pleases, to accomplish his just works, that they nonetheless in the meantime do not obey the will of God at all, but indeed resist it utterly." Ibid. p. 390.

units.la: 43. Sexta calumnia est, testari aperte scripturam maleficia designari Deo non solum volente, sed auctore. Ad hanc Beza respondet. Quoties jam ostendi mille restimoniis ex ipso Calvino petitis, hoc ipsum quod ei objicis ab eo oppugnari? Non repetam igitur quod jam millies dixi. p. 391.
units.tr: 43. The sixth calumny is that Scripture openly testifies that wicked deeds are done by God's will and authorship, not merely by his permission. Beza answers this: "How often have I already shown, from a thousand testimonies taken from Calvin himself, that this very thing you object to him is opposed by him? I will not therefore repeat what I have already said a thousand times. P. 391."

units.la: 44. Septima calumnia est, quod homines faciunt dum peccant, ex voluntate Dei facere: liquidem saepissime pugnat Dei voluntas cum praecepto. Hanc Beza refutat. pag. 392. &ff.
units.tr: 44. The seventh calumny is that what men do when they sin they do by the will of God, since God's will very often conflicts with his precept. Beza refutes this, p. 392 ff.

units.la: 45. Octava calumnia est, induratio nem Pharaonis, atque adeo pertinaciam animi & rebellionem opus Dei fuisse vel Moses testimonio, qui totam Pharaonis rebellionem Deo ascribit. Hanc diluit Beza. pag. 398. &c.
units.tr: 45. The eighth calumny is that the hardening of Pharaoh, and thus the obstinacy and rebellion of his mind, was the work of God, as even Moses testifies, who ascribes the whole of Pharaoh's rebellion to God. Beza dissolves this, p. 398 etc.

units.la: 46. Nona calumnia est, voluntatem Dei summam esse indurationis hominum causam. Hanc abstergit ibidem.
units.tr: 46. The ninth calumny is that the will of God is the chief cause of the hardening of men. He wipes this away, ibid.

units.la: 47. Decima calumnia, est, Satanam medacem dacem esse ex imperio Dei. Hanc damnat Beza.p.400.
units.tr: 47. The tenth calumny is that Satan is a liar by the command of God. Beza condemns this, p. 400.

units.la: 48. Undecima calumnia est, Deum non solum velle dare operantibus mala, sed etiâ suggerere pravos affectus & inhonestos, non solum permisisse, sed efficaciter, idque propter suam gloriam. Hanc refutat Beza p.401.&f.
units.tr: 48. The eleventh calumny is that God not only wills to give evil things to those who work, but also suggests wicked and dishonourable desires; that he not only permits them but effectively brings them about, and this for his own glory. Beza refutes this, p. 401 f.

units.la: 49. Duodecima calumnia est, impios in impietate potius opus Dei quàm suum facere, Hanc expungit Beza p.409.
units.tr: 49. The twelfth calumny is that the ungodly, in their ungodliness, do the work of God rather than their own. Beza strikes this out, p. 409.

units.la: 50. Decima-tertia calumnia est, Necessario peccare ex sensu Dei quum ex nostro sive fortuito peccamus.
units.tr: 50. The thirteenth calumny is that we sin of necessity according to God's purpose, when we sin by our own will or by chance.

units.la: 51. Decima-quarta calumnia est, Quae prava sua voluntate perpetrant homines, illa etiam procedere à voluntate Dei Utramque diluit Beza.p.410.&f. Hactenus quatuordecim Castellionis calumniae fuerunt.
units.tr: 51. The fourteenth calumny is that whatever wicked things men perpetrate by their own depraved will also proceed from the will of God. Beza answers both, p. 410 f. So far are the fourteen calumnies of Castellio.

units.la: 52. Sed iniquum est, dices, praecipere quod praestari non posse scias, perinde ac si quis pater filio praecipiat ut rupem comedat. Miram vero argutiam. Nunquam ita creati sunt homines, ut posint rupes vorare. Iniquum igitur fuerit ab eis flagitare ut rupem vorent. Ista vero peccandi necessitas, ista impotentia, quae facit ut ne idonei quidem ad bona cogitanda simus, num à prima illa creatione proficiscitur? imò à viciosiviciositate. Unde autem haec viciositas, nisi quid is sponte defecit à suo opifice, ex quo peccandi necessitas in omnes invasit? Hujus defectionis si merito rei tenentur universi homines, inquit Calvinus, ne se necessitate excusatos putent, in qua ipsa luculentissimam habent damnationis suae causam. Item alibi, quid faciat miser homuncio, inquit, quando cordis mollities, quae ad obedientiam necessaria cerat, illi denegatur? Imo quid tergiversatur, quum duritiem nulli nisi sibi ipsi possit imputare? Denique ut semel recum transigam, audi (si quid audire potes) quàm breviter & quàm appositè omnem hanc controversiam decidat Calvinus ille per cujus latus veritatem oppugnas. Pretendere, inquit, excusationem non licet quod facultas defit, & velut exhausti debitores, solvendo non simus. Non enim convenit ut Dei gloriam metiamur ex nostra facultate. Qualescunque enim simus, manet ille sui similis semper, amicus justitiae, iniquitati infensus. Quicquid a nobis exigat (quia non potest nisi rectum exigere) ex natura obsignatione obsequendi necessitas manet. Quod autem obsequi non possumus, id vitii nostri est. At propria enim cupiditate in qua peccatum regnat, si vincti tenemur, ne soluti simus in patris nostri obsequium, non est cur necessitatem pro defensione causemur, cujus malum
units.tr: 52. "But it is unjust," you will say, "to command what you know cannot be performed, just as if a father should command his son to eat a rock." What a remarkable piece of cleverness! Men were never created in such a way that they could devour rocks; it would therefore be unjust to demand of them that they devour rocks. But does this necessity of sinning, this impotence which makes us unfit even to think good things, arise from that first creation? Rather it arises from vice. And whence this vice, unless man of his own accord fell away from his maker, from which the necessity of sinning has crept upon all? "If all men are rightly held guilty of this defection," says Calvin, "let them not think themselves excused by necessity, in which they have the most manifest cause of their own damnation." Likewise elsewhere: "What," he says, "is a wretched little man to do, when the softness of heart which is necessary for obedience is denied him? Nay, why does he make excuses, since he can impute his hardness to no one but himself?" Finally, to bring this matter to a close once and for all, hear (if you can hear anything) how briefly and how aptly that Calvin, through whose side you attack the truth, settles this whole controversy. "It is not allowed," he says, "to plead as an excuse that the ability is lacking, and that, like exhausted debtors, we are not able to pay. For it is not fitting that we should measure God's glory by our own ability. For whatever we are, he remains always like himself, a friend of justice, hostile to iniquity. Whatever he demands of us (since he can demand only what is right), the necessity of obeying remains by the very nature of the obligation. But that we cannot obey, this is the fault of our vice. For if we are held bound by our own desire, in which sin reigns, so that we are not released into the obedience of our Father, there is no reason for us to plead necessity in our defence, whose evil is both within us and to be imputed to us."

units.la: {Inst.} Calv. lib. 2. c. 3. & 4. cujus malum & intra nos est, & nobis imputandum. Beza p. 415.
units.tr: {Inst.} Calvin, Institutes bk. 2, ch. 3 and 4, whose evil is within us and is to be imputed to us. Beza p. 415.

units.la: CAP. VII. Quodnam sit primum Dei decretum.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. Which is the first decree of God?

units.la: QUamvis decreta Dei omnia ab æterno facta sint, ordo tamen quidam prioris & posterioris secundum illorum naturam & mutuum inter ipsa respectum merito ponitur. In eo theologi variant, qui Christiano clarent nomine. Nec mirum in re divina, & quidem divinarum abstrusissima & sapientissima hominem, lumbricos de terra variare, & qua omnes sumus hebetudine, quando ad lucem illam inaccessam licet in verbi speculo refulgentem, animorum aciem erigimus, nimis caligare. Hanc vero communem humani ingenii imbecillitatem atque caliginem nolle deplorare, sed ex ea ad triumphalem coronam flores colligere velle, quid aliud est, quam laureolam in mustaceo quaerere? Quid vero est, quaeso te, quod hic tibi palmarium putas? Sed & altius, inquis, positis iis hypothesibus provehatur necesse est. Nam si absoluta sunt & inconditionata Dei decreta de singulis rebus, primumque adeo decretum Dei (cui subordinatur postea decretum creationis) est salvare hos, illos; perdere hos
units.tr: Although all of God's decrees were made from eternity, a certain order of prior and posterior is rightly posited, according to their nature and their mutual relation. Theologians who are famous for the Christian name differ on this. Nor is it surprising that in a divine matter, and indeed one of the most abstruse and most wise of divine matters, we who are worms of the earth should disagree, and that we, with all the dullness that we share, grow too dim when we raise the sight of our minds toward that inaccessible light, though it shines in the mirror of the Word. But to refuse to lament this common weakness and darkness of the human mind, and to want to gather from it flowers for a triumphal crown, what else is it than to look for a little laurel wreath in a honey cake? What, I ask you, is it that you think is the prize here? But, you say, with those hypotheses laid down, one must necessarily be carried on higher. For if the decrees of God concerning single things are absolute and unconditioned, and the first decree of God (to which the decree of creation is afterwards subordinated) is to save these, and to destroy those

units.la: hos illos, ad suam gloriam sequitur decretum Dei primum esse de non subiecto, sive de non ente ὧν ὡς: sicut enim subiecta non exsistunt nisi per creationem, ita in conceptu & mente divina non possunt esse nisi per decretum creationis. Docent ergo, Deum ante quam proposuisset creare, statuisse hos, illos servare, hos illos perdere. Cur necesse est, ut altius provehamur? Hypothesis audivisti, quas commodè explicatas autumamus. Interea non habemus, omnia decreta Dei esse absoluta.
units.tr: those, to his own glory, it follows that the first decree of God concerns the non-subject, or non-being [ὧν ὡς]. For just as subjects do not exist except through creation, so in the conception and mind of God they cannot exist except through the decree of creation. They teach, therefore, that God, before he had purposed to create, decided to save these and to destroy those. Why is it necessary that we be carried on higher? You have heard the hypotheses, which we think are conveniently explained. Meanwhile, we do not hold that all of God's decrees are absolute.

units.la: Deinde cogita Arminium in declaratione sua de praedestinatione sententiae, quatuor theologorum de decretis Dei opiniones recitare, ex quibus unam duntaxat, decretum praedestinationis anteponit decreto creationis, quam tamen, ut ipse alibi fatetur, paucissimi amplectuntur. Cur igitur eam urges, Berti? Si tam pauci sunt, qui eam defendunt, nihil attinet eam cum odio theologorum de ecclesia Dei alioqui optime meritorum publice & frequenter impugnare. Nihil enim ab ea periculi erit, si no sint qui amplectantur, nisi paucissimi. Equidem fateor, decretum creationis antecedere ordine naturae decretum praedestinationis, quapropter nemini litem moveo, qui hoc affirmat, sed potius assentipulor, idque suffragantibus plerorumque theologorum calculis, qui in syste-
units.tr: Next, consider that Arminius, in his Declaration on predestination, recites the opinions of four theologians about the decrees of God, and that he alone places the decree of predestination before the decree of creation, which, as he himself admits elsewhere, very few embrace. Why then do you press it, Berti? If there are so few who defend it, there is no point in publicly and repeatedly attacking it with hatred of theologians who have otherwise deserved very well of the Church of God. For there will be no danger from it if there are none who embrace it except a very few. Indeed, I admit that the decree of creation precedes the decree of predestination in the order of nature; therefore I bring no quarrel against anyone who affirms this, but rather I assent to it, and that with the support of the votes of most theologians, who in the system

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAP. VII.

units.la: systematis theologiæ decretum providentiæ, quod est creationis & gubernationis, decreto prædestinationis anteponere consueverunt. Quòd si illi ipsi aliquando aliù decretorum ordinem constituant, non ideo debent sacri fieri & intestabiles. Res enim est sublimis & ardua, nequead salute præcise scitu necessaria: Illi etiam nituntur principio omnium sapientiū calculo approbato: priorem nempe cogitationem de fine esse quàm de mediis. Hinc probabilius ipsis visum est, omnia alia Dei decreta ad hoc unū prædestinationis in quo Deus gloriam justitiæ ac misericordiæ suæ manifestat, tanquam ad scopum referre, uti cætera tanquā media sapienter & sancte subordinentur.
units.tr: Theologians of system have customarily placed the decree of providence, which concerns creation and government, before the decree of predestination. But if some of them at times set up a different order of the decrees, they ought not for that reason to be branded as accursed and detestable. The matter is lofty and difficult, and not strictly necessary to know for salvation. They also rest on a principle approved by the judgment of all the wise, namely that thought about the end comes before thought about the means. Hence it seemed more probable to them that all the other decrees of God should be referred, as to a goal, to this one decree of predestination, in which God displays the glory of his justice and mercy, while the rest are wisely and holily arranged as means.

units.la: Quapropter vim thesis 19. & 20. non sententia, quæ opinione eorum, qui prædestinationis decretum omnium esse primum asserunt, absurdis onerant consequentiis, à quibus tamen te abstinuisse præstaret. Nosti enim quid D. Arminius de ejuscemodi more & modo consequentiarum morojudicet in responsione ad 31. articulos p. 393. Injustitia species est, inquit, impingere alicui consequentias, quas quis ex ipsius dictis nectit, ac si ille sic sentiret, & injustitia major si illa consequentia ex dictis concludi nequeant bona consequentia. Hæc te, Bertii monita Arminii meditameditari & sequi decet, atq; ab odiosis cō-sequentiis deinceps abstinere.
units.tr: Therefore the force of theses 19 and 20 burdens with absurd consequences not the opinion itself but the view of those who assert that the decree of predestination is first of all. From these consequences you would have done well to refrain. You know what Arminius judges of this manner and mode of drawing consequences, in his reply to the 31 articles, p. 393: It is a species of injustice, he says, to fasten upon someone the consequences which a man draws from his statements, as if that person held such views; and it is a greater injustice if those consequences cannot be validly concluded from what was said. You ought to meditate on and follow these admonitions of Bertius and Arminius, and from now on to refrain from hateful consequences.

units.la: CAP. VIII. De forma decretorum Dei.
units.tr: CAP. VIII. On the form of God's decrees.

units.la: PRæclarè imperator Manuel Palæologus: Πίφυκε, inquit, τὸ ἀληθὲς οἰκεῖον τῆς ἀφοεμῆς ἑαυτὸ συνάπτει, i.e. Ea est veritatis natura, ut occasiones & causas stabiliendi se-ipsum ex se quasi ex fonte quodam profundat. Eas si homo non videat vitium non est in in vero, sed in homine. Quapropter, mi Berti, quid cogere pergis? Coguntur, inquis, etiam formam ipsam decretorum aliter concipere, quàm in verbo Dei proponitur. Nos certè non cogimur, si autem alii summi viri Calvinus & Beza id cogerentur maximè, tamen indignum esset eos exagitare, qui nō hostes veritatis, sed patroni fuerunt. Nec oblivioni erat tradendum, quod Calvinus sapienter alicubi monet: Præcipuum religionis nostra caput esse, ut inter nos simus concordes. Alibi idem rectè: Ubi cum professis veritatis hostibus nobis negocium, duo vitia nobis cavenda sunt, ne tacendo aut conniventes videamur blandiri: perfidum enim esset illud silentium, quo proderetur veritas. Rursum ne efferamur petulantia aut immodico calore, quemadmodum sæpe animi plus quam par
units.tr: The Emperor Manuel Palaeologus put it admirably: "Πέφυκε τὸ ἀληθὲς οἰκεῖον τῆς ἀφορμῆς ἑαυτὸ συνάπτειν" (It is the nature of truth to furnish from itself, as from a kind of fountain, the occasions and causes of establishing itself.) If a man does not see these, the fault lies not in the truth but in the man. Why, then, my Berti, do you keep pressing? You say they are compelled to conceive the very form of the decrees otherwise than it is set forth in the Word of God. We certainly are not compelled. But even if the eminent men Calvin and Beza were compelled, it would still be unworthy to harass those who were defenders of the truth, not its enemies. Nor should it be forgotten what Calvin wisely warns somewhere: The chief point of our religion is that we be of one mind among ourselves. Elsewhere he rightly says the same: When we have to deal with those who openly profess enmity to the truth, we must guard against two faults, lest by keeping silent or conniving we seem to flatter them; for that silence would be treacherous, by which the truth would be betrayed. Again, let us not be carried away by petulance or immoderate heat, as the minds of men often boil over in contention more than is fitting.

units.la: In 1. Cor. 1. V. 10. In act. 4. v. 1. par est, in contentione ebulliunt. Jam vero utrerque auctor, Calvinus pariter & Beza, licet alicubi iudicio aut lingua, ut homines œspitent, optimè tamen erga veritatê sunt animati, imò & alios plurimos ore & scriptis animarunt. Vide quid animi sit Calvino: Hoc unum, inquit, solide docendi principium est nihil proferre, nisi quod ex ore Dei prodiisse convenit. Audi quâ mente sit Beza. Nos, inquit, discamus ex Dei verbo non tantum sapere, sed etiam loqui. Unde cõstat, eos decreta Dei non nisi ex Dei verbo concipere voluisse. Quid ergo cogis? quid urges eos aliter? Nos decretorum Dei formam non aliunde petimus quàm ex Dei verbo. Decretum electionis & reprobationis summam euangelii complectitur. Eam habet promissio, quæ ad baptismi institutionem appensa legitur Marc. 16. v. 16. Qui crediderit & baptisatus fuerit, servabitur: qui vero non crediderit condemnabitur. Eam ultimi iudicii processus evidenter exprimit, Matth. 25. ver. 31. & s. Eam ostendit Paulus, quantum ad electionem plenè ad Rom. 8. 28. 29. Novimus autem, iis, qui diligunt Deum omnia simul adiumento esse ad bonum iis videlicet, qui ex proposito ipsius vocati sunt. Nam quos præ novit, etiam prædestinavit, conformandos imagini filii sui; ut sit primogenitus
units.tr: On 1 Cor. 1:10; on Acts 4:1. Indeed each of the two authors, Calvin and Beza alike, though in some places they stumbled in judgment or speech, as men do, were nonetheless most devoted to the truth, and even inspired very many others by their voice and writings. See what Calvin's mind was: This one thing, he says, is the solid principle of teaching: to put forward nothing except what ought to have come forth from the mouth of God. Hear with what mind Beza spoke: Let us learn from the Word of God, he says, not only to be wise but also to speak. From this it is plain that they wished to conceive the decrees of God only from the Word of God. Why, then, do you compel them, why do you press them otherwise? We seek the form of God's decrees from nowhere else than from the Word of God. The decree of election and reprobation comprises the sum of the gospel. The promise that is attached to the institution of baptism has it, read in Mark 16:16: He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned. The course of the last judgment expresses it plainly, Matt. 25:31 and following. Paul sets it out fully as regards election, Rom. 8:28, 29: We know that to those who love God all things work together for good, namely to those who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn

units.la: In act. c. 16. v. 31. tus inter multos fratres. Et Ephes. 1. 4. Sicut elegit nos in ipso ante jacta mundi fundamenta, ut essemus sancti & inculpati coram eo cum charitate. Eam denique quantum ad reprobationem describit Judas v. 4. Nam subrepserunt quidam homines, prius jam olim descripti ad hanc damnationem; impii qui Deinostri gratiam transferunt ad lasciviam & solum illum verum Deum ac Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum negant. Hinc minime approbamus eorum opinionem qui indefinite ac confuse docent electionem factam citra respectum meritorum Christi et fidei, tantum quia Deo ita libuit. Reprobationem quoque factam sine consideratione peccati aut inobedientia, incredulitatis aut impoenitentia, tantum quia ita libuit &c. Sed tamen semper hoc addendum, neminem emergere ex damnatione & fidelem fieri sine gratia singulari Dei; & neminem relinqui nisi juste.
units.tr: On Acts 16:31; among many brothers. And Eph. 1:4: Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love. Finally, as regards reprobation, Jude describes it, v. 4: For certain men have crept in unnoticed, who were long ago marked out for this condemnation: ungodly men, who turn the grace of our God into licentiousness and deny the only true God and our Lord Jesus Christ. Hence we by no means approve the opinion of those who teach, indefinitely and confusedly, that election was made without regard to the merits of Christ and to faith, merely because it so pleased God. Reprobation too was made without consideration of sin or of disobedience, of unbelief or of impenitence, merely because it so pleased God, and so on. Yet this must always be added: no one emerges from condemnation and becomes a believer without the singular grace of God; and no one is left behind except justly.

units.la: CAP. IX. An credentes postquam semel vera fide donati sunt, possint peccatis suis gratia Dei & sua salute excidere?
units.tr: CAP. IX. Whether believers, once they have truly been granted faith, can by their sins fall from the grace of God and from their salvation?

units.la: ARcem controversiae, quae inter nos hactenus fuit, aggrederis, verumtamen non directe, sed oblique, dum interabsurda eam habes, quae occultae theologiae falsitas
units.tr: You approach the citadel of the controversy that has existed between us hitherto, yet not directly but obliquely, while you hold it among the absurdities, which is the falsehood of that hidden theology

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: sitas pariat. Etsi autem alibi hac de re multa dixerimus, & mox plura sint dicenda: tamen hic obiter est, quod monendum arbitror. Nimirum ne ita confuse & indistincte nobis attribuas, quod sine justa distinctione nemo prudens admittit. Postremum, ais, quum Deus ubique nos admoneat, ut salutem nostram in timore operemur, ne deficiamus & excidamus salute, audent isti contendere, credentes postquam semel vera fide donati sunt, non posse peccatis suis gratia Dei et sua salute excidere. Asimiliter Hyperaspistes tuus calumniatur mentem meam: Nam quum ABSOLUTAM, inquiens, & irrevocabilem posuisses perseverantiam in iis qui semel crediderunt perseverantia necessitatem, vidisti ipsis non posse proponi rejectionis periculum. p. 184. Neque aliter verba mea depravasti: Qui absolutam, scribens, perseverantiae necessitatem oppugnant, videntur sibi errorem & humanam aliquam confidentiam invadere. p. 180. Hic ita sententiam orthodoxorum recitas, asti absolute & omni modo negent credentes deficere posse; id quod nunquam &is aut mihi in mentem venit. Ex praecipuis vide clarissimum d. Piscatorem, qui in responsione apologetica ad parasceven D. Vorstii cap. 9. multo aliter ac distinctius eam rem disceptat. Vide etiam, si placet, ejusdem
units.tr: produces. Although I have said much on this matter elsewhere, and more is still to be said, I think it worth a brief reminder here. You must not attribute things to us so confusedly and indiscriminately, which no sensible person accepts without a proper distinction. You say at the end: Since God everywhere admonishes us to work out our salvation in fear, lest we fail and fall away from salvation, these men dare to contend that believers, once they have been granted true faith, cannot by their sins fall from the grace of God and their salvation. In the same way your Hyperaspistes slanders my meaning: For when you had laid down, he says, an ABSOLUTE and irrevocable perseverance in those who have once believed, you saw that no danger of rejection could be set before them. p. 184. You have distorted my words no differently: Those who oppose the absolute necessity of perseverance, I write, seem to themselves to be invaded by error and some human confidence. p. 180. Here you recite the opinion of the orthodox as if they absolutely and in every way deny that believers can fall away, which never came into the mind of either them or me. Among the chief authorities see the most distinguished Mr Piscator, who in his apologetic answer to the Parasceve of Dr Vorstius, chapter 9, treats that matter in a far different and more distinct manner. See also, if you please, his notes on Dr Vorstius's friendly comparison, section 114, p. 194.

units.la: notas ad amicam collationem D. Vorstii sect. 114. p. 194. Ego quidem ad quaestionem propositam citra distinctiones e verbo Dei petitas non posse convenienter respondere si semper judicavi & adhuc judico. Hinc est quod tractatu 1. de perseverantia sanctorum cap. 3. non una, sed decem conclusionibus sententiae nostrae veritatem pronunciare necesse fuit. Accuratissime enim distinguendum hic est, sed tenente ipso D. Vorstio, non modo inter defectionem ipsam & deficiendi potentiam; sed etiam inter potentiam non-deficiendi proximam & remotam, sive mavis naturalem & supernaturalem; interque causas tum deficiendi, tum cavendi intrinsecas & extrinsecas; sive quae a nobis ipsis vel ab aliis extra nos exsistunt. His talibus observatis, dextereq; explicatis citra omnem contradictionem pronunciari poterit, Credentes posse deficere, &, credentes non posse deficere. Tu quidem haec in hyperaspistę tuo vulpium paria vocas: sed in eo ne erraveris: mox, Deo gratiam largiente, efficiam, & ostendam vulpes quidem esse eas, atque opinionum tuarum & errorum segetes validissime exurant. Nunquam id tentasem, si tuus Hymenaeus desertor intra modestiae abs D. Arminio olim observatas limites continere voluisset. Omnia illa
units.tr: For my part, I have always judged, and still judge, that the question proposed cannot be answered properly without distinctions drawn from the Word of God. That is why, in the first treatise on the perseverance of the saints, chapter 3, I found it necessary to set forth the truth of our view not in one conclusion but in ten. For this matter must be distinguished most carefully, and, with Dr Vorstius himself holding to it, not only between the defection itself and the power of falling away, but also between the power of not falling away that is proximate and that which is remote, or, if you prefer, natural and supernatural; and between the causes, both of falling away and of guarding against it, which are intrinsic and extrinsic, that is, those which exist in ourselves or in others outside us. With these distinctions observed and skilfully explained, it can be stated without any contradiction that believers can fall away, and that believers cannot fall away. You, in your Hyperaspistes, call these pairs of foxes; but do not be mistaken in that. Soon, with God granting grace, I will show that they are indeed foxes, and that they will most powerfully burn up the crops of your opinions and errors. I would never have attempted this if your deserter Hymenaeus had been willing to keep within the limits of modesty once observed by Dr Arminius. All those things

units.la: {*} Ad Arminium. ille pro sanctorum apostasia calidè, quan- quam frigidis saepè ratiunculis, definit, quae D. Arminius in dubiis suis numerabat. Con- sessio illius est. Sed utrum ii (Credentes intelligit) per negligentiam initium suae in Christo existentiae deserere non possint, praesenti huic mundo rursus adhaerere à sana doctrina semel illis tradita deficere, bonam conscientiam amittere, gratiam irritam facere, id vero uti ex scriptura diligenter inquiratur, utile esse arbitror, simulque etiam necesse fore ut de eo in primo nostro conventu agamus. Ingenuè tamen affirmo, nunquam me docuisse quod vere credens aut totaliter aut finaliter à fide deficiat, sicque pereat; quamvis non dissimulem esse loca scripturae quae id videantur praeseferre: ad quae responsiones ejusmodi videre mihi non licuit, quae sese mihi per omnia probaverint; quemadmodum etiam ab altera parte loca quaedam adducuntur observatu etiam illa non indigna.
