Assimiliter in examine libelli de praedestinationis modo & ordine editi à Perkinso: Quod fides vera, ait, & salutifera totaliter vel finaliter excidat, non facile audim dicere: licet plerique ex patribus saepe id dicere videantur, p. 224. Tibi vero, clarissime Berti, qui absteindisentiunt, non aliter nisi Borboritae, Manichaei, Stoici clarè audiunt. Nempe hi nec dissentire à te salva gratia, nec consentire salva conscientia possunt. Quid ergo facto opus est? Id quod Bernhardus suadet sermone 23. in cant. Facile praesit qui matrem virtutum Discretionem perfecte fortitudinis est; vino charitatis usque ad contemptum sui gloriae inebriatus. Virtus liquidem discretionis absque charitatis fervore jacet: & fervor vehemens absque discretionis temperamento precipitat. Utinam vero, o Bernarde, mortalibus, ut suades, ita persuaderes idomnibus! Si forte apud patres incommoda distio, apud recentiores Dei servos duriuscula phrasis occurrat, aut sententia quam aut non capiamus, aut digerere nequeamus, age cogitemus nos eorum filios esse, quos deceat navos illorum non prodere, non cum degenere Chamo aliis deridendos propinare, sed nosse, sed tegere, sed tolerare, semper quo animo repetamus, prius suam autoram habere cujusque fidem, quam ad meridiem perveniat, imo quum exquisitissimi judicii theologi in quaestionis alicujus difficilioris decisione convenire inter se non possint, non illico sibi invicem libellum repudii mittere debere, & tanquam ab ecclesia Christi separatis fratrum jus renunciare, etiam infirmioribus fili acrimonia hujus vel auctorem esse vel occasionem praebere.
units.tr: {*} To Arminius. He, concerning the apostasy of the saints, defines warmly, though often with cold little arguments, what Dr Arminius counted among his doubts. His statement is this: But whether they (he means believers) through negligence can abandon the beginning of their existence in Christ, turn back to the present world, fall from the sound doctrine once delivered to them, lose a good conscience, make grace void: this, I think, is useful to inquire into carefully from Scripture, and at the same time it will also be necessary for us to deal with it at our first conference. Yet I frankly affirm that I have never taught that one who truly believes falls from faith either totally or finally, and so perishes; although I do not deny that there are passages of Scripture which seem to suggest this, to which I have not been able to see replies of such a kind as have proved themselves to me in every respect; just as, on the other side, certain passages are adduced which are also not unworthy of notice. Similarly, in his examination of the little book on the mode and order of predestination published by Perkins: That true and saving faith should wholly or finally fall away, he says, I do not readily hear said; although many of the Fathers often seem to say it, p. 224. But to you, most distinguished Bertius, who disagree with these men, they clearly sound like nothing other than Borborites, Manichaeans, or Stoics. For these men can neither disagree with you without loss of grace, nor agree with you without loss of conscience. What then must be done? What Bernard advises in sermon 23 on the Song of Songs: that he who is drunk with the wine of charity, to the point of contempt for his own glory, easily becomes perfect in fortitude, since discretion is the mother of the virtues. For the virtue of discretion lies dead without the fervour of charity, and a vehement fervour without the moderation of discretion rushes headlong. Would that, O Bernard, you could persuade all mortals to what you urge on them! If perhaps among the Fathers an inconvenient expression, or among more recent servants of God a rather harsh phrase, or a statement which we either do not grasp or cannot digest, comes to hand, let us then think of ourselves as their sons, who ought not to betray the nakedness of their fathers, nor hand them over to others to be mocked like degenerate Ham, but to know, to cover, and to bear with them; and always with this attitude let us recall that each man's faith has its own dawn before it reaches its noon. Indeed, when theologians of the most exquisite judgement cannot agree among themselves in deciding some more difficult question, they ought not straightway to send one another a bill of divorce, and renounce the rights of brethren as if they were separated from the Church of Christ, nor, by the bitterness of this, give occasion or cause for offence even to the weaker brethren.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: Quòd Bertius quemadmodum theologi, quorum sententiam arrodit, revera duplicem DEI voluntatem asserat.
units.tr: That Bertius, like the theologians whose opinion he gnaws at, in fact asserts a twofold will of God.

units.la: Quî fit, doctissime Berti, ut postquam in publica theologorum opera sævitum est, tua tandem sententia cum illorum mente coalescat? An interposito tempore tam brevi in locum irae subiit verecundia? Neque, verò, ais, haec nostra eo spectant ut velimus negare, esse aliquam in Deo voluntatem arcanam aut omnia quae agit aut agere vult Deus, verbo expressa esse, sed ut intelligentes aliam esse voluntatem in Deo, rerum quas ipse agere vult, aliam rerum quas à nobis fieri vult, sciamus, nos ad illam PRÆCIPUE respicere debere: utque ostendamus nullam esse voluntatem in Deo, quae à verbo patefacto dissentiat, imò verò fieri non posse, ut rem eandem Deus occulta voluntate fieri à nobis nolit, revelata velit. Plura revelatæ & occultæ theologiæ, quos appellas, patronis, quàm velint ac postulent, hîc cedis & assentiris. Omnia enim ista accipiant, nisi quòd fritinnis, nos ad illam, purà revelatam Dei voluntatem PRÆCIPUE respicere debere. Imò ad illam solam nos respicere. spicere oportet, nō autem rimari eam quæ in Deo latet. Revelávit autem Deus tum quæ ipse de nobis fit facturus, tum quæ nos facere velit, quantum ad salutem nostram satis est. Fateris præterea arcanam esse Dei voluntatem, quantum ad omnes eventus singulares, quos ipse vel facit vel ab aliis fieri vult. Alii non concederent id de omnibus, sed de iis duntaxat, quos in verbo suo non præcise ac perspicuè prædixit. Fateris denique permissionem peccati, ejusque ad bonum finem directionem esse abstrusæ sapientiæ opus. Ita sanè est, & omnes theologi confitentur: & imprimis Calvinus, quem hic reum agis, sæpissime erumpit in vocem Augustini: Magna Dei opera & exquisita, in omnes voluntates ejus, ut miro & ineffabili modo non fiat praeter ejus voluntatem, quod fit contra ejus voluntatem. Post hæc omnia diffiteri te posse aut velle non puto, duplicem in Deo voluntatem considerari à te, quemadmodum alii theologi, aliam approbantem bonorum, malorum verò permittentem aliam considerant. Ita enim exserte docet Zanchius lib. 3. de nat. Dei cap. 4. thes. 7. & 8. pag. 348. 349. Deum peccata proprie non velle, sed tantum permittere. Quamvis autem volens Deus permittat peccata, non tamen sequitur quod velit fieri peccata, & quidem voluntate efficaci. Aliud enim est velle aliquid fieri, & aliud velle permittere ut aliquid fiat, id quod eleganter explicatum legitur apud Rupertum Tuicensem lib. de voluntate Dei cap. 3. & in lib. de omnipotentia Dei cap. 23. 24. 25. Omitto hic sciens prudens Lombardum, omitto scholasticos doctores, qui hanc rem satis erudite ac bene explicuerunt, omitto Bellarminum & alios pontificios, inter quos iste licet à syrtibus sibi cavere voluit, in eas tamen periculosissime impegit. Unus esto ex nostratibus instar omnium D. Zacharias Ursinus, felicissimus Philippi discipulus & imitator, multorum cum honore ac perpetua nominis gloria praeceptor, qui confessionem nostram proprie expediat: Deus, ait ille, dupliciter velle & nolle aliquid dicitur, videlicet velle vel quoad approbationem & effectionem simul, aut quoad approbationem tantum, sub qua & mandatum comprehenditur: non autem quoad effectionem (nempe quando non vult absolute, sed cum conditione, ibi non operatur etiam, nisi conditio sit impleta, & tamen ibi fit voluntas Dei & est efficax semper eo modo, quo vult, sed conditione impleta: qua non impleta non vult). Nolle autem dicitur quippiam, quoad impro-
units.tr: How does it happen, most learned Bertius, that after such savage attacks on the public works of the theologians, your opinion has at last come into agreement with their mind? Has modesty come into the place of anger after so short an interval? "Yet," you say, "these remarks of ours do not aim to deny that there is in God some secret will concerning all the things he does or wills to be done, which is not expressed in the Word. They aim rather to make us understand that there is one will of God concerning the things he himself wills to do, and another concerning the things he wills us to do, and that we must chiefly look to the latter; and to show that there is no will in God that dissents from the revealed Word, nor can it be that God wills a thing to be done by us in his hidden will and does not will it in his revealed will." In this you yield and agree with more than the defenders of the so-called revealed and secret theology, whom you name, would wish or demand. For they would accept all of this, except that you say "we must chiefly look to that" and then, in a sense, "the purely revealed will of God." Indeed we ought to look to that alone, and not to pry into what lies hidden in God. God has revealed both what he himself will do concerning us and what he wills us to do, and this is enough for our salvation. Moreover you admit that the will of God is hidden as regards all particular events, which he either brings about himself or wills to be brought about by others. Others would not grant this of all events, but only of those which he has not foretold precisely and plainly in his Word. Finally you admit that the permission of sin, and its direction to a good end, is a work of deep wisdom. So it is indeed, and all theologians confess it; and especially Calvin, whom you here accuse, very often breaks out into the words of Augustine: "The great and exquisite works of God are such that, in all his wills, in a wonderful and ineffable manner, nothing is done outside his will which is done contrary to his will." After all this, I do not think you can or will deny that you consider a twofold will in God, as other theologians do: they distinguish one will which approves good things, and another which permits evil things. Zanchius teaches this plainly in book 3 on the nature of God, chapter 4, theses 7 and 8, pages 348 and 349: that God does not properly will sins, but only permits them. Yet although God, willing, permits sins, it does not follow that he wills them to be done, and indeed with an efficacious will. For it is one thing to will that something be done, and another to will to permit that something be done; this is explained elegantly in Rupert of Deutz, in his book on the will of God, chapter 3, and in his book on the omnipotence of God, chapters 23, 24 and 25. I pass over here the wise and learned Lombard; I pass over the scholastic doctors, who explained this matter learnedly and well; I pass over Bellarmine and the other Papists, among whom that man, though he wished to beware of the quicksands, has nonetheless most dangerously run aground. Let one of our own men stand for all, the venerable Zacharias Ursinus, the most fortunate disciple and imitator of Philip, teacher of many with honour and lasting glory of name, who expounds our confession precisely: "God," he says, "is said to will and not will something in two ways: namely, to will either as regards approval and effecting together, or as regards approval only, under which a command is also included, but not as regards effecting" (namely, when he does not will absolutely but with a condition; then he does not work unless the condition is fulfilled, and yet there the will of God is present and is always efficacious in the way he wills, but when the condition is fulfilled; if it is not fulfilled, he does not will it). "But something is said not to be willed, as regards disapproval together with the hindrance of the effect, or as regards disapproval only, and not as regards hindrance." And a little after: "God can will nothing except what agrees with his own nature and goodness; nor does Scripture say anywhere that God wills those things which are contrary to his nature, insofar as they are such." I would therefore prefer this one theologian, so judicious, so grave and so pious, to a thousand curses from Castellio or others, from whom most of those calumnies come by which pious teachers are torn to pieces. Let Calvin be added to this as well, whom many hate undeservedly, yet to whom very many owe much. For, I beg you, what moderation or what conscience or shame is there in accusing Calvin, the most bitter enemy of the Libertines above all others, and all our churches which profess one and the same doctrine, of impiety, as if we made God the author of evil? I hope, my dear Bertius, that since charity hopes all things, you will not in future tear apart the sincere and pure doctrine of the Church with this biting of yours, but that, mindful of the apostolic admonition, you will remember with me always: "The whole law is fulfilled in one word, namely, You shall love your neighbour as yourself. But if you bite and devour one another, take heed lest you be consumed by one another."

units.la: § 4. bationem hationem per inhibitionem effectus simul, aut quo ad improbationem tantum, non autem quoad inhibitionem. Et post paulum; Nihil Deus velle potest nisi ipsius natura & bonitati conveniens; nec usquam quae natura ipsius advertantur, quatenus talia sunt, velle Deum sacra scriptura dicit. Hunc ergo unum theologum, tam cordatum, tam gravem, tamque pium vel mille maledictis Castellionibus, aut aliis, a quibus plerisque illae calumniae quibus pii doctores proscinduntur, praetulerim. Huc etiam accedat Calvinus, quem immerito oderunt multi, cui tamen debent plurimi. Cuius enim obsecro moderatio est, aut cuius etiam conscientiae & pudoris, Calvinum, si nihil aliud, certe Libertinorum hostem unum omnium acerrimum & nostras omnes ecclesias unam & eandem doctrinam profitentes impietatis accusare, quasi nos Deum faciamus malī auctorem? Te quoque spero, mi Berti, quum charitas omnia speret, deinceps sinceraм & castam ecclesiae doctrinam venato hoc morsu non esse laceraturum, sed apostolici moniti mecum perpetuo memorem fore: Tota lex uno verbo completur, ipso videlicet, Diliges proximum tuum, ut teipsum. Quod si alii alios mordetis & devoratis, videte ne vicissim alii ab aliis consumamini.
units.tr: § 4. improbation, by inhibiting the effect together with it, or as to disapproval only and not as to inhibition. And a little later: God can will nothing except what agrees with his own nature and goodness, and Scripture says nowhere that God wills those things which are contrary to his nature, insofar as they are such. I would therefore prefer this one theologian, so judicious, so serious and so pious, to a thousand curses from Castellios or others, from whom most of those calumnies come by which the pious teachers are torn apart. Let Calvin also be added, whom many hate undeservedly and yet very many owe a great deal to. For, I beg you, what restraint is there, or what conscience or shame, in accusing Calvin, the most bitter enemy of the Libertines at least if of nothing else, and all our churches that profess one and the same doctrine, of impiety, as if we made God the author of evil? I hope too, my Berti, that since charity hopes all things, you will not tear the sincere and pure doctrine of the Church with this biting, but will remember with me always the admonition of the apostle: The whole law is fulfilled in one word, namely, You shall love your neighbour as yourself. But if you bite and devour one another, take heed that you are not consumed by one another.

units.la: QVemadmodum humanae societati, cui natura devinxit omnes, nihil tristius, nihilq; funestius est discordia: ita Christianae rei- publicae, cujus nos cives fecit gratia, nihil desiderabilius, nihilque melius obtingere potest quàm concordiae in religiosa veritate stabilis concentus & harmonia. Istud gentilium prudentissimi viderunt, qui concordia res parvas crescere, discordia maximas dilabi, uno ore confessi sunt omnes. Hoc coelestissimae humani generis deliciae, unicus servator noster Iesus Christus supremâ lege suâ sancivit: Mandatum, inquiés, novum do vobis ut alii alios diligatis: sicut, inquam, dilexi vos ut etiam diligatis alii alios. Ex hoc omnes cognoscent vos esse discipulos meos, si charitate habueritis alii in alios. Hoc insignissimus servatoris nostri typus, regius psaltes decantavit: Ecce quam bonum & quam amoenum est, habitare fratres etiam unâ. Est ut ut unguentum illud optimum superfusum capiti, descendens super barbam, barbam Aharonis; quod descendit usque ad oram vestimenti ejus. Ut ros Hermonis, ut qui descendit super montes Zionis: nam illic mandat DOMINUS benedictionem suam, vitamque usque in seculum. Hoc divinus apostolus Paulus diligentissime suadet: Satis solicitint servetis consensionem spiritus in vinculo pacis. Ut sitis in unum corpus & in unum spiritum, quemadmodum vocati estis in unam spem vocationis vestræ.
units.tr: As nothing is more sad or deadly to human society, to which nature has bound us all, than discord, so nothing more desirable or better can befall the Christian commonwealth, of which grace has made us citizens, than a stable harmony and concord in religious truth. The wisest of the Gentiles saw this, and all of them agreed with one voice that small things grow by concord and great things fall apart by discord. Our only Saviour, Jesus Christ, the heavenly delight of the human race, sanctioned this by his supreme law: "A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another; as I have loved you, so also love one another. By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another" [John 13:34-35]. The royal psalmist sang this as a most notable type of our Saviour: "Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity. It is like the best ointment poured on the head, running down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which ran down to the hem of his garment; like the dew of Hermon, which falls upon the mountains of Zion, for there the LORD commands his blessing, and life for evermore. The divine apostle Paul urges this most earnestly: "Be diligent to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace; that you may be one body and one Spirit, as you were called in one hope of your calling" [Eph. 4:3-4].

units.la: Quod si alii alios mordetis & devoratis, videte ne vicissim ab aliis consumamini. Precor autem vos, fratres, ut observetis dissidiorum et scandalorum auctores, contra doctrinam, quam vos didicistis: & declinetis ab eis. Nam qui ejusmodi sunt, Domino nostro Jesu Christo non serviunt, sed suo ventri: & per blandiloquentiam & assentationem corda hominum minime malorum seducunt. Hoc Petrus apostolorum similiter monet: Deinde omnes estote concordes, mutuo misericordiam proni, compatientes: fraterna ...
units.tr: But if you bite and devour one another, take care lest you in turn be consumed by one another. I beg you, brothers, to mark those who cause divisions and offences, contrary to the doctrine you have learned, and to turn away from them. For such men do not serve our Lord Jesus Christ but their own belly, and by smooth speech and flattery they seduce the hearts of the unsuspecting. The apostle Peter likewise admonishes this: "Finally, be all of one mind, sympathetic, loving the brothers, compassionate, brotherly ..."

units.la: Non reddentes malum pro malo, aut convicium pro convicio, sed contrà benedicentes: ut qui sciatis vos ad hoc vocatos esse ut benedictionis hereditatem possideatis. Itaque qui vult vitam diligere, & videre dies bonos, coerceat linguam suam a malo, & labia sua ne loquantur dolum. Declinet a malo, & faciat bonum: quaerat pacem, & persequatur eam. Item, Ad hoc ipsum vero vos omni praeterea collato studio, adjicite fidei vestrae virtutem, virtuti vero scientiam, scientiae vero continentiam, continentiae vero tolerantiam, tolerantiae vero pietatem, pietati vero animum in fratres propensum, animo vero in fratres propensio, charitatem. Haec enim si vobis adsint & exuberent, non inertes vos nec infructuosos efficient in Domini nostri Jesu Christi cognitione. Nam cui haec non adsunt, is caecus est nihil procul cernens, oblitus sese a veteribus peccatis suis fuisse purgatum. Hoc illustrissimus princeps ac dominus, D. Fridericus III. felicissimae memoriae, comes palatinus ad Rhenum sacri Romani imperii archidapifer & elector in confessione fidei suae testamento inserta pie ac prudenter inculcavit: Tertio, & praecipue, inquiens, moneo & hortor charissimos filios meos ut sibi quam diligentissime a turbulētis tam ecclesiarum, quam scholarum ministris cavent, qui nunc in religionis & fidei negociis omnis generis contentiones, logomachias, et exitiales condemnationes in pias ecclesias & scholas, quae tamen in fundamento ac praecipuis Christiana religionis capitibus consentiunt, & salutem suam una nobiscum in unicum nostrum servant. servatorem Jesum Christum collocant, ex mera ambitione & pervcrso zelo, ac pratextu ministerii sui, per quod spiritum sanctum mundum arguere videri volunt, idque indicta causa, necsine scandalo introducere, & non minus atque in exsecrando papatu factitatum est, tam in magistratuum, quam in subditorum conscientias dominari, & sibi novum quendam primatum passim erigere atque constituere conantur. Ex qua resane non tantum & in politica & in ecclesiastica gubernatione distractiones et exulcerationes animorum, et utriusque illius gubernationis perturbationes & interitus sequuntur, verum etiam papa & ejus satellitio praebetur occasio veram nostram Christianamque religionem ferro flamma, exsulibus, aliisque innumeris supplicis persequendi, suamque Tyrannidem hoc modo stabiliendi; qua res quantas et quam miserandas pepererit distractiones, miserias & calamitates, etiam nostra hac atas nimis, proh dolor, multa in electorum aliorumque Germaniae principum provinciis, nec non apud exteras & vicinas gentes exstant exempla, ex quibus merito omnes Christiani principes ecclesiae & schola exemplum sibi quod exsufit capere, ideoque summopere a turbulentis illis hominibus & pacis ac tranquillitatis publicae inimicis sibi cavere, nec permittere, ut ab illis occupentur, & vel inter se, vel contra alios exacerbentur, aut a se invicem divellantur ac distrahantur, sed multo potius ejusmodi homines vitare & fugere, & si nulla emendationis in illis spes appareat, prorsus a se removere, nec se horrenda illius & exsecranda persequutionis & indigna innocentium hominum cædis, quæ in imperio Germanico, & apud alias exteras nationes ex his minime Christianis condemnationibus consequuta sunt, socios & participes facere debebant, sicuti hac de re inter me aliosque electores & principes non semel ex jam dictis, aliisque pluribus piis & gravibus causis convenit, sic tamen, ut hac ratione nihil piis ecclesiarum ministris quod attinet ad debita eorum, quæ quotidie offeruntur, vitiorum reprehensionem, & correctionem, & errorum Christiana adhibita moderatione & æquitate ex verbo Dei desumtam refutationem, quæ non ad destructionem, sed ad ædificationem & emendationem dirigenda & instituenda est, derogetur.
units.tr: "Not rendering evil for evil, or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary blessing, knowing that you were called to this, that you might inherit a blessing. For he who wishes to love life and see good days, let him restrain his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit. Let him turn from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it" [1 Pet. 3:9-11]. Likewise: "To this very end, bringing all diligence, add to your faith virtue, to virtue knowledge, to knowledge self-control, to self-control patience, to patience godliness, to godliness brotherly affection, and to brotherly affection love. For if these things are in you and abound, they will make you neither idle nor unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For he in whom these things are not present is blind, seeing nothing afar off, having forgotten that he was purged from his former sins" [2 Pet. 1:5-9]. This most illustrious prince and lord, D. Frederick III of most happy memory, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Archsteward of the Holy Roman Empire and Elector, piously and prudently inculcated this in the confession of his faith inserted in his testament: "Thirdly, and above all, I say, I advise and exhort my dearest sons to guard themselves most carefully against the troublemaking ministers of both churches and schools, who now in matters of religion and faith stir up contentions of every kind, word-battles, and deadly condemnations against pious churches and schools, which nevertheless agree in the foundation and chief heads of the Christian religion, and keep their salvation together with us in our one Saviour Jesus Christ, placing it in him, out of sheer ambition and perverse zeal, under the pretext of their ministry, by which they wish to appear to convict the world of the Holy Spirit; and they do this without a hearing of the case and not without scandal. It has been done no less than in the accursed papacy: they seek to lord it over the consciences of magistrates as well as subjects, and they strive to set up and establish for themselves a certain new primacy everywhere. From this there follow not only divisions and festering of minds in both political and ecclesiastical government, and the disturbance and ruin of both kinds of government, but also an occasion is given to the pope and his satellites to persecute our true Christian religion with sword, fire, exile, and countless other torments, and thus to establish their tyranny. What great and miserable divisions, miseries and calamities this has produced, our own age, alas, has too many examples of, in the provinces of the electors and other princes of Germany, and also among foreign and neighbouring nations. From these examples all Christian princes should rightly take warning for themselves, and therefore should greatly beware of those turbulent men, enemies of public peace and tranquillity, and not allow themselves to be occupied by them, nor be provoked by them against one another or against others, nor be torn and pulled apart from one another. Rather, they should avoid and flee such men, and if no hope of amendment in them appears, remove them utterly from themselves; nor should they make themselves partners and sharers in that horrible and accursed persecution and unworthy slaughter of innocent men which followed in the German empire and among other foreign nations from these by no means Christian condemnations. Just as concerning this matter it has been agreed between me and other electors and princes more than once, for the reasons already stated and many other pious and weighty causes, yet in such a way that by this arrangement nothing is taken away from the pious ministers of the churches as regards the reproof and correction of vices, which are owed and offered daily, and the refutation of errors drawn from the Word of God, applied with Christian moderation and fairness, which is to be directed and undertaken not for destruction but for edification and amendment."

units.la: Hoc denique piissimus juxta & prudentissimus memoriæ nostræ theologus, D. Franciscus Junius olim in ipsa Leidensi Academia professor celeberrimus pro sua prudentia animadvertit & expendit. Postea quam enim annos xxv. in Germania, communi & charissima patria nostra vixisset, irenicum scripsit, & permanus illustrissimi ac potentissimi principis, dn. dn. MAURI-TII Hassiae Landgravii &c. veluti τὸ φιλοσ-ῶν ... ἀπ' ἀλλήλων ... ei ab internecinis theologorum digladiantium contentionibus, si potest, pacandae obtulit. Inibi pacem suadet, concordiam optat, dissensiones sopit, redimendae pacis conditiones exponit, rixatum in commoda enumerat, concordiae commoda commendat, nihil non agit ut aeternum veritatis & charitatis conjugium impetret. O laudabilem summi theologi laborem! o sus-piciendum conatum! o consiliorum ampletendam prudentiam! Sed quotusquisque nostrum est, qui ad ista omnia tam bona, tam honesta, tam utilia, tam jucunda, tamque necessaria & salutaria animum advertat? Christiano nomine gaudemus & gloriamur omnes, pontificii pariter & protestantes. At quam parum, pro dolor, tanti nominis mensuram implemus: iidem omnes, pontificii pariter & protestantes? Quam acerbe scribimus, quam amarulenter dicimus in nos invicem & invehimur? Ubi moderatio Christiana haeret? ubi charitas obdormivit & prope dixerim omnis exstincta jacet? Hanc oportet morum feritatem exuere, & homines induere & viscera Christi. E multis seculi nostri litigiis unum longe maximum & horrendum ut producam resipsa postulat. Innocentissimis Dei fer- vis, viris Christianis imputatur hoc plusquam diabolicum paradoxum: Deum esse peccati auctorem. Hoc illis imputatur a viris in papatu & extra eum, quitamen omnes Christiani volunt videri, & vero etiam multi revera sunt. Triftisfimam hac de re querelam legimus apud doctissimum D. Bogerman- num in annotationibus ad pietatem ordinum Hollandiae & Weftfrisiae a clarissimo D.Hug.Grotio vindicatam: Vel hoc solum nomine plerique odium alicui conflant quod Calvini & Bezae fit studiosus: quin etiam in eo toti sunt, ut hos Dei servos velut Turcis & Maranis crudeliores, totosque sanguinarios plebi reddant exosos, & apud multos hoc jam dedere effectum, ut ab ipso horum doctorum nomine abhorreant, uti quotidiana testatur experientia. Videat lector inter alia quamplurima hujus farinae scripta, campanam incendiaria, perspicillum cryptallinum, &c. nec mitius hoc genus hominum tractaret ipsum magnae Britanniae regem, nisi fastigium formidaret regium. Quem vero hominem sana mente praedictum inter Judaeos, Turcas & paganos a Christiana fide non absterreat vel sola hujus tae Christianorum cotroversiae auditio? Ab omni enim religione imo ab omni ratione alienum est summum bonum esse mali, quod cum virtute pugnat, causam. Quem igitur non modo fana sed & per fidem illuminata ratione ornatum & orthodoxa religione imbutu non offendat has voces inter Christianos audiri? Hujus erroris & blasphemiæ à Papistis, à Lutheranis, &c, quod vehementer deplorandum est, ab iis etiam qui in puerioribus ecclesiis educati sunt, accusantur viri quibus tamen nihil ejusmodi in mentem venit unquam. Damnat enim blasphemiam hanc uti & alias omnes quas illis multorum ira & γλωσσαλγία falso objectat, horum publica scripta, damnant publicæ confessiones, publicæ conciones damnant, damnant ecclesiarum, quibus præsunt, publicæ praxes, damnant tot paratissimæ mortes & martyria. Quid ergo est, obscro vos viri Christiani, quod in tanta testimoniorum luce & multitudine adhuc malignis suspicionibus indulgemus, alii aliorum dicta & scripta pervertimus, & viros alioqui piissimos deque ecclesia Dei meritissimos leviter arrepta unius aut alterius vocula occasione posthabitis mille quaju-ratis, qua injuratis tam horribiliu dogmatum negationibus & publicis refutationibus, tam temere tamque crudeliter condemnamus? Quid est, quod δυσψης illa & vere barbara ἀλλοφωνία tam paucis displi-cet. cet?. Ah mitiores simus, qui Christiani su- mus! Ah leniores simus, qui Christi corpus simus, ut Christi spiritus in nobis veluti corpore suo vires suas exserere videatur! Mirum quod non videamus dissidia nostra esse amicorum dispendia, hostium compe- dia (ut cum Hieronymo loquar) & publi- ca irae divinae incendia. Audiamus verbis Augustini tam augustis, tam piis in psal. 122. quibus Christianos dissidentes in fide affatur: Quid litigamus? fratres sumus. Non intestatus mortuus est pater: fecit testa- mentum, & sic mortuus est, & resurrexit. Tam- diu cotenditur de hereditate mortuorum, quam- diu testamentum proferatur in publicum, ta- cent omnes ut tabula operiantur & recitentur. Iudex intentus audit, advocati silent: pracones silentium faciunt: universus populus suspensus est, ut legantur verba mortui, non sententiis in monumento. Ille sine sensu iacet in monumento, & valent verba ipsius: sedet Christus in caelo et contradicitur eius testamento? Aperi, legamus, fratres sumus, quare contendimus? placetur animus noster? Non sine testamento dimisit nos pater: qui fecit testamentum, vivit in aeternum: audit voces nostras, agnoscit tuas. Legamus, quid litigamus? ubi inventa fuerit hereditas, ipsum teneamus. Aperi, lege. His simillima dixit Optatus Milevitanus Donatistas ita comcompellans: & annunciant populo Christi va-nas seductiones, qui nostri sunt fratres. Sed ne quis dicat me inconsiderate eos fratres appellare qui tales sunt: quamvis & illi non negent & omnibus notum sit quod nos odio habeant & exsecrentur & nolunt se dici fratres nostros: tamen nos recedere a timore Dei no posumus, quos hortatur Spiritus sanctus per Esaiam prophetam dicens: vos qui timetis nomen Domini, audite nomen Domini; hi qui vos odio habent & exsecrantur & nolunt se dici fratres vestros, vos tamen dicite eis, fratres nostri estis. Sunt igitur sine dubio fratres, quamvis non boni. Quare nemo miretur eos me appellare fratres, qui non possunt non esse fratres.
units.tr: This, finally, is what that most pious and at the same time most prudent theologian of our memory, Dr. Franciscus Junius, once a most celebrated professor in the Leiden Academy itself, observed and weighed in keeping with his prudence. For after he had lived twenty-five years in Germany, our common and most dear fatherland, he wrote an irenicum and, through the hands of the most illustrious and powerful prince, Lord Maurice, Landgrave of Hesse, etc., offered it to the church as a lover of wisdom [τὸ φιλοσοφῶν ... ἀπ' ἀλλήλων], to be pacified, if possible, from the mutually destructive contentions of the wrangling theologians. There he urges peace, desires concord, lulls dissensions, sets out the terms on which peace is to be bought back, enumerates the drawbacks of quarrelling, commends the advantages of concord, and leaves nothing undone to obtain an eternal marriage of truth and charity. O the praiseworthy labour of that great theologian! O the admirable effort! O the prudence of counsels worth embracing! But how few of us there are who give heed to all these things, so good, so honourable, so useful, so pleasant, and so necessary and salutary! We all, Papists and Protestants alike, rejoice and glory in the Christian name. But how little, alas, do we live up to the measure of so great a name, we who are all alike Papists and Protestants! How bitterly we write, how bitterly we speak, and rail at one another! Where has Christian moderation stuck fast? Where has charity fallen asleep, and, I might almost say, lies utterly extinguished? We must put off this savagery of manners and put on the bowels of Christ. Out of the many quarrels of our age, the matter itself demands that I bring forward one by far the greatest and most dreadful. This more-than-diabolical paradox is imputed to the most innocent servants of God, Christian men: that God is the author of sin. It is imputed to them by men within the papacy and outside it, who nevertheless all wish to appear Christians, and indeed many really are. We read a most sorrowful complaint on this matter in the most learned Dr. Bogerman, in his notes on the piety of the Estates of Holland and West Friesland, vindicated by the most distinguished Hugo Grotius: "Many stir up hatred against a man on this ground alone, that he is a zealous follower of Calvin and Beza. Indeed, they are wholly intent on making these servants of God more cruel than Turks and Marranos, and altogether bloodthirsty, and hateful to the common people; and among many they have already brought it about that they shrink from the very name of these teachers, as daily experience attests." Let the reader look, among very many writings of this sort, at the Incendiary Bell and the Crystal Spectacles, etc. Nor would this kind of men treat the king of Great Britain himself more gently, were it not that they feared the royal dignity. What man of sound mind, among Jews, Turks and pagans, would not be deterred from the Christian faith by the mere hearing of such a controversy among Christians? For it is alien to every religion, indeed to all reason, that the highest good should be the cause of evil, which fights against virtue. Who, then, endowed not only with sound reason but with reason enlightened by faith, and imbued with orthodox religion, would not be offended to hear such voices among Christians? Men are accused of this error and blasphemy by Papists, by Lutherans, etc., which is greatly to be deplored, and even by those who were brought up in the purer churches; yet such a thing never came into the minds of these men. For their public writings condemn this blasphemy, as they condemn all the others which the anger and "gossip-pain" [γλωσσαλγία] of many falsely lays upon them. Public confessions condemn it, public sermons condemn it, the public practices of the churches over which they preside condemn it; so many most ready deaths and martyrdoms condemn it. What is it, I beg you, Christian men, that in such a blaze and multitude of testimonies we still indulge malicious suspicions, each of us perverting the sayings and writings of others? Why do we condemn so rashly and so cruelly men otherwise most pious and most deserving of the church of God, seizing upon the single word or phrase of one or another, and passing over a thousand solemn professions and the sworn denials and public refutations of such horrible doctrines? Why is it that so few are displeased by that ill-speaking [δυσφημία] and truly barbarous "speaking otherwise" [ἀλλοφωνία]? Ah, let us be gentler, we who are Christians! Ah, let us be milder, we who are Christ's body, so that the Spirit of Christ may seem to exert its powers in us as in its own body! It is strange that we do not see our dissensions to be the losses of friends, the gains of enemies (to use Jerome's words), and the public fires of divine wrath. Let us hear the words of Augustine, so majestic and so pious, in Psalm 122, with which he addresses Christians who disagree in faith: Why do we quarrel? We are brothers. Our father did not die intestate: he made a will, and so he died, and rose again. As long as there is contention over the inheritance of the dead, all keep silent while the will is brought out in public, so that the tablet may be opened and read. The judge listens attentively, the advocates are silent, the heralds call for silence; the whole people is hushed, so that the words of the dead man may be read, not the opinions of the tomb. He lies in the tomb without feeling, and yet his words have force: is Christ sitting in heaven, and is his testament contradicted? Open it, let us read it; we are brothers, why do we contend? Let our mind be calmed. Our Father did not leave us without a testament: he who made the testament lives for ever; he hears our voices and recognises yours. Let us read it; why do we quarrel? Where the inheritance is found, let us hold to it. Open it, read. Optatus of Milevis, addressing the Donatists, spoke in very similar words: "And they announce to the people of Christ vain seductions, they who are our brothers." But lest anyone say that I rashly call them brothers who are such men: although they do not deny it, and it is well known that they hate and curse us and refuse to be called our brothers, yet we cannot depart from the fear of God, whom the Holy Spirit exhorts through the prophet Isaiah, saying: "You who fear the name of the Lord, hear the name of the Lord; those who hate you and curse you and refuse to be called your brothers, yet say to them, You are our brothers." They are therefore without doubt brothers, though not good ones. Let no one wonder, then, that I call them brothers, since they cannot but be brothers.

units.la: Terreat nos b. Hilarii in libro adversus Constantium imperatorem, expostulatio: Dum in verbis pugna est: dum de nominibus quaestio est: dum de ambignis occasio est: dum de auctoribus querela est: dum de studiis certamen est: dum in consensu difficultas est: dum alter alteri anathema esse cepit, prope jam nemo Christi est. Credamus & dicamus tandem illud tritum:
units.tr: Let the expostulation of the blessed Hilary in his book against the emperor Constantius frighten us: While there is fighting over words, while there is questioning about names, while there is occasion from ambiguities, while there is complaint about authors, while there is strife over studies, while there is difficulty in agreement, while one begins to be anathema to another, hardly anyone is any longer Christ's. Let us believe, and at last say that well-worn line:

units.la: Nulla salus bello; pacem te poscimus omnes.
units.tr: There is no safety in war; we all demand peace from you.

units.la: Qui natura ἐξ ἀγαλλόμενοι, iacundi & vehementiores sumus, culpam candide agnoscamus & humiliter deprecemur, solitusque veritatis studium cum charitate deinceps connectamus, vinculo nunquam solvendo. Eam ad rem quum pernecessarium & apprime appositum mihi videatur magni istius Junii consilium, non abs re fore sum arbitratus si ex Irenico illius excerptum in vulneratae quin imo exulceratae ecclesiae usum huc reponerem. Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, Deus pacis & concordiae efficiat, ut ardentissimo odiorum camino, quibus ecclesia nunc flendum in modum flagrat, oleum irarum affundamus nulli, purissimas vero charitatis aquas, non ad fabriles carbones, qui magis eo inardescunt, sed ad corda Christianorum dissidiis inflammata, incendio tam acerbo tempestive restinguendo afferamus omnes, Amen.
units.tr: Since we are by nature quick-tempered and rather vehement [ἐξ ἀγαλλόμενοι], let us candidly acknowledge our fault and humbly beg pardon, and from now on join the pursuit of truth with charity, by a bond never to be dissolved. Since the counsel of that great Junius seems to me most necessary and most fitting for this purpose, I have thought it not out of place to set down here an extract from his Irenicum for the use of the wounded, nay rather ulcerated, church. May the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the God of peace and concord, grant that we pour the oil of wrath on no one into the most ardent furnace of hatreds, in which the church now burns in a manner to be wept over; but that we all bring the purest waters of charity, not to the smith's coals, which are only kindled the more by them, but to the hearts of Christians inflamed by dissensions, so as to quench in time so bitter a fire. Amen.

units.la: D. FRANCISCI JVNII Biturigis theologi gravissimi consilium de pace & concordia in ecclesia Dei colenda, deque moderando rerum theologicarum judicio, apprime necessarium ex Irenico ipsius exsignatum.
units.tr: The counsel of the most serious theologian D. FRANCIS JUNIUS of Bourges on cultivating peace and concord in the Church of God, and on moderating judgment in theological matters, most necessary, set out from his Irenicum.

units.la: Psalm. cxxii. 6,7.
units.tr: Psalm. cxxii. 6,7.

units.la: Expetite pacè Hierosolymorum, dicentes, Tranquilli sint amantes tui: Sit pax in praemunitione tua, & tranquillitas in palatiis tuis.
units.tr: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: "May those who love you be at rest. Let there be peace within your walls, and tranquillity in your palaces."

units.la: Iàm multis circumsidea- mur bonis à Domino in ecclesia ejus, & quantam laetitiam in animis nostris ex eo percipiamus, hacte- nus satis, judicio meo, ex verbis prophetae audivimus. Nam quum & privatis singulorum membrorum officiis, H 3 & & communibus Dei in corpus totum eccle-siæ summisque beneficiis intus & foris de-monstratis,potentissimè proph-eta se & ec-clesiam prisca m suis temporibus ad hanc lætitiam excitaverit:nos,qui Deum esse no-vimus constantissimum in promissionibus gratiæ,& salutari beneficentia in ecclesiam suam, iisdem argumentis uti necesse est,ut confirment ipsi, & alios in cognitione ac conscientia ejusdem boni, quoad ejus per- nos fieri potest,confirmemus.
units.tr: Already we are surrounded by many blessings from the Lord in his Church, and, in my judgment, we have heard well enough so far, from the words of the prophet, how great a joy we receive in our minds from this. For since the prophet, by the particular duties of the individual members, and by the common benefits of God shown to the whole body of the Church, and by the greatest blessings both within and without, has powerfully stirred up both himself and the Church of old in his own times to this joy, we, who know God to be most constant in the promises of grace and in his saving kindness toward his Church, must use the same arguments, so that they may confirm themselves, and that we may confirm others, as far as we can, in the knowledge and conscience of the same good.

units.la: Atque hæc quidem Christiana lætitia in- nobis ejusmodi est, ut omnem metum omnemque dolorem eximere ex mentibus nostris & fugare possit, si eam animo veré concepimus.Sed quia illius gratiæ virtutis-que divinæ( quæ in se ēstabsolutissima per-fectissimaque) sensus est in nobis imperfe-ctissimus: propterea visum est spiritui san-cto,expositæ prophetarum lætitia spiritu-ali nostra, certissimisque illius argumentis, effectum lætitiæ illius conjunctissimum re-liquo psalmo exponere nimirum publica denunciationem lætitiæ illius ex studio Christiano, procuratione-mque diligentissimam illius lætitiæ propagandæ in univer-sitatem ecclesiæ; ex quo ingeneratum est in nobis spirituale gaudium, de quo ante di-ximus. Id enim naturale est, ut lætitia ho-minem minem quasi fundat & dilatet modis omnibus; ut contra, tristitia contrahit hominem, & quodammodo in angustum cogit: qui laetatur, diffunditur in se & extra se, nec potest quin erumpat apud alios in testificationem laetitiae suae: quam rem sensus naturae docet, & parabolis evidentissimis expressit Christus, viri qui ovem perdiderat, foeminae quae drachmam & patrisfamilias qui filium, Luc. 15. 4, 8, 11. Secundum hanc igitur rationem propheta suam ipsius & communem ecclesiae laetitiam cum descripsisset verbis antecedentibus, jam venit ad illam inclinationem naturalem laetitiae, nimirum ad publicam denunciationem illius, & saluberrimam adhortationem ad pacem, qua laetitia alitur atque continetur ad Dei gloriam.
units.tr: Indeed, this Christian joy, when we have truly conceived it in our souls, is of such a kind that it can remove and drive away from our minds every fear and every sorrow. But because our sense of that grace and divine power (which in itself is most absolute and most perfect) is most imperfect in us, the Holy Spirit has therefore seen fit, after setting out the joy of the prophets as our spiritual joy and by its most certain proofs, to set out in the remaining psalm the effect of that joy, which is most closely joined to it: namely, the public proclamation of that joy from Christian zeal, and the most diligent effort to spread that joy throughout the whole extent of the Church, from which the spiritual gladness we spoke of before has been engendered in us. For it is natural that joy should expand and enlarge a man in every way, just as sorrow contracts a man and in some measure drives him into narrowness. He who rejoices is poured out into himself and beyond himself, and cannot but break out among others in witness of his joy. Nature's own sense teaches this, and Christ expressed it in the most evident parables: of the man who had lost a sheep, of the woman who had lost a drachma, and of the father of the family who had lost a son (Luke 15. 4, 8, 11.). Accordingly, having described his own joy and the common joy of the Church in the preceding words, the prophet now comes to that natural tendency of joy, namely its public proclamation, and to a most wholesome exhortation to peace, by which joy is nourished and maintained to the glory of God.

units.la: Docturus autem propheta illud officium pacis ad laetitiae conservationem perneces-sarium, duobus modis credentes instruit de hac Christiana pace. Nam primum hortatione utitur vehementissima, tanquam praeco religiosissimus voluntatis Dei, versu sexto & septimo, quos ante exscripsimus. Deinde vero suum ipsius exemplum spondet, & ante oculos piorum exhibet se velut ducem futurum ex facto ad ista pietatis officia, non autem vocalem solum praeconem, spectatorem torem, hortatoremque ociosum, duobus versibus ultimis. Quum autem sermone instituit docere alios Christianam pacem; tanquam doctor fidelissimus in schola Domini; primum tem ipsam imperat, deinde praecit verba singulis ad rem quam imperavit pertinentia, Rem enim ipsam imperat summatim, dicens; Expetite pacem Hierosolymorum. Verba autem praecit credentibus quibus hoc imperat, quum subjicit, tranquilli sint amantes tui. &c. oratione conversa ad Hierosolymam.
units.tr: Now the prophet, wishing to teach that the duty of peace is necessary for the preservation of joy, instructs believers about this Christian peace in two ways. For first he uses the most vehement exhortation, as the most devout herald of the will of God, in the sixth and seventh verses, which we have transcribed above. Then, in the last two verses, he pledges his own example and presents himself before the eyes of the godly as one who will lead the way by deed in these duties of piety, and not merely as a vocal herald, an idle spectator and an idle exhorter. Now when he sets out to teach Christian peace to others by word, like a most faithful teacher in the school of the Lord, he first states the matter itself and then adds the words relevant to the thing he has enjoined. For he enjoins the matter itself in brief, saying: "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem." And he adds the words to believers to whom he enjoins this, when he subjoins "may those who love you be at rest," etc., his speech being turned toward Jerusalem.

units.la: Ac primum quidem quid sibi velit psaltes Hierosolymorum appellatione, satis (opinor) constat ex praecedentibus. Nam v. 2. & 3. rem totam copiose explicavimus.
units.tr: As for what the psalmist means by the name of Jerusalem, that is, I think, sufficiently clear from what has gone before, for in verses 2 and 3 we have explained the whole matter at length.

units.la: Pax vero quid significet, nobis videndum est; ut singuli suum officium, ad quod excitantur his verbis, tenere possint. Ut itaque paucis absolvamus, quum desiderium pacis universe hoc loco praecipiatur, & hujus ipsius pacis sequentibus verbis tradatur narratio, ne longius abeamus, pacis nomine intelligimus constitutionem vacuam ab omni malo, & in omni bonorum genere intus & foris quiescentem. Ac proinde, quia pax certa homini esse non potest, qui non solum intus abundat malis & bonis vacuus est, sed etiam foris omnibus malis appetitur, & ab omni bono quasi refugitur: ita è diverso pacem homini illi esse statuimus, quem bona certatim appetiit & fugiunt mala. Eademque ratione de ecclesia dicimus, quam urbs Hierosolymorum olim adumbravit; hanc dici pacem illius, quum ipsi bene est ac non male. Quomodo autem ecclesiæ bene esse possit, superiora docuerunt. Bene est ecclesiæ; quæ lætatur de filiis suis: ad quam filii adeunt & adhærent; cujus forma interna, est Deus: externa, communio sanctorum cum Deo verbo salutis & precibus, & piorum inter se justo ordine quæ Deus instituerit ad coagmentationem sanctorum, ad ædificationem corporis Christi. His rebus vera pax ecclesiæ continetur: quemadmodum vera pax & justa corporis constitutio in optima formæ interne atque externæ & actionum omnium, accidentiumque commoditate versatur. De hac pace quam pii cum Deo habent, cum animis suis cum ecclesia tota, & cum membris singulis ejus, & cum omnibus hominibus, propheta nunc demum loquitur, & omnia antegressa bona comprehendit hac una pacis appellatione, dicens: Expetite pacem Hierosolymorum.
units.tr: We must now see what peace means, so that each person may hold to the duty to which these words stir him. To be brief, since the desire for peace is enjoined here in general, and the narrative of this peace is given in the words that follow, let us not stray too far: by the name of peace we understand a state free from every evil, and resting within and without in every kind of good. And therefore, since there can be no certain peace for a man who is not only filled with evils within and empty of goods, but is also assailed without by every evil and, as it were, shunned by every good, we hold that peace belongs rather to the man whom good things eagerly seek and evils flee. And by the same reasoning we say of the Church, which the city of Jerusalem once foreshadowed, that she has peace when it is well with her and not ill. How the Church can be well, the earlier passages have taught: it is well with the Church which rejoices in her sons, to which the sons come and cling; whose inner form is God, and whose outward form is the communion of the saints with God, through the word of salvation and prayers, and the orderly fellowship of the godly among themselves, which God has instituted for the joining together of the saints and the building up of the body of Christ. In these things the true peace of the Church consists, just as true peace and the right constitution of the body lie in the best arrangement of its inner and outer form and in the convenience of all its actions and accidents. It is of this peace, which the godly have with God, with their own souls, with the whole Church, with its individual members, and with all men, that the prophet now at last speaks, and he comprehends all the goods already mentioned in this one name of peace, saying: "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem."

units.la: Hierosolyma, id est, ecclesiam Dei bonā esse confitemur omnes, tanquam Dei viventis domum : tum pacem illius domus bonam & jucundam esse. Unum a nobis desideratur; ut quum bonam esse ecclesiā, & bona ecclesiæ pacem sententiamus omnes in nostra conscientia, nos quoque bonum officium erga ecclesiam, quam prædicamus bonam, & ad pacem, quam natura bonam esse docet, faciamus. Huc nos hortatur & vocat propheta dicens, Expetite pacem Hie-rosolymorum: tanquam si diceret : Ita estis singuli a natura comparati, ut neque bonum privatum vestrum, neque commune novc-ritis : ac ne illud quidem expetatis, aut etiam procuretis, si quando novisse datum est: adeo magnæ sunt in vobis tenebræ. Quòd si in ipsis humanis rebus non videtis, quid vobis, quid publico utile esse possit: multò magis aberraturi estis a bono spirituali vestro, & ecclesiæ Dei, quarum rerum notitia nemini nisi ex revelatione Dei potest obtingere. Nunc verò quum per Dei gratiam ex præcedentibus constet, Deum ecclesiam, & fratres germanos vestros a Deo in ecclesia genitos, & vos denique ipsos a vobis cognosci præluce nte face divini verbi: videte, ne in modo naturæ vestræ torpentes hæreatis, neve a bono profequedo, cujus notitiam impertivit Deus, abstinea-tis impie, sed bonum publicum ecclesiæ, privatum spirituale vestrum in ecclesia procurate, quibuscunq; modis pote est. Quod si plura non potestis (quemadmodum revera non sumus idonei per nos ipsos ad cogitandum quidquam velut ex nobis ipsis: sed quod idonei sumus, illud ex Deo est, 2. Corinth. 3. 5.) saltem date operam, ut vobis ardentibus ex animo, religiosissimisque precibus coram Domino contendatis, & intus studia vestra quam diligentissime accendatis ad pacem, id est bonum publicum ecclesiae, & in ea privatum vestrum procurandum. Hoc igitur summum praeceptum est, ad quod pios hortatur psaltes ex antecedentis laetitiae causarumque laetitiae argumento.
units.tr: We all confess that Jerusalem, that is, the Church of God, is good, as the house of the living God; and that the peace of that house is good and pleasant. One thing is required of us: that since we all judge in our conscience that the Church is good and that the peace of the Church is good, we should also perform a good duty toward the Church, which we proclaim good, and toward the peace which nature itself teaches is good. The prophet urges and calls us to this, saying: "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem," as if he said: "You are so constituted by nature that you know neither your private good nor the common good; and you do not seek or even bring about that good, even when it has been given you to know it; so great is the darkness in you. But if you do not see in human affairs what can be useful to you and to the public, you will be far more astray from your spiritual good and from the Church of God, the knowledge of which can come to no one except by the revelation of God. Now, however, since it is clear from what has gone before, by the grace of God, that God is the Church's, and that your brothers born of God in the Church, and finally yourselves, are known to you by the light of the divine word, see that you do not cling sluggishly to the manner of your nature, nor impiously hold back from pursuing the good whose knowledge God has given. Instead, promote in the Church the public good of the Church and your own spiritual good, in whatever ways you can. But if you cannot do more (as indeed we are not, of ourselves, fit to think anything as if from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, 2 Cor. 3. 5), at least take pains to strive before the Lord with fervent hearts and the most devout prayers, and to kindle your inner zeal as diligently as you can for peace, that is, for the public good of the Church and the promotion of your own good within it. This, then, is the chief precept, to which the psalmist exhorts the godly from the cause of the joy he has just described and from the evidence of that joy."

units.la: Quum autem praeceptorum divinorum omnium ejusmodi sit auctoritas, ut quicunque buscunque praecepta dantur, ii praeceptis illius obsequi reueatur[?] sine exceptione ulla: profecto nos, qui singulari Dei beneficio in ecclesiam ad perceptionem voluntatis ejus vocati sumus, necesse est de obsequio fideli cogitare, ut pacem ecclesiae petamus, quemadmodum nobis praecepit Deus. Ac propterea ne forte in petendo incerti simus, tanquam si nesciremus quid a quo peti oporteat, indidit propheta piis velut in os sanctissimam petitionis formulam, quum dicit: tranquilli sint amantes tui, sit pax in praemunitione tua, &c. Hujus enim petitionis loci duo sunt a propheta indicati, incremento convenientissimo, quum pacem ecclesiae docet peti a nobis oportere & foris & intus, communiter & singulariter. Foris quidem etiam iis qui amat ecclesiam communiter, quamvis nondum sese illi adjunxerint: intus vero singulariter, domesticis fidei & ecclesiae catholicae. Nam quemadmodum si quis pacem habitationis suae desideraverit, circumspiciat opus est foris, quae impedimenta arcenda, quae adjumenta retinenda: deinde vero dispiciat intus quid ipsae partes habitationis postulent: ita etiam pios omnes post omnem hominum memoriam Deus informavit, ut in hoc domicilio mundi omnibus bene cupiant & pace coiant cum omnibus, quoad ejus fieri poterit, ut Romanis scribebat apostolus, c. 13. v. 18. deinde ut ipsi ecclesiae ante omnia bene cupiant secundum Deum. Quin etiam hunc ipsum ordine, quem nobis praescribit psalmes, Deus in suis promissionibus quas enunciavit Abrahamo distincte servavit, ne quem quam Christianum taedeat illud postulare, quod in promissionum numero recensuit Deus. Dicebat enim primum de omnibus etiam exteris, Benedicam iis, qui benedicent tibi: tibi : postea vero de ecclesiae Christianae membris subjecit illud alterum, Benedicta erunt in te omnes familiae terrae, Gen.12.3. De omnibus ergo promiscue, etiam exteris, ab ecclesia Dei pronunciatur haec verba: tran- quilli sint amantes tui: de ipsis vero domesticis sequentia enunciata sunt.
units.tr: Since the authority of all God's commands is such that, whatever commands are given, we must obey them without any exception, surely we who have been called into the Church by God's singular kindness to receive his will must think about faithful obedience, and seek the peace of the Church, as God has commanded us. So that we may not be unsure in our asking, as if we did not know what we ought to ask for and from whom, the prophet has placed in the mouths of the godly, as it were, a most holy form of petition, when he says: tranquilli sint amantes tui, sit pax in praemunitione tua, etc. In this petition the prophet indicates two aspects, most fittingly arranged, when he teaches that we ought to seek the peace of the Church both outside and inside, in common and in particular. Outside, in common, we seek it even for those who love the Church but have not yet joined themselves to it. Inside, in particular, we seek it for the members of the household of faith and of the catholic Church. For just as, if someone desires peace for his dwelling, he must look outside to see what hindrances are to be warded off and what aids are to be kept, and then look inside to see what the parts of the house themselves require, so God has from the beginning of human memory so disposed all the godly that in this dwelling of the world they wish well to all and live in peace with all, as far as it can be done, as the apostle wrote to the Romans (13:18), and then that they wish well above all to the Church itself, according to God. Indeed God has kept this very order, which the psalm prescribes to us, distinctly in his promises which he declared to Abraham, so that no Christian should be weary of asking for what God has included among his promises. For he first spoke of all, even outsiders: Benedicam iis, qui benedicent tibi: tibi; afterwards he added, concerning the members of the Christian Church, that other saying: Benedicta erunt in te omnes familiae terrae (Gen. 12:3). So the words tranquilli sint amantes tui are pronounced by the Church of God on all without distinction, even outsiders, but the following words are spoken concerning its own household.

units.la: Ac prius quidem perspicue est evidens: si tantum illud observemus, amantium ecclesiae tantum duo esse genera, prout distincte a psalte enumerantur paulo post octavo versu, dicendo: propter fratres meos & amicos meos, &c. Sunt enim hi fratres, i.e. germana ecclesiae membra, & jam jam ex facto ad eam pertinentia in Christo Jesu, aut etiam in ea degentia secundum formam externa & ordinem aspectabilem illius: illi vero amici, quamvis extra ecclesiam positi, qui nec oderunt ecclesiam animo, nec sermone aut obsunt: sed aut bene cupiunt ipsi ex animo, quamvis ipsi sibi id non cupiant boni, aut certe amice ferunt, ut ecclesia sit, atque tranquilla sit: de quo genere dicebat Christus, Qui non est adversum nos, pro nobis est, Luc. 9.50. Pro his ergo omnibus ecclesia postulat, ut ipsis bene sit, & tranquillitate fruantur, denique communibus secum beneficiis magis ac magis cumulentur a Domino.
units.tr: The first point is plainly evident if we observe that there are only two kinds of those who love the Church, as the psalmist distinctly enumerates them shortly afterwards in verse 8, saying: propter fratres meos & amicos meos, etc. For these are the brethren, that is, the true members of the Church, who already belong to it in fact in Christ Jesus, or who dwell in it according to its outward form and visible order. The others are friends, who, although they are outside the Church, do not hate the Church in their hearts, nor harm it by word or deed, but either wish it well from their heart, though they do not wish themselves well, or at least bear it kindly that the Church should exist and be at peace. Of this kind Christ said: Qui non est adversum nos, pro nobis est (Luke 9:50). For all these, therefore, the Church asks that they may fare well, enjoy tranquillity, and finally be increasingly heaped by the Lord with the common benefits he bestows on the Church.

units.la: Alterum vero optatum in versu 7. quod ad domesticos ecclesiæ pertinet, duas partes illas pacis evidenter notat, de quibus ante dicebamus in definienda pace. Ad justam enim & veram pacem desiderantur duo: defensio à malo & bonorū pacis perceptio. De utroq; preces concipiendas ostendit psaltes verbis paucissimis; & servata typi illius, qui tum ad figurandam ecclesiæ fuerat datus, allegoria. Jerusalem typus erat ecclesiæ; ad tranquillitatem urbis illius duo hæc fuerunt opus, tum ut adversus mala foris minantia & irruentia circummunita esset urbs, tum ut intus abundaret bonis. Defensionem à malo propheta suis verbis docuit expetendam: sit pax in promurnitione tua. Constitutionem vero stabilem in bono ac florentissimam postulare docuit illis; Sit tranquillitas in palatiis tuis. Etsi ne hoc quidem prætereundum videtur silentio, quod in hoc utroque genere præstantiam summam bonorum ad pacem pertinetium amplissimis vocibus denotavit. Nam de illa defensione à malo acturus, non simpliciter murum, fossam, vallum, aut aliquid simile appellavit; sed voce amplissima usus est, quodvis munimentum idque potentissimum & commodissimum ad defensionem significante. De interna vero bonorum copiatam pia tam magnifice loquitur, ut dignitatem ecclesiæ non possit quisquam amplius extollere, quum palatia nominaret. Videbat enim propheta omnes pios in Christum & ecclesiam insitos, reges & sacerdotes apud Deum patrem in Christo factos, regale sacerdotium, ut appellat Petrus 1. Petr. 2. 9. Exod. 19. 9. sive ut Moses, regnum sacerdotale. Huic dignitati piorum dignas stationes voluit demonstrare à Deo attributas, ac velut praetoria & regales domos, quum tranquillitatem inesse palatiis ejus expeteret: de rebus videlicet spiritualibus tam magnifice in fide sentiens, ut sibi ipse non posset satisfacere, nisi res illas in spiritu magnificas vocibus magnificis secundum corpus exprimeret.
units.tr: The second wish, in verse 7, which pertains to the members of the household of the Church, clearly marks those two parts of peace of which we spoke before when defining peace. For a just and true peace requires two things: defence from evil and the enjoyment of the good things of peace. The psalmist shows in very few words that prayers must be offered for each, keeping to the allegory of that type which was given at that time to figure the Church. Jerusalem was a type of the Church, and two things were needed for the tranquillity of that city: that it should be fortified outside against evils threatening and assaulting it, and that it should abound inside with good things. The prophet taught that defence from evil is to be sought in his words: sit pax in praemunitione tua. He taught that a stable and most flourishing condition in good things is to be asked for in the words: sit tranquillitas in palatiis tuis. Yet it seems that this must not be passed over in silence either: in each of these two kinds he expressed, in most ample terms, the great excellence of the goods that belong to peace. For when he was about to speak of that defence from evil, he did not simply name a wall, a ditch, a rampart, or anything similar, but used a most ample word signifying any fortification whatever, and that most powerful and most convenient for defence. Concerning the inner store of good things, he speaks of it so magnificently, calling it palaces, that no one could raise the dignity of the Church higher. For the prophet saw that all the godly are implanted in Christ and in the Church, and are made kings and priests before God the Father in Christ, a royal priesthood, as Peter calls it (1 Pet. 2:9; cf. Exod. 19:6), or, as Moses calls it, a kingdom of priests. He wished to show that suitable stations are assigned to the godly by God, to match this dignity, and like praetorian and royal houses; for he sought tranquillity to dwell in his palaces. Clearly he thought so magnificently in faith of spiritual things that he could not satisfy himself unless he expressed those things, magnificent in spirit, in magnificent words drawn from bodily things.

units.la: Videmus ergo ex prophetæ verbis, quidnam illud sit quod expeti à nobis omni tempore necesse est. Sed à quo expetamus nisi à Deo, qui potest explere petitionem nostram? Deus igitur, Deus ille noster, auctor ecclesiæ, custos & hospes constantissimus illius, ad quem ecclesia respiciens nihil non habet boni, à quo respicens aliorsum nihil non sentit mali: is ergo ipse est, qui hæc curare potest ecclesiæ efficacissimè, & à quo nos indesinenter opus est petere quæcunque ad pacem & tranquillitatem illius pertinent. tinent.neque dubium est,fi examino fidem & misericordiam illius imploremus his ipsis ferreis & luctuosissimis temporibus, quin oculi ipsius super justos invigilaturi sint, & aures ipsius attentæ futuræ ad pias preces & susspitia illorum.
units.tr: We see therefore from the words of the prophet what it is that we must always ask for. But from whom are we to ask it, if not from God, who can fulfil our petition? God, then, that God of ours, the author of the Church, its guardian and most constant host, to whom the Church, looking up, lacks no good thing, and from whom, looking elsewhere, it perceives no evil: he is the one who can most effectively look after these things for the Church, and from him we must without ceasing ask whatever pertains to its peace and tranquillity. Nor is there any doubt that, if we call upon his faithfulness and mercy even in these iron and most doleful times, his eyes will watch over the just, and his ears will be attentive to the pious prayers and sighs of those who are his.

units.la: Sed quia Deus pacem & tranquillitatem ecclesiæ suæ non solum procurat immediate (ut loquuntur) arbitratu suo, verum etiam quibuscunque visum est mediis utitur ad præstandam pacem & tranquillitatem illius; videamus ne singuli nostri deficiamus ab officio nostro, si forte Deus nobis, tanquam instrumentis, indignis quidem, sed sanctificatis ab ipso per gratiam, ad tantum opus dignetur uti. Nam quid nobis miseris futurum est, si quod ore petimus, illud manibus pedibusque obnixè oppugnemus? aut si nec manu nec pedem admoveamus, quum honorem istum Deus nobis habuerit, & ad opus immerentes gratiosissimè vocaverit? quod ergo petimus sermone, petamus animo; quod animo & sermone petimus, idem etiam modis omnibus appetamus, & studium, operam, laborem, industriamque nostram eo conferamus, ut id ipsum quod petimus, tandem beneficio Dei, ut benedicturi officio ministeriique nostro, assequamur. Hoc autem ut faciamus sanctè, meminememinerimus ab eo qui omnia dat; expeti omnia; ab iis vero qui possunt aliquid ministrare secundum voluntatem Dei donatoris omnium, aliqua postulari secundum Deum oportere. Itaque omnia omnino à Deo petimus; ab aliis, aliqua secundum Deum. Quum autem ab aliis dicimus; quis adeo desipit, ut aliorum officiū merito desiderari putet, & dissimulare nostrū? Quæcunque creaturæ sunt, tenentur secundum Deum ministrare voluntati ejus. quid ergo exigamus ab aliis, quod nos ipsi præstare minimè cogitamus? Utrumque opus est in expetenda pace & tranquillitate ecclesiæ: tum ut ipsi summo desiderio procuremus & colamus eam, tum ut proximos ad idem officium religiose excitemus. Proximos autem omnes universè provocari ad hoc officium erga ecclesiam Dei oportere docemur natura, & auctoritate scripturæ: quèadmodum Christum legimus præcepisse, Diligite etiam inimicos vestros, benedicite iis qui devovent vos &c. Matth. 5. 44. & Paulū præcipientem, si fieri potest, quantum in vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus in pace vivite. Sed quia varia est proximorum ratio, & ipse quoque propheta in hoc loco aliquam distinctionem affert; paucis de ordine eorum dicendum
units.tr: But since God does not only procure the peace and tranquillity of his Church immediately (as they say), by his own decision, but also uses whatever means seem good to him to bestow peace and tranquillity upon it, let us see that we, each one of us, do not fail in our duty, should God perhaps deign to use us as instruments, unworthy indeed, but sanctified by him through grace, for so great a work. For what will become of us wretches, if we vigorously oppose with our hands and feet what we ask for with our mouths? Or if we do not move hand or foot, when God has granted us this honour and has graciously called us, undeserving, to the work? What we therefore seek with our speech, let us seek with our heart; what we seek with heart and speech, let us also seek by every means, and direct our zeal, effort, labour and diligence to this end, that what we ask for we may at last, by the gift of God, attain, as those who are to be a blessing in the office and ministry we hold. But that we may do this rightly, let us remember that from him who gives all things, all things are to be sought, while from those who can supply something, according to the will of God the giver of all, some things are rightly to be asked, according to God. Therefore we ask all things from God, and some things from others, according to God. But when we say "from others," who is so foolish as to think that the duty of others is rightly demanded while he neglects his own? Whatever creatures there are are bound, according to God, to serve his will. Why then should we require of others what we ourselves are in no way inclined to perform? Both tasks are necessary in seeking the peace and tranquillity of the Church: that we ourselves with the greatest desire procure and cherish it, and that we stir up our neighbours to the same duty with godly zeal. Now we are taught by nature and by the authority of Scripture that all our neighbours in general are to be summoned to this duty towards the Church of God, as we read that Christ commanded: Diligite etiam inimicos vestros, benedicite iis qui devovent vos, etc. (Matt. 5:44), and Paul bidding, si fieri potest, quantum in vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus in pace vivite (Rom. 12:18). But since the relation of neighbours is varied, and the prophet himself makes some distinction in this passage, we must say a few words about their order, so that it may be clearer what ought to be asked for and what ought to be granted to whom.

units.la: Omnes universè provocari debent ad pacem. cendum est, ut melius constet, quid quibus peti & praestari oporteat. Proximi omnes alii aliis secundum speciem a natura sumus: sed proximorum duo genera statuimus, nos quidem qui in ecclesia sumus. Nam alii in ecclesia sunt nobiscum, alii absunt ab ea: quorum illos apostolus vocat domesticos fidei, ad Galatas scribens cap. 6. v. 10. hos ad Timotheum exteros vel extraneos appellavit. Tim. 3. 7. Externorum vero rursum duo sunt genera: Nam alii sunt amici ecclesiae Dei, alii inimici. Qui amici sunt, aut ira sunt amici, ut bonum citent ecclesiae humano animo, aut saltem amici eatenus, ut malum illius non expetant: sed simpliciter in eo acquiescant, ut si poterit bene esse ecclesiae bene sit. Inimicorum vero qui ecclesiam oderunt atque persequuntur, alii ignoratione sunt inimici, alii perturbatione & studiis particularibus, alii denique malitiosa voluntate. Quid faciamus cum istis omnibus, quicunque ad expetendam pacem ecclesiae vocati sumus? Argumetum grave & odiosum: sed tamen tam necessarium in hoc tempore quàm quod maxime. Quapropter de eo dicturi sumus quam brevissime potterimus, ut rationem pacis expetendae procurandaeque in tot tantisque impedimentis certam teneamus: & dicemus diverso ordi-
units.tr: All people without exception must be called to peace. It must be said, so that it may be clearer what ought to be sought and granted to whom. We are all neighbours to one another in kind, but we set up two kinds of neighbour: those who are within the Church, and those who are outside it. Some are with us in the Church, others are absent from it. The apostle calls the former the household of faith, writing to the Galatians in chapter 6, verse 10; to Timothy he called the latter outsiders or strangers (1 Tim. 3. 7). Outsiders, moreover, are of two kinds. For some are friends of the Church of God, others are enemies. Of the friends, some are truly friends, wishing well to the Church from a sincere heart, while others are friends only in this respect, that they do not desire its harm but simply rest content that, if it can prosper, it should prosper. As for enemies, those who hate and persecute the Church are of three sorts: some are enemies through ignorance, some through agitation and private interests, and some finally through malicious will. What are we to do with all these, we who are called to seek the peace of the Church? It is a grave and unpleasant subject, yet in this time it is as necessary as anything. Therefore we shall speak of it as briefly as we can, so that we may hold a sure account of how peace is to be sought and promoted amid so many and so great hindrances; and we shall proceed in a different order, step by step, so that we may gradually come to examine the degree of each.

units.la: Proximorum duo genera.
units.tr: Two kinds of neighbours.

units.la: Tropos consilii de pace. ordine, ut ita paulatim ad singulorum gradum explorationem veniamus.
units.tr: The method of counsel on peace, in order: so that we may gradually come to examine the degree of each.

units.la: Primum igitur est, quid facto opus adpa-cem ecclesia fires nobis cum iis futura est, qui voluntarie certaq; malitia inimici sunt illius? Stat sententia, pacem ecclesiæ a nobis pro-curari oportere: quumque pax sit in va-catione a malo & fructu boni posita, non esse cum iis aut apud eos de pace ecclesiæ agendum, qui malitiose procurant malum ipsius. Qua propter si pacem ecclesiæ vere procuremus, & instrumenta ejusmodi no-bis oblata videamus quæ pacem impeditura sunt, non sunt commovenda. Sic enim præce-pit Christus dicens: Ne date quod sanctum est canibus, nec projicite margaritas vestras coram porcis, ne quando conculcent eas pedibus suis, & conversi lacerent vos Matt. 7. 6. Nam tu qui pacem expetis, quorsum eos como-veas, qui nihil nisi oppugnent ecclesiæ pa-cem? Sed hic tamen duplicem a Christiano homine cautionem desidero; ne quado pru-dentiæ opinione veniat contra charitatem, quam omnibus debemus, teste apostolo Rom 13. 8. Una est, ne temere judicium fe-ramus de ullo homine, quod certa malitia & deliberata, sive (ut Moses loquitur Num. 15. 30.) elata manu oppugnet Deum, & veritatem & ecclesiam ejus. Altera, si judica-dum
units.tr: First, then, what must be done when we are to deal with those who are willingly and knowingly enemies of the Church? The principle stands that we must promote the peace of the Church; and since peace consists in freedom from evil and the enjoyment of good, we must not treat of the Church's peace with those, or among those, who maliciously promote its harm. Therefore, if we truly care for the peace of the Church, and see instruments of that kind offered to us which are likely to hinder peace, they must not be stirred up. For Christ commanded thus, saying: "Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet and turn and tear you" (Matt. 7. 6). For you who seek peace, why stir up those who attack nothing but the peace of the Church? Yet here I require a twofold caution from the Christian man, lest by a show of prudence he go against the charity that we owe to all, as the apostle witnesses (Rom. 13. 8). The first is this: we must not rashly pass judgement on any man whom deliberate and settled malice, or (as Moses speaks, Num. 15. 30) a hand raised high, assails God, the truth and his Church. The second is this: if judgement must be passed, we must not suppose that we know those bad trees from one fruit or two; rather let us learn from very many and very serious fruits what is enough for our caution, but not for their condemnation.
