units.la: 1 2 dum est, ne ex fructu uno aut altero putemus nos arbores illas malas cognoscere: sed potius ex fructibus plurimis & gravissimis discamus cognoscere quod satis est ad cautionem nostram, non autem ad illorum condemnationem. Hunc ordinem nos docuit Christus diligentissime, dicendo: Primum quidem, ex fructibus eorum agnoscetis eos: postea vero subiiciendo cautionem illam pernecessariam, ut judicium Deo permittamus, quum inquit: Non quisquis dicit mihi, Domine Domine, introibit in regnum coelorum: sed qui facit quod vult pater meus qui in coelis est. Multi dicent mihi die illo, Domine, Domine, nonne per nomen tuum prophetavimus? & in nomine tuo daemonia ejecimus? & per nomen tuum multas virtutes edidimus? Tunc autem profitebor eis, certe nunquam novi vos: discedite a me qui operam datis transgressioni legis.
units.tr: Christ taught us this order most diligently, saying: "First, indeed, you shall know them by their fruits"; afterwards, however, he added that most necessary caution, that we leave judgement to God, when he said: "Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Many will say to me on that day, Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name? And then I will profess to them: I never knew you; depart from me, you who work lawlessness" (Matt. 7. 21–23).

units.la: Quod si res nobis cum eo futura est, qui singulari perturbatione vitium & cedens infirmitati suae, ecclesiae adversabitur, eadem plane ratio a nobis observanda est, dum homo id ipsum tamen discrimen illud adhibendum, quod Christianum hominem perturbationi praesenti oportet ad tempus cedere, & dare operam ut prudenter ac commode misfer miser homo jamjam ex perturbatione animi sui revocetur, aut exspectetur dum fidat quodammodo illa animi perturbatio, prout homini ebrio fieri a nobis solet. Id enim natura docet, salubrius remedia ægroto adhiberi, quum acres illæ morborum ἀχηρ & perturbationum impetus quasi refracti sunt: & notum est illud dictum Cleoftrati, qui quum ebrius esset graviter, cuidam sibi dicenti; Non te pudet, quod ebrius factus es? respondit illico, Et te non pudet, quod monies ebrium? Hic enim vere dictum illud est a Salomone adhibendum, velut mala aurea cum figuris argenteis est verbum dictu commode, ut monile aureum & ornamentum ex insigni auro est reprehensor sapiens apud aurem auscultantem.
units.tr: But if we have to deal with one who, through some peculiar agitation of mind, gives way to his own weakness and opposes the Church, we must observe exactly the same plan, with this distinction added: a Christian ought for the time being to yield to present agitation and take care to deal prudently and fittingly with the wretched man, until he is recalled from the disturbance of his mind, or is waited for until that agitation of mind has in a sense worn itself out, as we are wont to do with a drunken man. For nature teaches that remedies are applied more healthfully to the sick when the sharp fits of diseases and the onsets of the passions have, as it were, been broken [ἀχηρ]. There is the well-known saying of Cleostratus, who, being gravely drunk, was told by someone, "Are you not ashamed that you are drunk?" and at once replied, "And are you not ashamed that you admonish a drunken man?" Here, truly, is that saying of Solomon to be applied: as apples of gold in settings of silver is a word spoken fittingly; and as an earring of gold, or an ornament of fine gold, is a wise rebuke to a listening ear.

units.la: Quod si ignorantia veritatis hominem vi- debimus Deo, ecclesiæ & veritati Dei in eccle- sia adversari: omnino videndum nobis est, ut in charitate expetamus institutione ho- minis illius: nitendum ut præbeamus, quam prudentissime modestissimeq; poterimus, lucem veritatis qua tenebras mentis illius depellamus. Sed cum his omnibus univer-se, qui inimici sunt, id semper nobis videndum est ut pacem ecclesiæ præoptemus, & ante omnia expetamus. Quod si cum bona ecclesiæ pace his prodesse possumus, facia-mus mus sanctissimo studio salutis ipsorum: sin autem pax ecclesiae aut membrorum ejus periclitabitur propter voluntatem, perturbationem, aut inscientiam iistorum, abstineamus potius ab eis commovendis, quàm ut pacem dimittamus ecclesiae, donec misericors ille Dominus, qui nostri misertus est quum sibi inimici essemus, viam patefecerit illis misericordiae. Ad summam, quod veteres monuerunt olim non esse movendum malum quod bene positum est, id in hoc hominum genere observari opus est accuratissime. Videndum ut ab iis qui semper mali sunt, certoque cohilio dant operam malo, ne bonum quidem expectamus, aut commoveamus magno sive ecclesiae, sive nostro ipsorum, aut aliorum malo. Ab iis vero qui infirmitate aut ignoratione rapiuntur in malum, movendis tantisper caveamus, dum ita se habent: sed potius studeamus iis benefacere, quum erit commodum, quàm malum ipsorum accedere, nec ipse beneficiorum nobis accersamus importunè malum.
units.tr: But if we see that a man, through ignorance of the truth, sets himself against God, the Church and the truth of God in the Church, we must by all means consider how in charity we may seek his instruction, and strive to present, as prudently and modestly as we can, the light of truth by which we may drive out the darkness of his mind. But with all those who are enemies in general, we must always see to this, that we prefer and above all seek the peace of the Church. If we can benefit them with the good peace of the Church, let us do so with the most holy zeal for their salvation; but if the peace of the Church or of its members will be imperilled on account of their will, agitation or ignorance, let us rather refrain from stirring them, than let go the peace of the Church, until that merciful Lord, who had mercy on us when we were enemies to him, opens a way of mercy for them. In short, what the ancients long ago advised, that an evil well placed is not to be stirred, must be observed most carefully with this class of men. We must take care not to expect good from those who are always evil and who with settled counsel labour at evil; nor should we stir them to the great harm of the Church, or of ourselves, or of others. But as for those who are carried into evil by weakness or ignorance, let us be cautious about stirring them while they remain so; rather let us study to do them good when it is convenient, than to bring on them harm; nor should we rashly invite upon ourselves the harm of benefits.

units.la: Sed quid sit homines erunt non inimico erga ecclesiam & pios animo? Horum duo genera, quae ante dicebamus, semper distinguì necesse est. Nam alii sunt non inimici, alii vero amici reipsa, & bono animo in ecclesiam Dei ac membra illius. Cum iis autem qui non inimici sunt, hic modus ad procurationem pacis in ecclesia tenendus est, ut potius vincas animos ipsorum & amicitiam concilies bonis sermonibus, officiis, exemplis, & rebus consimilibus, quàm ut importune ab illis exigas beneficia. Animum istorum adduci priusquam manus necesse est, qui secus fecerit, is præposterè de officio judicat illorum, & suo: quod magnæ est imprudentiæ.
units.tr: But what of men who are not hostile to the Church and are well-disposed? Of these two kinds, which we mentioned before, the distinction must always be kept. For some are not hostile, while others are truly friends, and of good will towards the Church of God and its members. With those who are not hostile, this method is to be kept in promoting peace in the Church: rather conquer their minds and win their friendship by good words, services, examples and similar things, than unseasonably demand benefits from them. Their minds must be brought over before their hands; whoever does otherwise judges wrongly both their duty and his own, which is great imprudence.

units.la: Sin autem homines amici sunt, qui animum ultro adiecturi sint ad benefaciendum ecclesiæ, hic utrumque fieri pro commoditate poterit, nostra officia in illos exerceri, & vicissim illorum erga ecclesiam occupari: ut cum nostris beneficiis lucrifiat Christo, præsertim fiducia nostra de ipsis explorata, tum etiam suis ipsorum factis quodammodo obstringantur ad constantiam illius sui in benefaciendo studii. Nam cur hoc modo non certemus benefaciendo cum illis hominibus? quibus Deus fecit promissiones causa ecclesiæ suæ, & amplissimâ quandam earum partem cum piis assignavit, Gen. 12.2,3. quos Christus pro nobis dixit esse, quandoquidem nō sunt adversus nos, Luc. 9. quibus promisit mercedem prophetæ, si vas frigidæ in nomine prophetæ ministraverint, Matth. 10. 42. quorum societatem Abraham, David, & pii omnes in testamento utroque conciliare sibi non dubitaverunt, quum & communitate naturae & promissionum divinarum consociatione hos sibi conjunctos esse boni animad verterint. Temeraria de his judicia interdum audivi plus satis: a quibus Christiani abstineant oro & obsecro, ne in veritatem divinam communemque charitatem impingant periculosissime.
units.tr: But if men are friends, who are about to bring their goodwill, unprompted, to doing good for the Church, then both can be done as occasion allows: our services can be rendered to them, and in turn their zeal for the Church be engaged; so that, with our benefits, they may be gained for Christ, especially since our confidence in them has been tested, and also that by their own deeds they may be in some measure bound to constancy in their zeal for doing good. For why should we not vie with those men in doing good? To them God gave promises for the sake of his Church, and assigned a very large part of them to the pious, Gen. 12. 2, 3; Christ said of them that they are for us, since they are not against us, Luke 9; he promised a reward to those who give a cup of cold water in the name of a prophet, Matt. 10. 42; Abraham, David and all the pious in both Testaments have not hesitated to win their fellowship, since they recognised that these men are joined to them both by community of nature and by the association of the divine promises. I have sometimes heard rash judgements about these men, more than enough; I beg and beseech Christians to abstain from them, lest they strike most dangerously against the divine truth and common charity.

units.la: "Quod si his bene fieri a nobis oportere (quantum quidem per eos fieri potest) pacem ecclesiae ab his secundum Deu convenit expeti: quanto magis & majore etiam fiducia hoc ipsum experiri ab iis necesse est, qui censentur in numero domesticorum ecclesiae? Atque haec causa est, cur nos passim apostolus ad Christiana erga fratres nostros germanos Dei in ecclesia filios officia accendit monitis saluberrimis, & hortationibus vehementissimis: modumque officiorum istorum praescribit diligentissime, ut cum omni modestia & mansuetudine, cum animi lenitate tolerantes alii alios per charitatem, studeamus servare unitate spiritus per vinculum pacis; & fundamenta principiaque horum officiorum quam accuratissime ascribit, dicens: Unum est corpus, & unus spiritus, sicut & vocati estis in una spem. ipsum vocationis vestræ: unus Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma, unus Deus & pater omnium, qui est super omnes, & per omnes & in omnibus nobis, Eph. 4.3.4.5.6.
units.tr: "But if we must do good to these people (as far as that is possible for us), and seek peace in the Church from them according to God, how much more necessary is it to try this with greater confidence towards those who are counted among the household of the Church? This is the reason why the apostle everywhere urges Christians to their duties towards their brothers, the other sons of God in the Church, with most wholesome warnings and most vehement exhortations. He prescribes most carefully the manner of these duties, that with all lowliness and meekness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, we should be eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. He also sets down most precisely the foundations and principles of these duties, saying: There is one body and one Spirit, even as you are called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all (Eph. 4.3, 4, 5, 6)."

units.la: Atque his quidem omnibus officiis omnes promiscuè fatemur alii erga alios in Domino: sed tamen quum ad eos respicio quos Deus singulari vocatione instruxit in ecclesia sua, ut faciant & doceant quæcunque sibi à Domino præcepta sunt, quo graviorem esse video obligationem illorum, eo graviorem quoque video & horreo condemnationem, si ab his officiis, quæ Deus docet, docedis & faciendis abscesserint. Quid enim? qui angeli sumus Domini, ministri Christi, & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei, qui non sumus nostri juris, sed Domini nostri Jesu Christi sumus, qui per ipsum mancipati Deo & patri & immisi ad colendum sanctam vineam illius, putamusne licere nobis quod vulgo non licet? aut quod in aliis culpamus, in nobis vacare culpa? Non cogitamus usquam exemplum illius instrumenti electi à Domino, dicentis, Quisquis certat, in omnibus est continens; illi quidem qui in stadio currunt, ut periturum coronam accipiant; nos autem, ut incorruptam. Ego igitur ita curro, ut non in incertum; ita pugilem ago, ut aerem non cedam, sed contundo corpus meum & in ser-
units.tr: We all acknowledge that all these duties are owed indiscriminately by one to another in the Lord. But when I look at those whom God has equipped by a special calling in his Church, that they should do and teach whatever the Lord has commanded them, I see that the heavier their obligation, the heavier also I see, and dread, their condemnation, if they have departed from those duties which God teaches and commands. For what of us? We who are the angels of the Lord, the ministers of Christ and the stewards of the mysteries of God, who are not our own, but belong to our Lord Jesus Christ, who through him have been handed over to God and the Father and sent in to cultivate his holy vineyard: do we think it lawful for us to do what is not lawful for the common people? Or that we are free from fault in what we blame in others? We do not consider anywhere the example of that chosen instrument of the Lord who says: Everyone who strives is temperate in all things; they indeed do it to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one. So I run, not aimlessly; I fight, not beating the air, but I punish my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become a castaway (1 Cor. 9.25, 26, 27).

units.la: Note: transfiguratio ab officiis Christiano-rum communibus ad propria docentium.
units.tr: Note: the transition from the common duties of Christians to the particular duties of those who teach.

units.la: in seruitute redigo, ne quomodo cum aliis prae-dicarim, ipse fiam reiectaneus 1. Corinth. 9. 25. 26. 27.
units.tr: I punish my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become a castaway (1 Cor. 9.25, 26, 27).

units.la: Quapropter mea nunc ad vos, o fratres charissimi & symmistae obseruandi, sese con-uertit oratio, qui praefecti estis ovili Domini, ni, ut agatis & pascatis greges qui vobis co-misi sunt ex auctoritate illius, & qui ratio-nem illi episcopo animarum nostrarum & summo pastori ovium estis reddituri, non solum de vita, verum etiam de administratione vestra. Nam quod omnes in populo Dei sive in ecclesia debent, id & vos debetis: ac pro-inde cum aliis omnibus pacem ecclesiae debetis postulare, & omnibus viribus, ut oves Christi propugnare. Sed quia amplius quam aliae oves Christi accepistis, sive dono, prout varie sua dona admerituit spiritus illius, sive vocatione, qua singulis imperata & commendata est sua administratio: propterea nobis supra quam aliis necessaria est accuratio in gerendis rebus, quas fidei nostrae commisit Dominus, sermonem suum commisit nobis: in ecclesia sua mandavit eloqui, & pascere oves suas: praestare iussit exemplo fidei: probare voluit exitum conversationis nostrae, propterea quoque nos id semper ante oculos habere, ut typi simus bonorum operum, quae grex Christi sequens consideret arq; imitetur.
units.tr: Therefore my speech now turns to you, brethren most dear and fellow ministers to be honoured, who have been set over the flock of the Lord, so that you may lead and feed the flocks committed to you by his authority, and who are to render account to that Bishop of our souls and chief Shepherd of the sheep, not only for your life but also for your administration. For what all in the people of God or in the Church ought to do, that you too ought to do. Accordingly, together with all others, you ought to seek the peace of the Church, and with all your strength to defend the sheep of Christ. But because you have received more than the other sheep of Christ, whether by gift, as the Spirit of God has variously apportioned his gifts, or by calling, by which your particular administration has been enjoined and entrusted to each of you, therefore a greater care in managing the affairs which the Lord has committed to our faithfulness is necessary for us than for others. He has committed his word to us; he has commanded us to speak in his Church and to feed his sheep; he has required us to give an example of faith; he has willed us to prove the outcome of our way of life. Therefore too we ought always to keep this before our eyes, that we be patterns of good works, which the flock of Christ may observe and imitate.

units.la: Ioan. 21. tur. Salterræ, lux mundi fuerunt apostoli: hac dignitate officii omnes communicant, qui sermonem illum Domini, quem tradiderunt apostoli, prout à Christo acceperât, præferunt in ovili ejus. Ambulent sane alii in vocatione sua sibi ipsis i.e. suo & paucorum quibus sunt conjuncti, commodo: at nos quibus dispensatio bonorum istorum fuit concredita, sive stamus, sive cadimus, non solùm Domino nostro & nobis (utalii) stamus aut cadimus; sed aliis quamplurimis, qui nobis labentibus collabuntur & consistunt stantibus. Optima quæque de omnibus concipio & opto ex animo: quum tamen ex priscis recentibusque exemplis incommoda plurima ecclesiis allata videam imprudenter multorum administratione, qui nec dignitatem sermonis divini, nec veritatem vocationis suæ, nec pacem eccle-siæ satis prudenter expenderint, dabitis veniam pro vestra in Deum ecclesiamq; pietate, si postquam de omnibus ecclesiæ membris in commune dixi, aliquid etiam speciatim de iis dixero, qui communi corpori ecclesiæ ex vocatione Dei tenentur consulere: ut pastores in ea dati ad coagmentationem sanctorum, ad opus ministerii, & ad ædificationem corporis Christi.
units.tr: John 21. You are the salt of the earth and the light of the world: the apostles were such. All share in this dignity of office who bring forward in his flock that word of the Lord which the apostles handed down as they had received it from Christ. Others, indeed, may walk in their calling for themselves, that is, for their own advantage and that of the few to whom they are joined; but we, to whom the stewardship of these goods has been entrusted, whether we stand or fall, do not stand or fall for our Lord and for ourselves alone, as others do; but for very many others, who fall when we fall and stand when we stand. I conceive and wish from my heart the best of all things for everyone; yet since I see from ancient and recent examples that many harms have come to churches through the imprudent administration of many who have not weighed sufficiently wisely the dignity of the divine Word, the truth of their calling, or the peace of the Church, you will pardon, out of your piety towards God and the Church, if, after I have spoken in common of all the members of the Church, I also speak in particular of those who are bound by God's calling to care for the common body of the Church: those pastors given in it "for the equipping of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ" (Eph. 4.12).

units.la: Est igitur munus commune omnium, ut communionem sanctorum colant, & pa- cem expectant illius: nostrum vero singula- re est, ut eandem communionem colamus singulari modo qui singulari vocationis le-ge à Deo præfinitus est. Ad hanc commu-nionem ante ostendimus primum formam internam, qua cum Deo coalescimus, per-tinere : deinde externam qua colligimur ad verbum ipsius percipiendum, preces ex-hibendas, præstandum obsequium, & ordi-nem honestatemque in his omnibus rebus procurandam. Nostrum est, ut in his ipsis rebus summa religione ac studio aliis omni-bus præeamus sermone & factis. Quid hic excusationis vel in speciem afferre possunt, qui aut sermone aut factis non ita procurat ædificationem illius corporis, quod Deus suo sanguine comparavit. Equidem per-horresco totus, nec sine dolore acerbissimo recolere possum cum animo meo, quantam ecclesiæ labem, quantam sibi ipsis ruinam accersiverint, qui sive prudentes, sive imprudentes ab hoc officio suo desci-verunt. Faxit DOMINUS, ne quis porro desciscat & se machinationibus satanæ ab hoc sanctissimo instituto vocationis suæ abripi patiatur. Gravissima sane vulnera non nobis solum infligimus, sed ipsi ec-clesiæ Christi, quam curæ nostræ Dominus com-
units.tr: It is therefore the common task of all to cultivate the communion of the saints and to look for its peace. But our task is singular: that we cultivate this same communion in a singular way, which is marked out for each by God through a singular law of calling. To this communion we have shown before that there belongs, first, the inward form by which we are joined to God; then the outward form by which we are gathered to hear his word, to offer prayers, to render obedience, and to secure order and decency in all these things. It is our task to go before all others in these very things, with the highest reverence and zeal, by word and deed. What excuse, even in appearance, can they offer, who by word or deed do not so promote the building up of that body which God has purchased with his own blood? Indeed I shudder through and through, and cannot recall without the bitterest grief what great ruin to the Church, and what great ruin to themselves, those have brought upon themselves who, whether wittingly or unwittingly, have deserted this duty. May the Lord grant that no one from now on desert it, or suffer himself to be snatched by the schemes of Satan from this most holy institution of his calling. Indeed we inflict most grievous wounds not only on ourselves, but on the very Church of Christ, which the Lord has entrusted to our care

units.la: commendavit : quum dictis aut factis ab illo fine quem Deus imperat, aberramus, oblivisce ntes illius pacis quam in ecclesia Dei nos constantissime oportet expetere. Nam cur non expendamus, quandoquidem administri summus Christi & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei, cur (inquam) non expendamus diligentissime dicta factaque nostra, quae ab aliis diligetissime novimus observari? Non laboro, utrum ea sic observet alii jure, an injuria: ex officio, an praeter officium: etsi quum lux jubemur aliis esse, ut videant: & sal esse ut veritate doctrinae ab omni corruptione homines vindicentur: non possunt dici ex officio non facere, qui ad nos respiciunt. Omnino ita nos oportet cum animis nostris statuere: si religiose dicta factaque nostra ipsi cogitemus circumspiciamusque, id nos ex officio facturos esse; sin minus, audaciam praesidentiamque inconsideratam nostram fore contra officium nostrum.
units.tr: when, by word or deed, we stray from that end which God commands, forgetting that peace which we must most steadfastly seek in the Church of God. For why should we not weigh most carefully our words and deeds, since we are the ministers and stewards of the mysteries of God, when we know full well that others observe them most carefully? I am not concerned whether others observe them rightly or wrongly, whether as part of their duty or beyond it; although, since we are commanded to be light to others, so that they may see, and salt, so that by the truth of doctrine men may be delivered from all corruption, those who look to us cannot be said not to act as part of their duty. Altogether we ought to resolve in our minds this: if we ourselves reflect and take care over our words and deeds in a religious spirit, we shall be acting as our office requires; but if not, our boldness and our careless presumption will be against our office.

units.la: Quid ergo dixerit quispiam in dictis factisque nostris attendi anobis necesse est? Expo-nam paucis, ad Deum, ecclesiam, mundum & ad nos ipsos oportet attendamus. Ad Deum, ut semper ab ipso pendeamus, & ad ipsum omnia referamus: ad ecclesiam, ut ipsi ad Deum iturae praeeamus: ad mundum, ut inculinculpati extra ipsum fugiamus & alios nobiscum evocemus: ad nos ipsos denique, ut in his omnibus nos occupemus constantissime, ad Deum, secundum Deum, per ecclesiam, & cum ecclesia contendentes, & adversus mundum armis iustitiae dimicantes ad nostram salutem, & eorum qui nos audiunt. Hic vero, Deus bone, quam multis modis peccatur ignorantia, imprudentia, & infirmitate nostra! Non libet, neque expedit omnia pertexere, quibus omnes graviter offendimus. Non libet ea, in quibus communiter cum aliis peccamus colligere. Id satis futurum arbitror, si de iis peccatis dixero, in quae contra singularem vocationem nostram plus satis (heu) incidimus, immemores gratiae Dei, pacis ecclesiae & vocationis nostrae; etsi fit plurimum ut hujus ipsius vocationis nostrae praetextu & specie peccata nostra contegamus. Tacebo de interna peccatis, quae videt Deus, & singulorum sentiunt apud se conscientiae: de externis dicam.
units.tr: What, then, must be attended to in our words and deeds? I will set it out briefly: we must attend to God, to the Church, to the world, and to ourselves. To God, so that we always depend on him and refer all things to him; to the Church, so that we go before it as those who are to go on to God; to the world, so that we flee its pollutions unstained and call others out with us; to ourselves, finally, so that we steadfastly occupy ourselves in all these things: to God, according to God, through the Church and with the Church striving, and fighting against the world with the weapons of righteousness; for our own salvation, and that of those who hear us. Here, good God, in how many ways we sin through our ignorance, imprudence and weakness! It is neither pleasant nor expedient to go through all the ways in which we all gravely offend. I do not wish to gather together those in which we sin in common with others. I think it will be enough if I speak of those sins into which we fall, alas, far too much against our particular calling, forgetful of the grace of God, of the peace of the Church and of our calling; although it very often happens that we cover our sins under the pretext and appearance of this very calling of ours. I will say nothing of the inward sins, which God sees and which individual consciences feel within themselves; I will speak of the outward ones.

units.la: Qui debemus ex vocatione, sanctimoniae & paci ecclesiae dictis & factis consulere, plerunque dictis & factis officimus, tum eas res, quae non sunt vocationis nostrae assumendo, tum eas, quae omnino ex vocatione sunt omittendo, tum contra jus vocationis alia committendo. Ac dictis quidem offendimus quà privatim aliqua ecclesiæ membra, quà publicè corpus ipsius, prout sese nobis res obtulerit. De privatis offen- sionibus quid dicam? aut unde incipiam? Alios offendit levitas sermonum qui nihil ad nos, alios silentium, alios importunitas.
units.tr: We who ought, by reason of our calling, to look after the holiness and peace of the Church by our words and deeds very often do harm by those words and deeds: by taking up matters that are not part of our calling, by omitting those things that are wholly part of it, and by committing other acts against the right of our calling. We offend by our words, both privately, against some members of the Church, and publicly, against its body, as the occasion presents itself. But what shall I say about private offences, and where shall I begin? Some are offended by the frivolity of talk that has nothing to do with us, others by our silence, others by our importunity.

units.la: Præsertim si qui doctrina, reprehensione, aut consolatione opus habuerint, incredibile est quàm facilè imprudentia nostra offendantur animæ, quę privatum Dei servorum officium desiderant in suis angustiis & perturbationibus gratissimis. Non solet enim illa cogitatio animos nostros incessere, quam ab exemplo Christi Domini & præceptoris nostri singulis momentis nos oportebat recedere non litigabit, neque clamitabit, neque audiet quisquam in plateis vocem ejus: arundinem quassatam non continget, & linum fumigans non exstinguet, Matth. 12. 19, 20. quæ omnia Christus fecit opere, & in ministerio fieri imperat. Nec valde, nec sæpe animos nostros afficiunt illius verba, qui zelo sanctissimo dixit, Quis affligitur, quin ego affligar? Quis offenditur, quin ego urar? 2 Cor. 11. 29.
units.tr: Especially when some people need teaching, rebuke or comfort, it is incredible how easily souls are offended by our thoughtlessness, when they long for the private office of God's servants in their distress and troubles. That thought does not usually stir our minds, the thought that at every moment we ought to withdraw from the example of Christ our Lord and Teacher: "He shall not strive, nor cry, neither shall any man hear his voice in the streets. A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench" (Matt. 12:19, 20). Christ did all these things in practice, and he commands that they be done in the ministry. Nor do the words of the man who said, with most holy zeal, "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is offended, and I burn not?" (2 Cor. 11:29) move our minds greatly or often.

units.la: Quid? quòd in hæc mala, graviora certè quàm putemus, in conscientias infirmorū & indignissima vocatione nostra, non solum lum ruimus apud eos, qui in grege nostrò sunt : verùm etiam tanquam si domi nihil essent in quo occupemur, agimus ἀλλότρια summa licentia, & in rebus alienis fumus oculatissimi? O nos miseros, quam pliffimos fines vocationis nostræ, quibus capiendis nunquam satis idonea aut sufficiens esse potest ingenii nostri tenuitas, delatari putamus oportere vanitate nostra: neque in sermone, quem Deus imperat tegi, neque in grege, quem Deus imperat pasci, conquiescimus ex officio nostro 1.Tim. 4.13. Act. 20.28. 1.Pet. 5.2.
units.tr: What then? Do we not fall, in these evils, which are certainly more serious than we think, into the consciences of the weak? And, most unworthy of our calling, do we not only fail among those who are in our flock, but also, as if there were nothing at home to occupy us, act with the greatest licence in other people's affairs [ἀλλότρια], and become most keen-eyed about things that are not ours? O wretched us! We think it right to take up very many ends of our calling, for which the poverty of our talent can never be sufficient or adequate, and we are carried off by our vanity. Yet we rest neither in the preaching that God commands us to keep up, nor in the flock that God commands us to feed, from a sense of our duty. (1 Tim. 4:13; Acts 20:28; 1 Pet. 5:2.)

units.la: Sed leviora sunt hæc privata vulnera, iis quæ publico sæpe imponuntur, partim fidentia, partimq; imprudentia nostra. Nam sive ad sermones in concionib. publicè habitos, sive ad reliquam administrationem oculos convertetis, incidunt sæpe quàm plurima; quibus nisi probè ad nos attendamus, nocemus publico & auctoritate vocationis illius nostræ, quam Deus eötemni facto nostro noluit, ipsi minuimus, 2 Tim. 2.13. Quàm multa interdum pro concione funduntur, quæ nihil ad nos pertinent aut vocationem nostram, quæ nihil ad ecclesiam? aut quę alienæ cognitioni sunt credita? Testes sunt ecclesiæ multę apud omnes gentes, testes magistratus, testes historiæ, testes libri etiam de jure divino & humano, scripti, plurimos eorum, qui finibus ecclesiasticæ vocationis suæ continere se debuerant quà se ipsos, quà ministerium suum sanctissimamque auctoritatem illius, quà multas animas, quà respublicas, quà ecclesias funditus perdidisse, dum ex angustia sui judicii (quod putabant amplissimum) omnia agi & ferri statuerunt oportere.
units.tr: But these private wounds are lighter than those that are often inflicted on the public, partly through our confidence, and partly through our thoughtlessness. For whether we turn our eyes to the sermons delivered publicly in assemblies, or to the rest of the administration, very many faults often occur, and unless we attend to them carefully, we harm the public and diminish the authority of that office of ours, which God did not want to be despised through our deed (2 Tim. 2:13). How many things are sometimes poured out in the pulpit which have nothing to do with us, nor with our calling, nor with the Church? Or which have been entrusted to the knowledge of others? There are many witnesses among all nations: witnesses in the Church, witnesses in the magistrates, witnesses in history, and witnesses in books written on divine and human law. They show that very many people, who ought to have kept themselves within the bounds of their ecclesiastical calling, have utterly ruined themselves, the ministry, and the most holy authority of it, many souls, commonwealths, and churches, while from the narrowness of their own judgement (which they thought very broad) they decided that everything had to be done and carried out their way.

units.la: Librum sacrum, fratres dilectissimi, libru sederis sive testamenti veteris & novi versandum habemus noctuna & diurna manu, ut dicebat satyricus; non libros hujus mundi forenses atque politicos: conscientias habemus curandas, ac non facultates ecclesias ac non respublicas. Putamus ne igitur Deum male prospexisse mundo, quia res civiles ab ecclesiasticis dispesceret? putamusne nobis factam a Deo injuriam, qui has res nobis, illas aliis curandas instituerit? putamusne sufficere metes cognoscendis & judicandis, corpora faciendi s tam multis rebus, quas Deus distribuit in multos propter earum infinitatem gravitatemque, & infirmitatem nostram? Nempe hoc illud est, miseret Deum nostri, & nos ipsos nostri non miseret. Videamus potius, obsecro ut tenuitate nostram serio coram Domino decepsrecordemur, gravitatem muneris nostri ex veritate cogitemus, & nobis ante oculos ponamus magnum illum Dei servum & Christi apostolum, dicentem: Fiduciam habemus per Christum (non autem per nos) apud Deum (non autem apud nos) ut quod idonei sumus per nos ipsos ad cogitandum quid-quam velut ex nobis ipsis: sed quod idonei su-mus, id ex Deo est, qui etiam fecit nos idoneos mi-nistros novi testamenti, non litterae, sed spiritus, vivificat. 2. Cor. 3. 4. 5. Hic, hic pes figendus est, in ministerio ad quod vo-cati sumus: non est curalio transvolemus, qui in opere nostro (si recte judicabimus) longe plus laboris sensuri sumus, quam ut nobis liceat animi nostri explendi causa in alienas curas irruere.
units.tr: Brethren most dear, we have the holy Book, the book of the Old and New Testament, to be handled with hand by night and by day, as the satirist said; not the forensic and political books of this world. We have consciences to care for, not property of the Church, not commonwealths. Do we think, then, that God has ill provided for the world, because he separated civil affairs from ecclesiastical ones? Do we think that God has done us an injury, who appointed these matters for us and those for others? Do we think that the limits of our knowing and judging, and our bodies, are sufficient for doing so many things, which God has distributed among many because of their infinite weight and our weakness? Surely this is what it means: God pities us, and we do not pity ourselves. Rather, I beg you, let us seriously remember our smallness before the Lord, let us think of the weight of our office in truth, and let us set before our eyes that great servant of God and apostle of Christ, saying: "We have such trust through Christ toward God; not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God; who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life" (2 Cor. 3:4–6). Here, here must we plant our feet, in the ministry to which we are called. We should not run across to care for other things, we who, if we judge rightly, shall feel far more labour in our own work than we would have if we were allowed to rush into other people's cares to satisfy our own minds.

units.la: Neq; vero hoc malum unum est in no-stra administratione quod alienis reb⁹ plus satis attendimus: sed ex eo alterum malum continuò nascitur, quòd alienis implicati occupationibus eas plerumq; omittimus, quae etiam flagitat inexcusabilis vocationis nostrae necessitas. Si qui in ecclesia sunt, quos docere à nobis oportet; ne p somniū quidem nobis in mentem venit nostri ossi-cii; si qui redarguendi à veritate doctrinae abludentes; si qui ad probitatem & sancti-moniam vitae cohortandi; si qui à viis malis & di stortis suis revocandi; si qui verbi divini conconsolationibus, ubi malis prostrati jacent, erigendi: si qui denique ullo modo verbis vitæ æternæ in Christo animandi (hic enim Rhodus hic saltus) sive privatim, ut lex charitatis jubet; sive publicè, ut ratio publica interdum postulat; tum vero nos hic nõ adsumus, & vere aliud agimus, quos hoc agere oportuit (ut in rebus sacris olim clamabat præco) & transfi-limus. Nimirum hic fructus illius ἁγνείας, hoc opus illius architectoris adversarii salutis nostræ, qui mille opifex rerum, & mille-artifex pro uno cogitato ad vocationem nostram pertinente infundit mille, ex quo nos ad mille potius alia quàm ad hoc ferri animadvertit ingenii nostri vanitate.
units.tr: Nor is this the only evil in our administration, that we attend too much to other people's affairs; from this a second evil immediately arises: because we are entangled in other occupations, we often neglect those duties which even the necessity of our inexcusable calling demands. If there are those in the Church whom we ought to teach, it never even enters our minds to do our duty; if there are those who need to be refuted because they depart from the truth of doctrine; if there are those who are to be exhorted to integrity and holiness of life; if there are those who are to be called back from evil and crooked ways; if there are those who are to be raised up by the consolations of the divine word, when they lie prostrate under evils; if there are, finally, any in any way to be encouraged by the words of eternal life in Christ (here is the Rhodes, here the leap), whether privately, as the law of charity commands, or publicly, as public reason sometimes requires; then indeed we are not present here, and we are truly doing something else, when we ought to be doing this, as the herald used to cry in sacred matters, and we pass by. Surely this is the fruit of that chastity, this is the work of that architect, the adversary of our salvation, who, the artificer of a thousand things and a thousand arts, pours a thousand thoughts into us in place of the one thought that pertains to our calling, and so turns us, by the vanity of our mind, to a thousand other things rather than to this.

units.la: Atq; utinam in his finibus mali hoc nostrum malum subsideret, ne ulterius abripe-remur à vocatione nostra. Gratisimum enim & indignisimum omnium experdi-to illo instituto id consequi solet maximo ecclesiæ damno, quod ii qui aliena curat & ad sua sibi imperata minime attendunt, eò tandem veniunt dementiæ, ut obliti plane vocationis suæ non dubitent ea facere in totum vocationi ipsorum adversantur. Quid enim obsecro facias mi homo qui forensia cum ecclesiasticis, profana cum sacris, hu-
units.tr: And would that this evil of ours might subside within these limits, so that we would not be carried further away from our calling. For it usually happens, by that most wretched and unworthy practice, that those who look after other people's affairs and pay little attention to what is commanded them, come at last to such madness that, quite forgetting their calling, they do not hesitate to do things utterly opposed to their own calling. For what, I ask you, will you do, my man, who most foolishly mix up the forensic with the ecclesiastical, the profane with the sacred, the human with the divine, unless, enticed by the honeyed poison and the weariness of this world, you strip away the zeal for holy things through the habits of profane ones? So it will happen to you, as was once said in the proverb: now asked to speak, now in a Greek cloak you walk about, and you, a man, wander about between your two pages of calling, while you seem to be making both pages of the world.

units.la: manacum divinis concurbas præsidentis- fimè; nisi ut inescatus mellito veneno fasti- dioque hujus mundi, exuas rerum sanctarum studium ex profanarum consuetudi- ne? Ita accidet tibi, quod olim proverbio dicebatur, ut modò rogatus, modò palliatus ambules, & utramq; paginam vir ἐπεγέ- μεγ ἐοπῦpas vocationis tuæ, dum utramque paginā mundi tibi videris facere. Deus bone quantum delirium mentes istorum hominum occupat, qui rerum adeo multarum se posse confidunt satagere! Non ita dilatabāt veteres illi poëtæ in ratione Deorum suorum, quos tamen hominibus longè potentiores esse fatebātur. huic cœlum, illi æthera, huic inferiorem aërem, illi mare, uni terram, alteri inferos tribuebat pro curandos: denique ordinem aliquem videbant in Diis suis commentitiis, quem tu, homo, in teipso videre non potes: ac proinde ubi ordinem non vides, in contraria studia, sententias, actionesque pro re nata, ut pluma in diversos ventos, quàm facillime abriperis. Nec verò aliter potest contingere; quum tibi in rebus nō constes, omnino necesse est eò delabaris, ut nec sermone, nec actionibus tuis perdiu idē esse possis. Quemadmodum autem in rebus error est proclivis, ubi tam multiplicem captura unica
units.tr: Good God, what madness occupies the minds of those men who trust that they can manage so many matters! The ancient poets did not extend their account of the gods so widely, though they confessed that these gods were far more powerful than men. To one they assigned heaven, to another the upper air, to another the lower air, to another the sea, to one alone the earth, to another the underworld, to be looked after. Finally, they saw some order among their fictional gods, which you, a man, cannot see in yourself. And therefore, when you do not see order, you are most easily carried off to contrary pursuits, opinions and actions, according to the circumstances of the moment, like a feather blown in different winds. Nor indeed can it be otherwise: since you are not consistent in your affairs, you must necessarily slip into such a state that you cannot be the same for long either in your speech or in your actions. Now as error in affairs is easily found, where we trust that we shall attain so many things with a single small thread of our wit and a single throw, so too a second evil must necessarily be born alongside it: that we lose the due measure of affairs just as we lose the affairs themselves. For those things which we ought to take care of privately for the salvation of souls…

units.la: Immo- deftia in rebus gerendis. unica ingenii nostri lineola & unico jactu nos asséquuturos esse confidimus, ita etiam alterum malum huic connasci tur necessario, quòd justum modum rerum peræquè ac res ipsas perdimus. Nam quæ privatim ad salutem animorum curari opus est, ea publicè funditamus; quæ in aurem insusurrari, ea super tecta pronunciamus; quæ sedato animo, ea cum fervore: quæ cum vehementia, ea remisso animo: quæ cum sale, ea insulsè: quæ cum auctoritate, ea ineptè ad scribarum & pharisæorum exemplum prædicantur. Nempe auctoritate nostram, non Christi quærimus plerique, & opinione freti auctoritatis nostræ utramque perdimus miseri. Et miramur, rebus ita stantibus, si verbum Dei parum fructus edit in ecclesiis Christianis hoc nostro tempore? quum tam parum in iis, per quos afferri ipsum oportet, plerumque radicetur: & radicatu adeo multis spinis & sentibus præsocerur, quas non ipsi plerumque facto nostro imprudentiaque in arvo Domini conferimus?
units.tr: Immoderation in conducting affairs. We are confident that we shall attain our goals with a single stroke of our one little wit, but a second evil is necessarily born alongside it: we lose the just measure of affairs just as we lose the affairs themselves. Things that ought to be handled privately for the salvation of souls, we broadcast publicly; things to be whispered into an ear, we proclaim from the housetops; things to be said with a calm mind, we say with heat; things to be said with vehemence, we say with a relaxed mind; things to be said with salt, we say without savour; things to be said with authority, we preach foolishly, after the manner of the scribes and Pharisees. Indeed, most of us seek our own authority, not Christ's, and trusting in our authority we wretchedly lose both. And are we surprised, with things in this state, if the word of God bears little fruit in the Christian churches of our time, since it so seldom takes root in those through whom it ought to be brought, and when it does take root it is so choked by many thorns and briars, which we ourselves for the most part bring into the Lord's field by our deeds and our folly?

units.la: Equidem non possum quin vehementissime commovear, quoties hæc mala apud me reputo: neque mihi voluptatis quicquam esse potest in iis perscribendis, quorum percursu horresco cogitatione: & quæ si qui indigne ferent
units.tr: Indeed I cannot help being very deeply moved whenever I reflect on these evils. There is no pleasure for me in setting them down in writing, and I shudder to go over them in thought; and if anyone takes this ill when I put it in writing,

units.la: ferant à me configuari scriptis: peto ex animo, ut ferant indignius ea fieri ab aliis quae à nobis perscribuntur. Deum oro, det nobis omnibus justum argumentum tollendi é medio his querimonias, & mihi ipsi delendi scripturam meam. Sed quid agam? taceamne in tanta perturbatione publica, tantoque incendio, quod plerisque custodib. dormientibus, aliud agentibus, aut varie in studia abreptis Satanas excitavit? certe in ce, diu est in orbe Christiano, nisi Deus è coelo prospexerit, omnia consumturum: animi humani foci sunt, in quibus peccatum flagrat: linguae hae folles sunt, illae fomites, quibus incendium magis ac magis inardescit: linguis succedunt chartarum virulentissimarum plaustra, quibus tanquam malleolis, perrumpit incendium in omnes partes, quaecunque lingua perflatin nō possunt: deniq; bona pars Christiani orbis hoc tempore bustum portus videtur esse pervadente & furente incendio, quam Christiani gregis domicilium. An ergo hi pastores? hae oves Christi? quas in suo miserabili busto miserè video contabescere? Sunt certe pastores adhuc, sunt oves Christi, & Christi sunt: sed multi in hoc tetro & letali incendio nec se Christi esse, nec oves esse, neces-se pastores meminerunt; usq; adeo Christus salutasalutarisque gratia illius gravitate istius incendii, & studiorum nostrorum in publico hoc modo vanitate, animorumq; tenebris, & mundi flagrantis fumo obscuratur. Quin igitur dicam, quod ille Elihu apud Jobum? plenus sum sermonibus, coarctat me spiritus ventris mei: ecce venter meus ut vinum cui no aperitur: sicut novi utres finderetur: eloquar, ut respiratio sit mihi: aperiens labia mea enun- ciabo ne, quaso, accipiam personam ullius, & apud quenquam non utar prafatione non enim novi prafationibus uti: paululum si disfimu- larem, tolleret me qui fecit me, Job.32.18.19. 20.21.22. Ac multos quidem viros bonos, Dei & ecclesiæ amantissimos, scio eadem verba mecum reputare sanctissimo religio- sissimoq; studio: quum ad mala tam mul- ta respiciut, quæ hoc nostro seculo, in Chri- stiano orbe grassantur licentiosissimè. Sed quia illi tacent coram hominibus, effundentes suos gemitus apud Dominum solum com- gnitorem omnium: spero me illis rem gratam facturum, si communes ipsis ac mihi dolores hoc scripto expressero, & Christianos omnes tandem testes appellavero tum doloris acerbissimi illius nostri, tum etiam officii, quod restarum facimus & sponde- mus in Domino, si forte ad restringendum incendium commodo Christianitati per volun-
units.tr: let them bear it, I beg from my heart, and let them take it more ill that such things are done by others, which we set down in writing. I pray God that he may give us all a just reason to remove these complaints from the midst, and me to erase my own writing. But what am I to do? Should I keep silent in such a public upheaval and such a conflagration, which Satan has kindled while most of the watchmen were sleeping, busy with other things, or carried off in various directions by their studies? Certainly, unless God looks down from heaven, this fire will in time consume everything in the Christian world. The hearts of men are hearths in which sin blazes; these tongues are bellows, those are kindling, by which the fire is fanned more and more; to the tongues are added wagonloads of the most virulent pamphlets, by which, as with firebrands, the conflagration breaks out in every direction wherever the tongue cannot blow it. In short, a large part of the Christian world at this time seems to be a burning pyre, with the fire raging and spreading through it, rather than the dwelling of the Christian flock. Are these the ministers? Are these the sheep of Christ, whom I see wretchedly wasting away in their miserable pyre? Certainly they are still ministers, they are still sheep of Christ, and they belong to Christ; but many in this foul and deadly fire no longer remember that they are Christ's, nor that they are sheep, nor that they are ministers. So far is Christ, and the saving grace of his name, obscured by the heaviness of this fire, by the vanity of our studies in such public matters, by the darkness of souls and the smoke of a burning world. Why then should I not say what Elihu said to Job? I am full of words; the spirit within my belly constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins it is ready to burst. I will speak, that I may have relief; I will open my lips and answer. Let me not, I pray, accept any man's person, nor use flattery toward anyone; for I do not know how to use flattery; if I kept silent a little, my Maker would soon take me away. Job 32.18, 19, 20, 21, 22. Indeed I know that many good men, most loving of God and the Church, reflect on these same words with a most holy and devout zeal, when they look upon the many evils which rage most unrestrainedly in the Christian world in this our age. But since they keep silent before men, pouring out their groans before the Lord alone, the knower of all things, I hope I shall be doing them a favour if I express in this writing the sorrows we share, and call all Christians to witness both to that most bitter grief of ours and to the duty we undertake and promise before the Lord, if perhaps by it, God willing, our work may serve to check the fire to the benefit of Christianity.

units.la: voluntatem Dei opera nostra futura est. Quid ergo agimus, ô fratres & peculiä Christi? quid, grex Christi? quid, pastores gregis? quousque tandem in Christum, in membra ipsius nostraque ipsorum viscera injiciemus violentas manus? alii alios con- teremus? dentibus unguibus lacerabimus? pedibus proculcabimus? & sæviemus o- mni conatu nostro, ut immanes feræ, quo- usque linguæ gladii acuti futuri sunt? quo- usque veloces pedes ad effundendum san- guinem procurrentes? quousque manus ad horrendam lanienam & carnificinam adji- cientur? Sunt enim quorum linguæ priva- tim ac publicè nihil nisi tubæ sunt ad cane- dum bellicum paratissimæ, inflammantes totum genituræ nostræ, & inflammatæ gehenna. Sunt quorum manus calamo & atramento armata profundit Christianum orbem telis planè letalibus: quibus nō cor- pora, sed corda hominum ad mortem sibi & aliis consciscendam furiosè adducuntur. Sunt quorum pedes ad excursiones & panegyres expeditissimi ministrant diabolicis furiis in Christianum gregem irruentibus sceleratissimè. Hæc tela jam in omnes partes Christianorum orbis volitant adeo confer- tim, ut quemadmodum nimbo vehemen- tissimo lux cœli, ita lux spiritualis denso te- lorum
units.tr: What then are we doing, brothers and the peculiar people of Christ? What are we doing, flock of Christ? What are we doing, ministers of the flock? How long will we lay violent hands on Christ, on his members and on our own bowels? How long will we crush one another, tear each other with teeth and claws, trample each other underfoot, and rage with every effort of ours like savage beasts, with sharp swords for tongues? How long will our swift feet run to pour out blood, and how long will our hands be set to horrible butchery and slaughter? There are those whose tongues, both in private and in public, are nothing but trumpets, most ready to sound the battle-cry, inflaming the whole course of our existence and themselves inflamed by hell. There are those whose hands, armed with pen and ink, pour out upon the Christian world weapons that are truly deadly, by which not bodies but the hearts of men are furiously driven to take death upon themselves and upon others. There are those whose feet, most nimble for raids and public assemblies, serve the devilish furies that rush most wickedly upon the Christian flock. These weapons now fly in every direction across the Christian world so thickly that, as the light of heaven is taken away by the most violent storm cloud, so spiritual light is taken away

units.la: Iorum istorum numero multis Christianis mentibus minime malis adimatur. An ergo tantum est in scribendo voluptatis, ut propter eam Christi, ecclesiae, & animarum tam multarum expungatur ratio? an voluptatem illam nostram, quam in scribendo capimus, tanti audemus emere? Quin potius cogitamus quod olim dicebat ille Satyricus, teneri multos scribendi cacoethe insanabili? Scripta non ex morbo animi, sed ex judicio certo exaranda atque edenda sunt. Alioquin raceri praestat: quum doceat Salomon etiam stultum, quando tacet, videri sapientem, Prov. 17. 18. Quod si certo judicio fiant, profecto ad veritatem & pacem, charitatemque spectare oportet omnia.
units.tr: by the number of these weapons from many minds that are by no means evil. Is there then so much pleasure in writing that for its sake the reckoning owed to Christ, to the Church, and to so many souls is wiped out? Do we dare to buy that pleasure of ours, which we take in writing, at such a price? Rather let us consider what that satirist once said, that many are seized by an incurable itch for writing. Writings must not be composed and published out of a disease of the mind, but out of sound judgement. Otherwise it is better to be silent, since Solomon teaches that even a fool, when he holds his peace, is thought wise (Prov. 17.28). But if writings are produced with sound judgement, then surely everything ought to look to truth, peace and charity.

units.la: Ac morbo quidem animi potius quam judicio scripta quam plurima hoc tempore in vulgus diffluari, multis argumentis probari potest. Verumtamen, ne longiores simus, paucula quaedam afferemus, ex quibus plurimorum scriptorum, quae hoc tempore circumvolitant in manus omnium, conditionem ostendemus; ut singuli videant quam impune grassetur hoc malum maximo ecclesiae malo. De iis autem perinde ac de actionibus internis & externis hominum, non ex genere materiaque (agimus enim de scripturis solum ad res sacras pertinentibus) sed ex spe-
units.tr: That very many writings are poured out upon the public today from a disease of the mind rather than from judgement can be proved by many arguments. Yet, not to make this longer, we shall set forth a few particulars from which we may show the condition of the many writings which now fly about in everyone's hands, so that each may see how freely this evil rages to the great harm of the Church. But concerning these, just as concerning the internal and external actions of men, we must judge not by their kind and matter (for we are speaking only of writings that pertain to sacred things), but by their species, circumstances and end.

units.la: {y} plurimorum scriptorum hodie, scriptorum fit editio. ex specie, ac circumstantiis & fine ipsorum fieri judicium necesse est. Primum enim scripta eduntur, ac potius voluntur quàm plurima ab ingeniis perturbatissimis: quæ pietati, veritati, charitati & paci publicæ re- ipsa adversantur, his bonis quæ modo dixi- mus, sed ipsa (ut cum vulgo loquar) in sub- stantia bona sint, tamen huic bonæ subsi- tiæ multum veneni sæpe infunditur, quum loco doctrinæ & dogmatum (ut vocant) veritatis justa circumstantia negligentur, & res personales injiciuntur, criminationes, convicia, contumeliæ, quàm plurima de- nique acerbissima judicia: quæ licet esse[nt] verissima, non jubet veritas dici, sed jubet reticeri charitas. Nam quid hoc ad veritatem propugnandam, aut medacium expugnan- dum facit, si forte hominem ex suis coloribus cuti mihi quidem videtur) depinxero? neque enim veritatem suam per homines Deus ita probari voluit, ut ex bono aut pravo huius, illius, aut cuius quam hominis instituto vitæ, de veritate divina judicent. Transcendit veritas omnem hominum ca- ptum: neq; per homines illa judicatur, sed homines per illam. Quapropter non dicebat Christus, ex fructibus hominum, aut ex hominibus cognoscetis veritatem: sed ex fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos. Et optime inquit.
units.tr: {y} Many writings are published today. First, writings are put out, or rather poured out, in greater number than ever by minds most disturbed, which are in fact opposed to piety, truth, charity and the public peace. Although, as I have said, these writings are good in their substance (to speak as the common people do), yet much poison is often poured into this good substance, when the proper circumstances of doctrine and of dogmas (as they are called) of truth are neglected, and personal matters are brought in: accusations, insults, reproaches, and finally very many most bitter judgements. Even if these were most true, truth does not require them to be said, but charity requires them to be passed over in silence. For what does it help to defend the truth or to overthrow a lie, if perhaps I have portrayed a man in his own colours (as it seems to me, at least, in his skin)? For God did not will his truth to be proved through men in such a way that people should judge the divine truth by whether this man or that man, or any man, lives a good or a bad life. Truth transcends all human comprehension; it is not judged through men, but men are judged through it. Therefore Christ did not say, "You will know the truth from the fruits of men, or from men," but, "You will know them from their fruits." And very well he says,

units.la: {¹} Cf. Matth. 7. inquit apostolus: Quid si infidi fuerunt quidam? Num ipsorum infidelitas fidem Dei inanem reddet? absit. imo esto Deus verax, omnis autem homo mendax: sicut scriptum est: ut justificeris in sermonibus tuis & vincas quando tu judicas. Rom. 3. 3. 4. Postremo ii ad finem, quem sibi in scriptis proponunt multi, aut ad eventum etiam respicimus, omnino copertum suimus, aut finem multorum qui scribunt iniquum esse, aut siquidem minime malus est, plurimum a fine discrepare scriptionis modum: ipsum denique eventum ab utroque abesse quam longissime. Cur autem? nisi quia in scribendo nec finis, nec modus servatur plurimum: & res tacendæ divulgantur in publicum; & incompetentes judices in rebus etiam gravissimis malitia hominum appellantur, copetentes vero multitudine oppressi in tanta rerum cotur-batione silent.
units.tr: {¹} Cf. Matth. 7. The apostle says: What if some were unfaithful? Will their unbelief make the faith of God without effect? God forbid. Yea, let God be true, but every man a liar; as it is written: That thou mayest be justified in thy words, and mayest overcome when thou art judged. Rom. 3. 3. 4. Finally, as for the end that many propose to themselves in their writings, or even the outcome to which we look, we have altogether concealed both: many who write aim at an unjust end, or if not an evil one, their manner of writing differs greatly from that end, and the outcome itself is as far removed as possible from both. Why so? Because in writing neither the end nor the manner is for the most part observed, things that ought to be kept silent are made public, and incompetent judges are summoned, in matters of the greatest importance, by the malice of men, while those who are competent, overwhelmed by the crowd, keep silent amid such a confusion of affairs.

units.la: Certe hæc mala, quæ modo à me ad-ducta sunt, si quis accurate fine perturbatione animi expenderit: mirabitur mecum summam illam Dei misericordiam, qui corpus illud lacerum Christianitatis, & in suam ipsius salutem conjuratum hactenus adeo gratiose, à meritissima ruina & peste conservaverit. Nam ut nihil de fine & modo scriptionum dicam, quia jam ante perstrinxistrinximus, quotus quisque est qui à rebus fundendis abstineat, quas taceri praestitis- set? Sed ad dogmata respexeris, hîc multa incommode, multa impropriè, multa falso deblaterantur ab his & ab illis, quae ubi fe- mel evolaverint, neque in scriptis revocari possunt, neque ex animis scribentium; qui se cupiunt victores esse, ac non victricé veritatem: neque ipsis in mentem venit sanctissimi illius dicti, quo Paulus utebatur, nihil posse nos contra veritatem, sed provveritate, 2. Cor. 13. 8. sin ad actiones hominum, quae perscribuntur, animum & cogitatione converteris, de quibus dicimus eò liberius, quò magis studiis in hanc autillam partem impellimur: quis nescit multa etiam bene facta non nisi tempestive enunciari oportere? malefacta verò nunquam, nisi ex necessitate? Atque hic ille campus est, in quo plerique delicias agunt hocipsò tempore: quo ad charitatem non solùm auctoritate divini verbi, sed etiam gravitate judiciorum eius, eventorum; lamentabilium, quae (pro dolor) videmus quàm plurima, nos omnes uno animo necesse habemus contendere.
units.tr: Certainly, if anyone weighs carefully and without disturbance of mind the evils I have just brought forward, he will marvel with me at that great mercy of God, who has so graciously kept that torn body of Christianity, which has so far conspired against its own salvation, from its well-deserved ruin and plague. For, to say nothing more of the end and manner of writings, since I have already touched on them, how few there are who refrain from pouring out the matters that they ought to have kept silent! But if you look to doctrines, here many things are babbled incorrectly, many improperly, many falsely, by these and those, and once they have flown forth they can be recalled neither from the writings nor from the minds of those who write, who wish to be victors rather than to see truth victorious; nor does it occur to them that saying of most holy Paul, that we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth, 2 Cor. 13. 8. But if you turn your mind and thought to the actions of men, which are written up, about which we speak all the more freely the more we are driven by zeal to one side or the other, who does not know that even many good deeds ought to be announced only at the right time, and evil deeds never, except out of necessity? And this is the field in which most people take their pleasure at this very time, when, for the sake of charity, we all must with one mind strive not only by the authority of the divine Word but also by the weight of its judgments, against the lamentable events which (alas!) we see in great number.

units.la: Deinde quàm grave est illud, obsecro, quod in illis omnibus scriptionum generibus judicet non competentes, non scientes, non aequi, appellantur? Quem enim, amabo te, mihi
units.tr: Next, I beg you, how serious is that which, in all these kinds of writings, they call judging those who are not competent, not knowing, not fair? For what judge, pray, do you summon for me, to decide either on doctrines or on matters pertaining to them, or to pronounce on the lives of men?

units.la: ap- dicès mihi appellas judice, sive de dogmatis aut rebus eò pertinentibus, sive de vita hominum institutas dicere? Nonne appellat ple-bem? cui nec vocationem impertivit Deus, ut de rebus istis cognoscat, nedum ipsa judicium faciat. An ignoramus inscientiam plebis aut populi, quem scriptis provocemus? an ignoramus studia & partes in quas post omnem hominum memoriam plebs quàm facillimè & levissimè per ejusmodi fl abella scissa est autu temerario? Quin illud ferme in more est populo, si judicium ad ipsum deferas de rebus gravissimis, ut statim ferat sententiam: sive ex opinione sui, quæ perpetua est ignorantiæ comes; sive ex studiis, quibus incòsulta plebs plurimum traducitur. Hi scilicet quorum non interest de multis cognoscere, qui necdonum habent, ut rectè judicent, nec vocatione, ut vel cognoscant, hi, inquam, competentes judices futuri sunt.
units.tr: Does he not summon the common people? To whom God has given no calling to know these things, let alone to pass judgment on them? Or do we not know the ignorance of the common people or the crowd, to whom we appeal in our writings? Or do we not know the factions and parties into which, since the memory of man, the common people have been most easily and lightly split by such firebrands, whether by rashness or by design? Indeed it is almost the custom with the people, if you refer to them judgment on the weightiest matters, that they at once pronounce sentence, either from their own opinion, which is the constant companion of ignorance, or from their party allegiances, by which the unadvised crowd is very much led astray. These, forsooth, whose interest it is not to know much, who have neither the ability to judge rightly nor a calling to inquire, these, I say, are to be the competent judges!

units.la: Quid verò, quod hoc ipso facto, dum plebem appellas & commoves, viris bonis prudentibus q; os plane obstruis? qui operâ dant ne adversò flumini, quo ferrur populus obniti videantur. Nam cur tibi hominí tribunitio & clamoribus fora & compita implenti, funemque longum trahenti imperitæ plebis, obloquantur boni intempestiva
units.tr: What is more, by this very act, while you summon and stir up the common people, do you not plainly stop the mouths of good and prudent men, who take care not to seem to resist the flood by which the people are carried along? For why do good men object to you, a man filling the forum and the crossroads with tribunician clamours and dragging the long rope of the untrained crowd, with untimely

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters] (marginal reference, bottom) stiva ob murmuratione? Tu in tuo foro tribi videris dicere: illi in justo cupiunt. Quid ergo? dixerit fortasse quis piam: tune populum judicem injustum dixeris? minime gentium. nam ne judicem quidem esse dico: alioqui cujus erit judex, nisi aut suiipsius, aut eorum quos habet judices? utrumque vero absurdum est. Quod si quis in populo judicium assumit sibi in plerisque rebus quae traduntur scripto hae licentia tem porum; is qua fide, quo jure faciat, viderit; quum omnes alios antevertit imprudentia sua; nec Deo ipsi, nec judicibus vocatis a Deo concedit locum. Nam in rebus dogmaticis, & quae cum fide conjunctae sunt, cur potius aliquem de stiva judicem audies, quam eum qui rebus sacris diligenter secundum Deum operam dederit? Cur potius tumultuarium plebis conventum, aut concursum, ac sibilum anhelantis audies, quam justum concilium exiis hominibus constitutum, quos Deus instruxerit donis & vocatione ad piam & sanctam rerum quae controvertuntur definitionem? quod si crimina sunt, convicia, contumeliae, aut vitae male gestae exprobrationes primum Deo injuriam facis qui ordinem humanum instituit, de rebus male gestis in vita humana cognituram: Deinde illis ad quos rei cognitio gnitio pertinet, injuriam facis, quam injuriam, ut illi dissimulent, non tamen dissimulabit Deus: praeterea populo injuriam facis, quem imprudentem incitas, ut convolet in jus publicum auctoritatem q; magistratus: Denique illi ipsi quem proscindis scripto, iniquus es. Si enim te offendit, habes mandatum Christi, ut arguas inter te & ipsum: si alium, quis te procuratorem instituit, & gestorem rei alienae? Sin autem non offendit te, cui offendis? Sin utrumque, cur ita agis ut palam testatum facias te non salutem, sed perniciem; non honorem, sed ignominiam, i.e. no ex charitate, sed ex perturbatione animi a charitate alienissima evetionem illius expetere. Interea vero ut de tertio capite adjiciam paucula, quis ferat dum populus ita appelletur silere bonos, qui justa scietia, imperturbato animo, donisque convenientibus instructi, aut judices a Deo sunt istarum rerum instituti, aut a te adhiberi possunt. Haec illa est Christiana ratio ad quam nos omnes oportet remis verbisque (quod ajunt) contendere, non aute ordinem divinum & humanum eadem operatione turbare. Aut ordinaria insistenda via, aut extra ordinem arbitraria deligeda: non pro imperio praescribenda a contendentibus: quod est iniquissimum. Atque hanc quidem [?]ἀξίως eo indigni-orem esse apud omnes constat, quo scripta revera longius a pietate, veritate & charita-te absunt. Sed tamen ne eos quidem ipsos qui tuentur veritatem, peccare velim fiducia cau-sa sua, & sic eam agere, ut in eadem peccata imprudentes ruant, quae in aliis reprehen-dunt. Multa enim interdum ad defensionem veritatis humanitus possunt nobis excide-re, quæ præstaret inhiberi. Sæpe fit ut res præter veritatem, præter necessitatem, præ-ter charitatem, præter officium ab iis effun-dantur, qui propugnant veritatem. Ignos-cat nobis gratiose Dominus, qui in multis offendimus omnes, Jacob.3.2. sed tamen certissimum illud est, fieri non raro, ut plus noceatur veritati, cum ista vitia in causa e-jus a nobis asperguntur, quam accedat ad-jumenti: non quod res ipsa interdum tan-ti sit momenti, sed quia tanti est quanti le-gentes esse voluerint: qui rem leviculam, si forte perturbato animo judicaverint, in gravissimam transformabunt. Quapro-pter omnes veritatis divinæ sacerdotes, at-que administros Christianæ pacis oro & obtestor per sanctissimum nomen Iesu Christi, cui servimus, ut quum ipsi de se & suis sermonibus, scriptisque cogitent quam diligentissime, ne forte cum veritate, aut charitacharitate, vel in speciem pugnent; tum vero ut in utriusque modo, sermonum inquâ & scriptorum, cancellos sibi circumdent quàm prudentissimè extra quos non patiantur se vel latum pedem abripi, quamvis clamantibus & provocatibus multis. Nam servos Dei armatos esse convenit invicta il-la patientia, de qua dicebat apud Salomonem Deus, Melior est longanimis robusto, & qui dominatur in animum suum eo qui capit civitatem, prov. 16.32.
units.tr: [illegible] ... murmurings? You seem, in your forum, to speak as a tribune; they desire what is just. What then? Someone may perhaps say: Would you call the people an unjust judge? By no means. For I do not even say they are a judge at all: otherwise, whose judge would they be, unless of themselves or of those whom they have as judges? Both are absurd. But if anyone takes to himself, from the people, a judgment in most of the matters that are handed down in writing, under this license of the times, let him see with what faith and by what right he does so, since his own thoughtlessness outstrips all others and grants place neither to God himself nor to judges called by God. For in dogmatic matters, and those joined with faith, why should you rather listen to some judge from the street, than to one who has diligently devoted his labour to sacred things according to God? Why should you rather listen to the tumultuous gathering of the crowd, or the crowd's shouting and hissing, than to a just council constituted of those men whom God has equipped with gifts and calling for a godly and holy definition of the matters in dispute? But if they are accusations, insults, reproaches or censures of a life badly lived: first, you do wrong to God, who established the human order, which will take cognizance of misdeeds in human life; second, you do wrong to those to whom the knowledge of the case pertains, a wrong which, though they may overlook it, God will not overlook; besides, you do wrong to the people, whom you incite, unwise as they are, to rush into public law and the authority of the magistrate; and finally you are unjust to the very man you tear apart in writing. For if he has offended you, you have Christ's command to reprove him between yourself and him; if another, who appointed you as agent and manager of someone else's business? But if he has not offended you, whom are you offending? If both, why do you act in such a way as openly to show that you seek not his salvation but his ruin, not his honour but his shame; that is, that you seek his overthrow not out of charity but out of a disturbed mind, most alien to charity. Meanwhile, to add a few words about the third head, who could bear it while the people are so summoned, and good men are silent, who, with a just knowledge and an undisturbed mind, endowed with fitting gifts, have either been appointed judges of these matters by God, or can be summoned by you? This is the Christian way, to which we all ought to strive with oars and words, as they say, and not to disturb the divine and human order by the same activity. Either we must keep to the ordinary path, or choose an arbitrary one outside the order; but the contending parties must not prescribe it by their own authority, which is most unjust. And it is certainly agreed by all that this manner is all the more unworthy, the further the writings are in fact from piety, truth and charity. Yet I would not wish even those who defend the truth to sin, relying on the justice of their cause and so acting that they fall unwittingly into the same faults they reprehend in others. For at times many things may, through human frailty, slip from us in defence of the truth, which it would be better to hold back. Often it happens that things are poured out by those who champion the truth beyond the truth, beyond necessity, beyond charity, beyond duty. May the Lord graciously forgive us, for in many things we all offend, Jas. 3.2. But this is most certain: it often happens that the truth is more harmed, when these faults are cast upon its cause by us, than it is helped; not because the matter itself is sometimes of such weight, but because it is of such weight as readers wish it to be; for they, if perhaps they have judged a trifling matter with a disturbed mind, will transform it into a most serious one. Therefore I beg and entreat all the priests of divine truth and the ministers of Christian peace, by the most holy name of Jesus Christ, whom we serve, that while they think as carefully as possible about themselves and their own speeches and writings, lest perhaps they fight against the truth or against charity, or even in appearance; so too, in the manner of both, of their speaking and of their writing, they should set about themselves, as prudently as possible, bounds beyond which they do not allow themselves to be dragged even a broad foot, though many cry out and provoke them. For it is fitting that the servants of God be armed with that unconquered patience, of which God said through Solomon: He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he that rules his own spirit than he that takes a city, Prov. 16.32.

units.la: Quid ergo? annon propugnabitur veritas a servis tuis? certè propugnari oportet ac non deseri veritatem: sed propugnari volo commodè: non autem imprudenter & sine fructu quasi lacinias veritatis discerpi importunitate hominum, qui veritati serviunt; propugnari eam à servis volo, quà loquendo, quà tacendo & manum Domini (qui Deus veritatis est) exspectando. Itaque quum veritas ipsa commodè velit dici: cuius commoditatis ratio ejusmodi est, ut ex natura ipsa ac fine veritatis & modo dicendi scribendique, & personis & circumstantiis temporis ac loci maximè observanda sit, ea omnia si observemus bene est: si non, in difficultates aut ipsi incidimus, aut alios injicimus.
units.tr: Well then, shall the truth not be defended by your servants? Certainly the truth ought to be defended and not abandoned. But I want it defended suitably, not imprudently and fruitlessly, as though the garments of truth were torn to pieces by the importunity of men who serve it. I want it defended by its servants, by speaking, by keeping silent, and by waiting for the hand of the Lord, who is the God of truth. Since truth itself wishes to be spoken suitably, the rule of that suitability is such that it must be most carefully observed in light of the very nature and purpose of truth, the manner of speaking and writing, and the persons and the circumstances of time and place. If we observe all of these well, all is well; if not, we either fall into difficulties ourselves or bring them upon others.

units.la: Ac primum quidem veritatem pro commodimoditate naturæ ipsius dici existimo, quùm dicitur id quod est: & id quod non est, ne-gatur fide & simplicitate summa; quam suis Dominus Deus veritatis semper imperavit: quemadmodum ostendit apostolus dicés, Deposito mendacio loquimini veritatem quisque proximo suo: Nam sumus alii aliorum membra. Enim vero labium veritatis stabilitur in æter-num: at donec momentum transigam lingua falsa, Prov. 12.19. Finem vero hujus veritatis charitate esse tota scriptura testis est. Nam ex charitate docuit nos veritate hæc Deus: quæ charitas effusa in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis, veri-tatem nos jubet eloqui, quoad ejus fieri in charitate potest & ex pedit, contra charita-tem eloqui veritate, impium est: præter cha-ritatem, otiosum: neutrum vero approbat Dominus.
units.tr: And first, I hold that truth is to be spoken in a manner suited to its very nature, when what is, is said, and what is not, is denied, with the utmost good faith and simplicity. The Lord God of truth has always enjoined this upon his people, as the apostle shows when he says: "Putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour, for we are members one of another." For "the lip of truth shall be established for ever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment." The end of this truth is charity, as the whole of Scripture witnesses. For God taught us these truths out of charity, and this charity, poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who is given to us, bids us speak the truth as far as it can and ought to be done in charity. To speak the truth against charity is impious; to speak it without charity is idle. The Lord approves of neither.

units.la: Hæc autem ipsa non raro contingit, ut in mente ejus qui dicturus aut perscripturus est, recte informentur, & tamen peccatum accidat in dicendi aut scribendi modo: præ-fertim quum perturbationibus animi aut sensus obscurantur quodammodo, aut verba objiciuntur dicenti & scribenti communi-ter: nisi accurate & cum delectu judicioque maximo dicturus circumspexerit, quæ res ad argumentum: quæ verba ad res, quia modo-dus [?] dus & ratio ad utrumque sit adhibendus, ut optata sequatur exitus aedificatio. Nam verba sapientum non solum recto & veritati opus est convenire, sed similia esse aculeis, similia clavis infixis, lectissima, ut ab eodem pastore tradita (ut Ecclesiastes docet cap. 12. verf. 11.) nimirum Domino.
