units.tr: It often happens, however, that what is rightly conceived in the mind of one who is about to speak or write is nonetheless spoiled in the manner of saying or writing. This is especially so when the perturbations of the mind somehow cloud the judgement or the feeling, or when words present themselves to the speaker and writer in general. Unless the one who is about to speak looks around carefully and with the greatest discernment and judgement, he must consider what matter suits the subject and which words suit the matter, since measure and method must be applied to both, so that the desired outcome, edification, follows. For the words of the wise must not only agree with what is right and true, but must be like goads and like nails firmly fixed, most carefully chosen, as given by one shepherd, namely the Lord, as Ecclesiastes teaches in chapter 12, verse 11.

units.la: Adhaec in personis observanda multa, citra quae plurimum offensionis dicentes scribentesque possunt incurrere. Nam & ad quos scribitur, & de quibus scribitur & in quos scribitur nonnunquam facto no‑stro ipsorum offenduntur: & (quod gravius est) offensiones illae quas saltem inter paucos latere oportuisset, eo deveniunt ut omnes fere offensioni sint. Quod si diligenter ad illud dictum Petri in his rebus attenderemus: Ante omnia charitatem alii in alios intensam habete: nam charitas operiet multitudinem peccatorum: item Augustini illud prudentissimum, Ubi natum est peccatum, ibi moriatur peccatum: neque diffundendis aliorum in fide erroribus, neque divulgandis peccatis ita operam daturi essemus, ut plurimum datur memoriā nostrā.
units.tr: Moreover, many things must be observed concerning persons, without which speakers and writers can incur much offence. For those to whom we write, those about whom we write, and those against whom we write are sometimes offended by our very conduct. And (what is more serious) offences which ought to have remained hidden, at least among a few, come to such a pass that almost everyone takes offence. If we attended diligently to Peter's saying on these matters, "Above all things have fervent charity among yourselves, for charity shall cover the multitude of sins," and likewise to Augustine's most prudent saying, "Where sin was born, there let sin die," we would not take such pains to spread abroad the errors of others in faith, nor to publicise sins, as we are wont to do so much of the time.

units.la: Atque huc maxime pertinet ratio illa circumstantiarum, quam ante diximus: ...
units.tr: And to this especially pertains that consideration of circumstances which we mentioned before:

units.la: in quibus principes circumstantiæ sunt temporis & loci, fi à modo quem ante actiones gimus (quæ summa est actionum circumstantia, etiam non raro dans speciem actionibus nostris) discessteris. Nam quorum intempestiva scripta? quorum gratia omnis eo ipso tempore quo edunt aut excidit, & quorum fructus aut damnosus aut nullus: quemadmodum enim necacerbo rum fructuum, nec verustate putrescenti um est voluptas neque utilitas, qui tempes tivè percepti futuri sunt grati & utiles: sic etiam intempestivarum scriptionum solet se habere ratio.
units.tr: in which the chief circumstances are time and place, if you depart from the manner which we laid down earlier (which is the principal circumstance of actions, and often gives a character to our deeds). For whose writings are not untimely? Whose purpose is lost at the very time they are published, and whose fruit is either harmful or nil? Just as neither the pleasure nor the usefulness of unripe fruit, nor of fruit rotting with age, is agreeable or useful, whereas fruit gathered at the proper season would have been both pleasant and useful, so it is commonly the case with untimely writings.

units.la: Nec minus judicii necesse est adhibere ad locorum discrimen explorandum: sit enim, ut qui sermo aut quæ scripta uno in loco prodest, eadem obsit in altero. Sermones & scripta pro ratione locorum ad quæ transmittuntur, ut venti regionibus, ita animis salubria sunt, aut insalubria. Ac propterea injuriam faciunt, qui aut suo judicio, aut suorum temporum loco rumve modulo omnia tempora & loca putant æstimanda. Una quidem est in se veritas, sed quæ se contemperat generis humani bono, sine sui ipsius detrimento.
units.tr: Judgement is no less necessary to discern the difference of places. For it may be that a sermon or writing which profits in one place does harm in another. Sermons and writings are wholesome or unwholesome to minds according to the places to which they are carried, just as winds are to regions. Therefore those do wrong who think that all times and places ought to be judged by their own opinion, or by the measure of their own time and place. Truth is indeed one in itself, but it accommodates itself to the good of mankind without any loss to itself.

units.la: Atque hæc omnia & alia consimilia quæ afferri possunt, profecto ejusmodi sunt, ut quisquis veritatis administer in charitate est, cogitaturus sit de eis diligentissime, quum aut sermonem dictarus, aut scriptum transmissurus est. Medicos o- mnes peritos & valetudinis humanæ stu- diosos videmus non solum de eo labora- re, ut veritatem materiarum simplicium, compositarumque & totius artis suæ tenent (quod theoricorum est) verum etiam quod practicorum est (ut vocant) ad constitutionem subjecti, id est, corporis humani tum communem, tum singularem attendere; eaque probè explorata res secundum artem justas, secundúmque veró corporis constitutionem mortificatas curationis causa admovere. Nos autem qui ad veritatis divinæ supernaturalisque dispensationem vocati sumus, & ad gregem Christi ovesque singulas illius, prout Dominus nobis fuerit admonensus, procurandas: an ita desipiemus, ut prudentiam rerum istarum medicis relinquamus & inconsideratè loquamur, scribamus, aut ambulemus in domo Domini? Fugiamus procul, ô fratres charissimi, insaniam istam, cum nobis ipsis tum aliis damnosissimam: & potius à scribenda litera unica totum vitæ hu-
units.tr: All these matters, and others of the same kind that might be brought forward, are truly such that whoever is a minister of truth in charity will consider them most diligently when he is about to dictate a sermon or send forth a writing. We see all skilled physicians, zealous for human health, attending not only to the knowledge of simple and compound remedies and the whole of their art (which belongs to theory), but also to what belongs to practice, as they call it: the constitution of the patient, that is, of the human body, both in general and in particular. Having explored this well, they apply remedies that are just according to the art, and tempered according to the constitution of the body, for the purpose of cure. But we, who have been called to the dispensation of divine and supernatural truth, and to look after the flock of Christ and each of his sheep as the Lord shall have admonished us, shall we be so foolish as to leave the prudence of such matters to physicians, and speak, write, or walk inconsiderately in the house of the Lord? Let us flee far away, most beloved brothers, from that madness, so harmful both to ourselves and to others, and rather refrain from writing a single letter

units.la: L jus curriculum abstineamus, quam ut animam ullam, vel minimam & infirmissimâ percellamus aut labefactemus officio inofficioso nostro.
units.tr: (for the whole course of human life), than strike or weaken any soul, however small and weak, by our ill-judged and unduly zealous office.

units.la: Si igitur, quid nonne veritas propugnanda est? dixerit quispiam. Est quidem ea propugnanda ubi oppugnatur: sed temperus est justum propugnationis, & tempus cessationis æquè in publico atque in privato labore nostro à Domino constitutum: quemadmodum in præliis tempus est petendi hostis depellendique, & tempus spe, & indi atque contemnendi, quum solido impetu gitdemens. Tyro consumit operam inaniter, veteranus prudens non nisi utiliter. Num certè fiqui naturam veritatis ex doctrina Dei didicerunt, eamque ex officio charitatis ad propinquorum ædificationem cupiunt exponere, vult Deus ad convenientem modum ad personas, & ad circumstantias ita ab illis & nobis respici, ut serviamus pacì & omnem morum contrarium paci sanctissima prudentia semper declinemus. Quapropter in privatis institutionibus, redargutionibus, hortamentis, reprehensionibus, consolationibus & siqua sunt præteréa hujusmodi, quid quomodo secundum rationem personarum & circumstantiarum fieri oporteat diligentissimè præscripsit Deus. Nam veritatem non solum expressit secundum naturam ipsius: verum etiam exprimendæ illius inter nos modum ex charitate circumscripsit, à piis singulis observandum, ut sale & gratia conditus sit sermo & scriptura nostra, Coloss. 4. personarum quoque respectum habere docuit oportere, ut peccantes moneantur; ac non traducantur: moneantur autem ordine charitatis, non inordinata illa imprudentia increpentur, quam cuique dictare solet offensi animi perturbatio: monean-tur toties, dum spes emendationis est: & moneantur locis, ex quibus cognoscant honori suo & saluti consuli: denique si repetitis monitis non acquieverint, sinantur aliquantisper, donec subsederit illa perturbatio animi quæ ipsos transversos rapit: aut si nunquam resipiscant, sinantur plane, ne discamus cum claudis claudicare, & contentiosi cum hominibus contentiosis & pertinacibus rixando efficiamur. Quid obstat, amabo vos, quo minus eundem ordinem in publicis nostris sermonibus & scriptis observemus? Nam hunc ordinem etiam in causis publicis nos docuit veritas: & eundem quoque præcipit omnino charitas: quumque natura charitatis ea sit, ut ad commodum respiciat eorum quibuscum cum agimus, certè & natura eorum postu-lat, ut agamus ex charitatis lege. Cogite-mus ergo,fratres dilectissimi, quotquot su-mus qui nomen Christo dedimus qua re-ligione, qua fide prudentiaque in his ac-tionibus publicis versari nos omnes oporte-at, qui in privatis tenemus magis earum modum: & deinceps demus examino o-peram, ut veritatem in charitate, & chari-tatem in pace ad salutem ædificationém-que communem procuremus, recordemur eorum quæ ante de capite illo nostro, typo fidei & conversationis nostræ & confessi-onis apostolo, Domino Jesu Christo di-cebamus: non litigabit, neque vociferabitur, &c. Matth. 12. 19. Respici amus ad Pauli monitum: qui hominem etiam hæreticum vult à nobis demum vitari post unam aut al-teram admonitionem, quum novimus eum eversum esse, & ita peccare, ut suopte judi-cio sit condemnatus, Tit. 3. vers. 10. 11. Me-minerimus denique amuleto certissimo nos instrui ab illo dicente, Quod si quis vo-let contentiosus esse, non est hic mos noster, neque ecclesiarum Dei. 1. Corinth. 11. 16.
units.tr: "If so, ought not truth to be defended?" someone will say. It is indeed to be defended where it is attacked. But the time for defending and the time for ceasing are equally appointed by the Lord, in public as in private labour, just as in battles there is a time for pursuing and driving off the enemy, and a time for holding back and not pressing the attack, when one is pressing forward with solid force. A raw recruit spends his effort in vain; a prudent veteran spends it only to good purpose. Surely, if those who have learned the nature of truth from the teaching of God, and who from the duty of charity desire to set it forth for the building up of their neighbours, God wills that they and we respect persons and circumstances in a fitting manner, so that we serve peace and always avoid, with holy prudence, every manner of conduct contrary to peace. Therefore, in private instruction, rebukes, exhortations, reproofs, consolations, and whatever else is of this kind, God has most carefully prescribed what ought to be done, and how, according to the nature of persons and circumstances. For he has not only set forth truth according to its nature, but has also prescribed from charity the manner in which it is to be expressed among us, to be observed by each of the pious, so that our speech and writing may be seasoned with salt and grace. He also taught that regard must be had for persons, so that sinners are admonished and not reviled. They are to be admonished in an order of charity, not rebuked with that disordered imprudence which the disturbance of an offended mind is wont to dictate. They are to be admonished as often as there is hope of amendment, and in places where they may recognise that their honour and salvation are being consulted. Finally, if they do not yield after repeated admonitions, they are to be left alone for a while, until that disturbance of mind which drags them askew has settled; or if they never come to their senses, they are to be left altogether, lest we learn to limp with the lame and become contentious by quarrelling with contentious and obstinate men. What prevents us, I beg you, from observing the same order in our public sermons and writings? For truth has taught us this order even in public causes, and charity commands the same absolutely. Since the nature of charity is such that it looks to the good of those with whom we deal, surely their nature too requires that we act by the law of charity. Let us consider, therefore, most beloved brothers, all of us who have given our name to Christ, with what religion, faith and prudence we ought to conduct ourselves in these public actions, we who hold to their measure even in private. Then let us take diligent care to secure truth in charity, and charity in peace, for salvation and common edification. Let us recall what we said before about that head of ours, the Apostle and type of our faith, conversation and confession, the Lord Jesus Christ: "He shall not strive, nor cry out," etc., Matth. 12. 19. Let us look to the admonition of Paul, who wills that even a heretic be avoided by us after one or two admonitions, since we know that such a man is perverted and sins in such a way that he is condemned by his own judgement, Tit. 3. vers. 10. 11. Let us remember, finally, that we are furnished with a most certain safeguard by his saying: "But if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God," 1. Corinth. 11. 16.

units.la: Neque verò propterea confingendus est nobis inanis metus. desertum hoc pacto iri veritatem: ac proinde nos divina, & alie-na & ha & nostra causa tenẽri scripta accumulare scriptis, & singulis vel ꝏblatrantibus cani- bus responsare. Nam hoc dudum profesto multorum éstμὴ ἐςίν, qui suis sive per- turbationibus, sive præposteris judiciis ex- istimentoportere ut alii dextera sua cadant. Longè aliter nos Christus, aliter prophetæ, aliter apostoli, aliter denique sancti & pru- dentes viri inde ab orbe condito docuerunt exemplo & sermone suo.
units.tr: Nor, however, should we invent for ourselves an empty fear that the truth will be abandoned in this way, and that we must therefore heap writing upon writing, both for the sake of divine truth and for our own cause, and answer every barking dog. For this has long been the habit of many, who think that by their disturbances or hasty judgments others ought to fall by their right hand. Christ has taught us quite otherwise, the prophets otherwise, the apostles otherwise, and finally holy and prudent men from the foundation of the world, by their example and their words.

units.la: Veritatem deseri Deus bone? magnum crimen, si quidem hic crimen est. Sed jam crimen esse definit, ex quo semel aut bis ve- ritatem scripto professus es, ac cultu publi- co semper doctrinæque communi in eccle- sia testatus palam. In hanc veritatem velut cippum firmissimum à Deo plantarum in- strumento manus tuæ, licet vel millies ad- versariis impingere, te testante & φιλοσοφικῶς quiescente Antecedente facto qui instituit veritatem & præsente monstrat, is nullo ju- re postea dicendus est eam destituisse, si ad singulorum clamores & vociferationes sese non obiecerit. Præposterum hoc judicium est, de quo sibi maximopere satanas gratu- latur, novit enim artifex dum ad clamores & contentiones aures advertimus, præter- mittit à nobis veram ædificationem quæ est in Christo. Adeo veteratorie hic antiquus draco imprudentiae nostrae novit illudere?
units.tr: God forbid that the truth should be abandoned! That would be a great crime, if indeed it is a crime. But it ceases to be a crime once you have professed the truth in writing once or twice, and borne open witness to it in public worship and in the common teaching of the Church. Against this truth, like a firm pillar planted by God, your hand, the instrument of planting, may strike at adversaries even a thousand times, while you bear witness and remain quiet philosophically [φιλοσοφικῶς]. Whoever has established the truth by an earlier act, and shows it present, is by no right to be said afterwards to have forsaken it, if he does not expose himself to the shouts and outcries of individuals. This is a preposterous judgment, and Satan greatly rejoices in it. For that craftsman knows that while we lend our ears to clamour and contention, he makes us let go of the true edification which is in Christ. So cunningly does this ancient dragon know how to exploit our lack of judgment!

units.la: Quòd si quis dixerit, licet non veritatis causa, quae rupes immota est, tamen aliorum causa quos vocat veritas, responderi nonnunquam oportere: equidem non negavero ejusmodi personas, causas, tempora, loca occurrere, quae respondendi necessitatem afferant: sed extra hanc necessitatem qui respondet, contentiosus est, aut ut efficiatur contentiosus, itidem metus est. Nam ut breviter de personis dicam, quorum causa judicas respondendum? aliena an tua? si aliena, utrum illius cui respondendum sittas? an vero eorum qui auditores & spectatores futuri sunt? Si illius causa cum ipso agendum est, non cum publico. Si aliorum causa, aut eorum qui nihil de re audiverint, aut qui de re aliquid perceperint. Qui nihil audiverunt, eos cur commoves? Qui audiverunt, certè eorum causa oportet instituì consilium istud, qui firmi in veritate sunt, aut qui infirmi sunt, aut qui in mendacium traducti sunt. Firmorum causa non putem: quid opus est? Infirmorum causa plus habet speciei: sed tamen postquam ex veritate semel, aut bis fuerit dissentientibus satisfactum; equidem magis metuero, ut infirmentur contentione in-firmi.
units.tr: But if someone says that, although not for the sake of the truth, which is an immovable rock, nevertheless for the sake of others whom he calls the truth, one must sometimes answer, I would not deny that such persons, causes, times and places occur as bring a necessity to answer. But whoever answers outside this necessity is contentious, or else fear makes him so. To speak briefly about persons: for whose sake do you judge that you must answer, your own or another's? If another's, whose? The one to whom you must answer, or those who are going to be hearers and spectators? If it is for the sake of that one, the matter must be dealt with with him, not with the public. If it is for the sake of others, either those who have heard nothing of the matter, or those who have perceived something of it. Those who have heard nothing: why do you stir them up? Those who have heard: surely this plan must be undertaken for the sake of those who are firm in the truth, or those who are weak, or those who have been led into falsehood. For the sake of the firm I think it unnecessary; what need is there? For the sake of the weak it has more of an appearance, but after satisfaction has once or twice been given to dissenters from the truth, I would rather fear that the weak will be weakened by contention than that they will be strengthened.

units.la: Ex: (ut) ..." firmi, quàm speravero fore, ut perscriptio- ne nova confirmentur. Et (quod gravius est) multiplex de eodem scriptio hoc habet incommodi, quod plerumque silvam of- fensionis infirmis atque imperitis, calu- mniae vero adversariis subministrat: quia (ut ait sapiens prov.8.14) multitudine ver- borum non cessat defectio. Quod si eorum causam adduxeris, qui jam malo errore im- plicentur, studium laudo, sed effectum non video. contra enim plurimum usuvenit, ut ea ipsa mala quae modò ostendimus, miseros confirment in malo, quemadmodum injecta aqua fabriles carbones solent inar- descere. Hoc quotidiana docet experientia: & insignibus duobus exemplis, nimirum suo & alterius cujusdam episcopi, Augustinus optimè demonstravit, qui ex Manichaeorum erroribus non ullo humano facto, sed singulari Dei testimonio, tanquam ex pestilentissima foetorum sentina erepti sunt, lib.3. confes. cap. ultimo. Omnino praestat in hoc genere mali antecedentia scripta & documenta commodè & quasi aliud agendo erratibus subjicere, ad testandam constantiam nostram in doctrina veritatis, quàm nova multa procudere.
units.tr: ...that the weak are confirmed by a fresh writing, as I had hoped they would be. And (what is more serious) a multiplicity of writings on the same subject has this disadvantage: it usually supplies a forest of offence to the weak and the unskilled, and a store of calumny to the adversaries, because (as the wise man says, Prov. 8.14) in the multitude of words there is no lack of transgression. If you bring forward the cause of those who are already entangled in a bad error, I praise the zeal, but I do not see the result. For on the contrary it very often happens that these very evils which we have just pointed out confirm the wretched in their evil, just as water poured on charcoal makes it glow all the more. Daily experience teaches this, and Augustine, by two notable examples, his own and that of a certain other bishop, showed it clearly: they were freed from the errors of the Manichaeans not by any human action but by a singular testimony of God, as if plucked from the most pestilential sink of filth (Conf. 3, last chapter). Altogether it is better, in this kind of evil, to set before the wandering the earlier writings and teachings, appropriately and as if doing something else, to attest our constancy in the doctrine of truth, than to forge many new ones.

units.la: Restat ut dicat is qui scripturus est, sua causa fit scri- benda.
units.tr: It remains to say that the one who is about to write ought to write for his own sake.

units.la: Multiplex de eodem scriptio quid incommodi habeat
units.tr: What disadvantage does multiple writing on the same subject have?

units.la: Anti-prid causa se scriptum publico daturum esse: nempe ut ea aut explicet quae ante scripserit, aut criminationes objectas diluat. Atqui jam eo peccatum est, si quis sua causa scriptiones ejusmodi immittat publico.
units.tr: Moreover, the reason why one gives a writing to the public is: namely either to explain what he has written before, or to dissolve accusations laid against him. But already it is a sin if anyone sends writings of this kind to the public for his own sake.

units.la: Quorsum enim in meis rebus cognoscendis homines occupem? Si veritatem quis scripsit & docuit, non sua, sed veritatis causa idem scripturus atque doctypus est. Hoc autem officium ab illo amplius non exigit veritas, ut ante ostendimus, quum uno aut altero scripto fecit satis. Quod si personarum causa veritatem mentis nostrae opus est explicari (nam aliud est veritatis in se testimonium edere, aliud ejus rei quam sententiam cum animis nostris) aut brevi additamento, non scriptorum centonibus praestari hoc potest (aut quod est certissimum) uni & alteri eorum qui rem in dubium vocant, testaram certis literis facere mentem nostram. Alioqui in causa fidei, quid est cur tantopere, si quid singulare credimus, aliis obtrudamus? quid, cur laboremus ut sententiam alii nos hoc aut illud credere & esse persuasissimos, modo nec ab expressa forma sanorum verborum (ut Paulus vocat 2. Tim. 1, 13.) abstinamus, merito omnia susque deque ferre posumus, quae ab aliis demente nostra cogitantur; & ipsi nobis (si ita placet) cavere sine motu publico.
units.tr: Why should I occupy people with the investigation of my own affairs? If someone has written and taught the truth, he will write and teach the same thing, not for his own sake but for the sake of the truth. Truth does not demand more of him than this, as we have shown before, since one or two writings have already done enough. But if the truth of our mind needs to be explained for the sake of persons (for it is one thing to bear witness to the truth itself, and another to set out our opinion on a matter with our own minds), this cannot be done by a patchwork of other men's writings, or by a short addition. Most certainly, it can be done by making our mind plain in clear letters to one or two of those who call the matter into doubt. Otherwise, in a question of faith, why should we press so hard to force on others whatever we believe that is peculiar to ourselves? Why should we labour to persuade others that we hold this or that opinion and are fully convinced of it, when we do not hold back from the set form of sound words (as Paul calls it, 2 Tim. 1:13)? Rightly, we can bear with equanimity everything that others think up against us, and can look to ourselves, if it pleases, without any public stir.

units.la: Jam vero convicia sint, injuriæ, crimina-tiones, quibus appetimur palàm, cur non potius ferimus, ut Corinthios monet apo-stolus; quàm ut ejulationibus & querimo-niis eorum aures oppleamus quorum non interest? 1. Cor. 6. 7. Aristotelem illum phi-losophum celeberrimum narrant historici, quum à quodam inimico absens graviter traductus esset, cuidam ad ipsum referenti & exstimulanti respondisse: Etiam licet ab-sentem verberet. Et nos Christianos usque adeo molles & fastidiosos esse, ut res eius-modi non possimus contemnere, & quasi pedibus terere? Deinde an nescimus quod olim prudenter monebat Tacitus: convi-cia, si irascare, agnita videri: spreta exolescere? Lib. 4. annal. Quod si id ab unoquoque natura exigit & dictat ratio, quo jure nos servi Christi, qui spiritu Christi vivimus, in corpore Christi, qui armis justitiæ dextrorsum & sinistrorsum per honorem & ignominiam Domino nostro debemus contendere, qui etiam beati dicimur hoc ipso fidei & patientiæ testimonio, desinemus à sequedo Christo, & salute nostra ipsorum, alienaque propugnanda ut de rebus studiisque nostris singularibus concertemus, atque invicem consumamus? cur potius non cogi-
units.tr: Now as for the insults, injuries and accusations by which we are openly assailed, why do we not rather bear them, as the apostle warns the Corinthians, than fill with our wailing and complaints the ears of those who have no concern in them? (1 Cor. 6:7). The historians tell of that most famous philosopher Aristotle, who, when he was gravely slandered by an enemy in his absence, answered a man who reported it to him and urged him to respond: Even though he is beating a man who is absent. And are we Christians so soft and fastidious that we cannot disregard things of this kind and trample them underfoot? Moreover, do we not know what Tacitus long ago wisely advised: If you are angry at insults, they seem to be admitted; if you despise them, they fade away. (Annals, bk. 4). If nature and reason dictate this to everyone, by what right, we who are servants of Christ, who live by the Spirit of Christ, who are in the body of Christ, who must fight with the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, through honour and dishonour, for our Lord, and who are even called blessed for this very testimony of faith and patience, shall we cease to follow Christ and to defend our own salvation and that of others, and instead contend over our own private affairs and interests, and consume one another? Why do we not rather think,

units.la: Tacitus.
units.tr: Tacitus.

units.la: cogitamus, si hic aut ille nos petunt convi-ciis, esse nobis contra locuplétissimum Dei, & animi nostri, & bonorum, apud quos vi-vimus, testimoniū, quo freti acquiescamus, & abstineamus ab ista inani solicitudine? quæ si nos torquet ipsi cum aliis perdimur: si non torquet, perduntur tela contradicen-tium. Taceo quod ante expositi iniquè facere eos qui convicia scriptis passim dis-seminant; ac proinde etiam iniquitatem eandem ab iis confirmari, qui coram iisdem testibus judicibusque constituunt respon-dendum esse, & quasi in foro incompeten-te (ut vocant) obeut vadimonium, si enim purgari me exempli causa ab alicujus ho-minis contumelia, no dico mea (prius ima dehiscat terra mihi) sed aliena & veritatis ipsius causa necesse est: equidem malim a-pud eos me legitime purgare, qui legitime possunt cognoscere, quàm miseram ple-bem eo nomine commovere quæ nec co-gnitionis instruendæ capax est, nec judicii faciendi sine cognitione legitima, nec sese denique ex miseris illis & horrendis fa-ctionibus, quæ hoc modo exoriri solent, potest commodè extricare. Prius igitur est, ut contemnamus convicia; postea-rius, si animum nostrum vincere ipsi non possumus, aut res postulaverit, ut convicia-tores tores legitima cognitione convincamus, docendo justitiā nostrā, non injuriā illorū persequendo. Væ nobis, qui primas eruditionis ambimus, fugimus silentii: in quo tamen etiam Christus, qui veritas est, bonam confessionem coram Pilato confessus est. Qui non respondet, conviciatorem confundit plane: qui autem convincit, hac existimationem sæpe conciliat sibi, ut ex impatientia & animi perturbatione adversarium persequi judicetur. id autem seu vere, seu falso judicetur, fructum ministerii impedit vehementissimè, totum non raro intercipit: Et satis magnas pœnas tum hoc ipso tempore apud bonos, tum futuro in posteritatem conviciatores reportaturi sunt, nobis tacentibus, & causam nostram committentibus Domino, cui servimus. De causis vero quibus ad respondendum sæpe adducimur, locus eadem opera explicatus est, quum de personis diximus. Nam aut ad Deum & veritatem illius, aut ad nos aut ad alios spectant. Quapropter judicium idem fieri de iis necesse est. Præsertim vero servos Dei per Christum oro, id semper cogitent, non persequendis injuriis, sed ferendis probari ministerium suum. Cujus probationes optimè demonstravit stravit Paulus dicens 2 Cor. 6. 3. &c. Nul-lam in re ulla prabentes offensionem, ne vitupe-retur ministerium: sed in omnibus nos approbantes ut Dei ministri, tolerantia multa in af-flictionibus, in necessitatibus, in angustiis, in verberibus, in carceribus, in exagitationibus &c. quae ille fidelissimus imitator Christi nos voluit atque mandavit imitari. Tempore & loco respondere quoque interdum oportere ante agno vimus: sed incredibile est quantum fallamur judiciis, quum de iis circum stantiis videndum est, det singulis prudentiam charitatemque Dominus. Et certe, quum rationem ecclesiae Dei, prout nunc se habet, cogito: corpus ita misere affectum est, ut in plerisque illius malis nihil magis periculosum judicem, quam immaturam medicinam. Et tamen hoc unum a plerisque videtur agi, ut quemadmodum apud Scythas olim & Babylonios per compita aegrotis consulebatur, tot sint ecclesiae medici, quot viatores ad salutandam ipsam quam primum accessuri ita plerunque evenit, ut quod dies curatura esset, vel potius Dei gratia successu temporis id hodie, Deo irato, ad solum aspectum velimus curatum esse, vel ad crepitum digitorum nostrorum: & quod quiete pos et cosanescere, id commotione intempestiva conturbemus: tanquam
units.tr: think, when this man or that attacks us with insults, that we have against him the most abundant testimony of God, of our own mind, and of the good people among whom we live, a testimony on which we may rest and so refrain from this empty anxiety? If it troubles us, we perish together with the others; if it does not trouble us, the darts of the gainsayers are wasted. I say nothing of the fact that those who scatter insults about in writings act unjustly, as I have said before, and that the same injustice is confirmed by those who maintain that one must answer before the same witnesses and judges who are present, and who, as it were, appear to answer in an incompetent court (as they call it). For if I must clear myself, by way of example, from some man's abuse, not of my own (may the earth open up and swallow me first), but of another's and for the sake of the truth itself, I would rather clear myself lawfully before those who can lawfully judge, than stir up the wretched common people on that account, who are capable neither of gaining the knowledge needed nor of forming a judgment without lawful inquiry, and who cannot conveniently extricate themselves from those miserable and dreadful factions which usually arise in this way. The order, therefore, is first that we despise insults; afterwards, if we ourselves cannot overcome our own feelings, or if the matter requires it, we should convict the reviler by lawful inquiry, teaching our righteousness rather than pursuing his injustice. Woe to us, who seek the first place in learning and flee silence, in which nevertheless Christ, who is the truth, made the good confession before Pilate. He who does not answer plainly confounds the reviler; but he who convicts him often gains for himself a reputation for impatience and agitation of mind, so that he is judged to pursue his opponent out of impatience and disturbance. Whether that judgment is true or false, it greatly hinders the fruit of the ministry and often wholly cuts it off. The revilers will incur, both now among good men and hereafter in posterity, penalties great enough, while we keep silent and commit our cause to the Lord whom we serve. As for the reasons which often lead us to answer, the place was explained at the same time when we spoke of persons. For they concern either God and his truth, or ourselves, or others. Therefore the same judgment must be made about them. Above all, I beg the servants of God, through Christ, always to bear in mind that their ministry is proved not by pursuing injuries but by bearing them. Paul showed this admirably when he said (2 Cor. 6:3 ff.): Giving no offence in anything, that the ministry be not blamed; but in all things approving ourselves as the ministers of God, in much patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, in stripes, in prisons, in tumults… which that most faithful imitator of Christ wished and commanded us to imitate. We have said before that it is sometimes fitting to answer at the right time and place; but it is incredible how greatly we are deceived in our judgments when we must consider those circumstances, and the Lord gives prudence and charity to each. And indeed, when I think of the state of the Church of God as it now stands, the body is so miserably afflicted that in most of its evils I judge nothing more dangerous than premature medicine. Yet this seems to be the one thing that most people are aiming at: just as once among the Scythians and the Babylonians the sick were consulted at the crossroads, so there should be as many physicians of the Church as there are travellers who are about to approach to greet her. And so it usually happens that what would be cured in time, or rather, by the grace of God, with the passage of time, we now wish, with God angry, to be cured at the mere sight of it, or at the snap of our fingers; and what could have recovered by rest, we disturb by untimely agitation, as though

units.la: quam pravis humoribus in corpore eccle- siæ irritatis, quos die & quiete commodâ spiritus Christi curaturus est solus. Atque hæc quidem mala quum in hunc locum af- fero, nemini speciatim male dictum volo. Nam Deus testis est me de singularis cujus- quam hominis, quem quidem noverim hoc tempore, notando facto minime co- gitare: sed licebit mihi per bonos (spero) deflere publica ecclesiæ mala, nostras omnium communes culpas, & meas quo- que ipsius: qui nos omnes & singulos tam multis intempestivis & importunis disci- plinis justissimo Dei judicio acerbissimoque agnosco flagellari. Quapropter deprecor iram flagellaque Dei communi causa ec- clesiæ, & mea per Christum Dominum nostrum Deum nostrum & patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi, ut singulorum mentes il- luminet in veritate, corda accendat charitate, & omnia simul regat ad finem pacis in unitate spiritus obtinendum. Deinde vero quia nos monet psalmes, thronos Dei inter homines ad hunc ipsum finem constitutos esse, ut singuli qui pacem ecclesiæ expetimus, ab illis thronis justa asequamur adjumenta pacis & prosperitatis: vos appello o servi Dei qui ex animo ad thronum spiritualem Christi in ecclesia procumbitis, & a & à Deo hauritis mysteria gratiæ & gloriæ, quam Deus timentibus se præparavit: vo-tem appello, ô servi Dei, qui ex officio ad thronum civilem in societate humana eve-ctis, ut regatis eos in pace, quos fidei ve-stræ commisit Deus. Expetite vos quoque pacem Hierosolymorum: curate ut amantes ecclesiæ fruantur prosperitate, ut pax sit præmunitioni & prosperitas palatiis ejus: facite ut qui non sunt adversus illam, pro illa habeantur, & indies illi adjungantur ad vitam æternam per salutis verbum. Nam si hoc cuique de populo, multo magis cuique de numero vestro præceptum est & impositum hoc munus à Domino. Experimini itaque singuli cum animis vestris pacem illam Dominilætificantem conscientias vestras: procurate ut vestræ illius pacis fructus etiam precedat foras ad eos in quorum societatem vos adduxit Deus.
units.tr: with evil humours stirred up in the body of the Church, which the Spirit of Christ alone will cure, in due time and in quiet. And although I bring up these evils at this point, I do not wish to speak ill of any one person in particular. For God is my witness that in censuring these faults I have no thought of any single individual whom I know at this time. Rather, I may, I hope, lament with good people the public evils of the Church, our common faults and my own as well, since I recognise that we all, each and every one, are scourged by God's most just and bitter judgment with so many untimely and troublesome disciplines. Therefore I beseech the wrath and scourges of God for the common cause of the Church, and for my own, through Christ our Lord, our God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that he may illuminate the minds of each in truth, kindle their hearts with love, and rule all things together toward obtaining the goal of peace in the unity of the Spirit. Then, since the Psalm reminds us that the thrones of God among men were set up for this very end, that we who seek the peace of the Church may obtain from those thrones the due aids of peace and prosperity: I appeal to you, O servants of God, who from the heart bow down before the spiritual throne of Christ in the Church, and from God draw the mysteries of grace and glory which he has prepared for those who fear him; I likewise appeal to you, O servants of God, who by your office are raised to the civil throne in human society, that you may govern in peace those whom God has committed to your faith. Seek peace for Jerusalem too. Take care that those who love the Church may enjoy prosperity, that there may be peace within her walls and prosperity in her palaces. See that those who are not against her are counted as on her side, and are joined to her daily unto eternal life through the word of salvation. For if this is enjoined on each person of the people, much more is this charge laid on each of you by the Lord. Therefore, each of you, test with your own souls that peace of the Lord which gladdens consciences; and take care that the fruit of that peace of yours also goes forth to those into whose fellowship God has brought you.

units.la: Conclusio paranetica.
units.tr: Paraenetic conclusion.

units.la: Studeamus, fratres dilectissimi, ut pacem Domini semper cogitemus, semper cogitamus, semper omnibus ostendamus, semper colamus, semperque defendamus strenuè, quum adversarium pacis videmus minimè ociantem, sed dies & noctes insidiantem aut appetentem corpus illud Christi, quod ad pacem in veritate & sanctimonia nia vocatus est. Invenit quidé ad versarius ille ad pacem ecclesiæ oppugnandā armorū plurimas (pro dolor) in ecclesia ipsa & membris singulis ipsius, ovibus & pastoribus. Mortificemus ergo veterē illum hominē, mortificemus membra carnis nostræ pacī illi cœlesti adversantia, & omnes aditus veteri illi serpenti, quàm diligentissimè fieri poterit, præcludamus: cavētes serio nobis ipsis & ad nos ipsos attendentes, & adovile Christi & ad oves singulas ipsius, ut pacem, quam suo sanguine peperit, frendente satana constantissimè teneamus. Vos autem oviri principes, qui orbem Christianum videtis tum gravissimis, incommodis pèr infirmitatem ipsius infestari, tum ab iis instrumentis sæpe torqueri & excarnificari miseras animas, quæ Deus sanctificaverat ut pacis instrumenta essent; rogo per sanctissimum nomen Domini nostri Jesu Christi, amplissimas miserationes illius, ad quarum communionem salutarem vocati estis, per suavissimum illud nomen Christianitatis, quo honoravit vos Dominus, & ab aliis cupitis honorari. perfruētum illum amplissimum, quem in hac vita spondet & exhibet atque in futura consummaturus est Deus; ut miseram Christianitatem, quæ plus satis theatrum dissidiorum & rixarum fuit.
units.tr: Let us strive, most beloved brothers, always to consider the peace of the Lord, always to think of it, always to show it to all, always to cherish it, and always to defend it vigorously, since we see that our adversary of peace is by no means idle, but day and night lays snares for or aims at that body of Christ which has been called to peace in truth and holiness. That adversary indeed finds, (to our grief) many weapons for assailing the peace of the Church, both in the Church itself and in each of its members, both sheep and shepherds. Let us therefore mortify that old man, let us mortify the members of our flesh that oppose that heavenly peace, and let us close, as carefully as can be done, all the entrances to that old serpent; being watchful and attentive to ourselves seriously, and to the fold of Christ and each of his sheep, so that we may hold most steadfastly the peace which he won with his own blood, while Satan gnashes his teeth. But you, the leading men of the Church, who see the Christian world troubled by very grave inconveniences through its own weakness, and by those instruments by which miserable souls, which God had sanctified to be instruments of peace, are often tormented and mangled; I ask you, by the most holy name of our Lord Jesus Christ, by his most ample mercies, to whose saving fellowship you are called, and by that sweetest name of Christianity with which the Lord has honoured you and which you desire to be honoured by others, and by the most ample enjoyment which God promises and bestows in this life and will bring to completion in the life to come: that you, by your counsel and help, may relieve wretched Christianity, which has been more than enough a theatre of dissensions and quarrels.

units.la: {Note: a catchword "fuit" appears at the foot right, and is not repeated in the text.} fuit, consilio & ope vestra allevietis humana ordine vestro ovibus Christi consula-tis pastores, quicunque tandem illi sint, ad honorem Dei prosequendum, & animarum salutem promovendam abjectis aliis cogitationibus, ex verbo Dei, urgeantis impediatis ne intempestivis imprudentibus-que remediis, vel potius vitiis adnaiscentibus vitia accendantur, & pax illa optatissima Christi in mentibus Christianorum omnium, in ecclesia ipsa (quemadmodum indignissimè adhuc fieri vidimus) tantopere infirmata & debilitata corruat. Vos huic sanctissimo Christianitatis aedificio sustinendo, tanquam tibicines; huic parti alendo & curando, tanquam nutricips; huic corpori tutando, tanquam parentes praefecit Deus. Quandoquidem ergo a Deo est corpus, & a Deo estis huic corpori praepositi, & utriusque Deo rationem redditur in ultimo illo die; ita rerum vestrarum & ecclesiae totius satagite, ut tanquam oves de instituto vitae, & tanquam pastores de instituto administrationis vestrae posthac Domino illi & Deo omnium respondere, freti praesidio gratiosissimo illius cui vos oportet servire, Domini nostri Jesu Christi.
units.tr: was; by your counsel and aid, in your own order, look after the pastors of Christ's sheep, whoever they may be, so that they pursue the honour of God and promote the salvation of souls, setting aside other concerns and acting from the Word of God. Hinder, lest by untimely and imprudent remedies, or rather by vices that arise from vices, further vices be kindled, and that most desired peace of Christ in the minds of all Christians, in the Church itself (as we have seen done most shamefully until now), be so greatly weakened and enfeebled that it falls. God has set you over this most holy edifice of Christianity to sustain it, as supporting pillars; to nourish and care for this part, as nurses; to protect this body, as parents. Since then the body is from God, and you have been placed over this body by God, and an account of both is rendered to God on that last day, so attend to your own affairs and to the whole Church in such a way that, as sheep in the pattern of your life, and as pastors in the pattern of your administration, you may hereafter answer to that Lord and God of all, relying on the most gracious protection of him whom you ought to serve, our Lord Jesus Christ.
